Katalog Berita (Halaman 42/58)

#3202. Can Robots Bring Stroke Surgery to Remote Hospitals?

Remedy Robotics is testing whether surgeons can operate from afar

At Remedy Robotics, the N1 System’s prototype console [lower left] awaits its operator, with cofounders Jake Sganga [left] and David Bell and the surgical robot in an adjoining room.

I am practicing brain surgery on a patient lying 6 meters away, out of my sight and reach. I press a foot pedal, activating the controller in my hand, and carefully steer a thin flexible tube called a catheter up through the patient’s blood vessels. I head for what I believe to be the brain, tracking my progress on the live X-ray feed. As I imagine finding a blood clot, David Bell, the surgeon seated to my right, helpfully reminds me that every minute a stroke goes untreated, millions of brain cells suffocate, swell, and die.

The patient under the X-ray in Bell’s office is not flesh and blood, but a plastic container holding long branches of silicone tubing. The controller I hold comes from an Xbox. But the surgical robot is real. The Remedy N1 is designed for emergency operations, including thrombectomies, the standard brain operation for acute ischemic strokes caused by blood clots. Ischemia, a restriction of blood flow, is the most common cause of stroke.

“We want it to feel a bit like a video game—a bit easy,” Bell says. “But we don’t want to dehumanize it as if there’s just another ‘game over.’ ” Bell, a clinician and former cardiac-surgery trainee from Australia, cofounded Remedy Robotics, based in San Francisco. With a team of engineers, he developed this robotic catheter and its related software to help ischemic stroke patients in remote and rural places, who lose crucial hours while being transferred away from hospitals incapable of providing care. According to 2025 data, at least 5 million people around the world suffer ischemic strokes every year. In the United States, stroke is the fourth leading cause of death.

When Remedy Robotics cofounders Jake Sganga [left] and David Bell initially met, they matched each other’s energy right away.Christie Hemm Klok

The screen shows my catheter at a fork in the narrowing road, and I decide to take a sharp right; I think I can make it. This device feels easier to drive than a typical robotic instrument that I controlled on a hospital tour the summer prior. I say to Bell that here my movements are smoother, more precise—exactly the talking point you’d expect to hear from a surgical robotics company. Never mind that, Bell corrects me: “Smoothness and precision are not clinical outcomes. Neither is a surgeon’s ergonomics.”

For Bell, the outcome that matters is whether the robot can get stroke treatment to patients who otherwise wouldn’t receive it in time. Today, only about 1 in 10 patients eligible for thrombectomy receive one. That’s where the long-unrealized promise of telesurgery is meeting an urgent problem: providing access to thrombectomies before life-threatening damage takes hold.

But can putting a robot in one hospital and a surgeon somewhere else actually close that gap? Remedy has already taken a first step, remotely testing its system on a small group of patients. “The remote stroke need is well known,” says Jake Sganga, who cofounded Remedy with Bell and leads the technology side. “It’s just a hard problem to take on.” Making telesurgery a practical part of stroke care will require more than a capable robot: It will depend on communications infrastructure, hospital resources and workflows, and ultimately, evidence that patients actually benefit.

As recently as the early ’90s, physicians who treated stroke struggled with “therapeutic nihilism.” A 1991 editorial by two lamenting neurologists expressed hope that a successful drug therapy for stroke would emerge that would “reverse the trend of nihilism.” Five years later, clot-busting drugs revolutionized stroke treatment, followed about a decade later by mechanical thrombectomy, in which a blood clot is physically removed from an artery.

In a standard thrombectomy a surgeon snakes a flexible wire through a small opening in the patient’s groin. This guide wire sets the route for a fine hollow tube around it, the catheter, to travel through the blood vessels to the brain, where instruments remove the clot. Suddenly a stroke was no longer a sentence of profound disability or death but a treatable event.

Yet decades later, thrombectomies remain inherently blind expeditions. The surgeon stands beside the patient, physically pushing these lines up, inch by inch. The only view comes from a live X-ray, which can’t see soft tissues like blood vessels. The surgeon shoots brief puffs of contrast dye through the catheter to illuminate the path ahead. A nimble operator can avoid scraping or piercing artery walls while bending the guide wire’s rounded tip around corners. But even these left or right turns are not intuitive. The guide wire can twist inside the body, and because the surgeon sees only a flat silhouette, steering it left may actually rotate the guidewire to the right.

The N1 robot feeds the catheter along a rail lined with seven modules, using a thin wire that allows precise control through a patient’s vascular system, even from kilometers away. Christie Hemm Klok

If all goes as planned, the doctor reaches the brain and pushes instruments through the catheter to dislodge the clot, then carefully pulls everything back out. Bell remembers how thrombectomies felt when he performed them. “I’m one and a half meters away from my catheter tip. I’m not in control of it. I can’t see where the blood vessels are. I thought, what is the ideal way to do these procedures? It’s certainly not what I’m doing now.”

Sganga and Bell want their robots to do two things: see what surgeons can’t see and be where surgeons can’t be. When I visited Remedy’s office in January, the team showed me their robotic arm and instruments that snap onto it. Motorized cartridges live on the robotic arm, one containing several actuators that use small gears to grip the threadlike instruments to move them in and out of a body. The instruments include a stent, an expandable wire-mesh tube used to pierce, grab, and yank a clot back out. It’s all typical stroke operation equipment—except for the catheter.

Remedy’s catheter is steerable, so it doesn’t need a guide wire to pave its path. Outside the body, a robotic arm advances the catheter while tiny wires tug its leading tip in any direction, as if an inquisitive worm is navigating the narrow branches of a bloodstream. As I maneuver the catheter with the Xbox controller, Bell and Sganga tell me they made wayfinding a priority. Sganga toggles on a CT scan to overlay on the X-ray feed. Suddenly I see the bright three-dimensional routes of blood vessels along a path that had been invisible on X-ray.

I noticed a pattern of small markings on the catheter. Sganga tells me they’re not for the surgeon, but for a computer-vision algorithm that tracks the catheter’s rotation inside the body. If an operator wants to steer right, Remedy’s software automatically translates that intention into the correct action. Instead of squinting at a 2D silhouette on an X-ray and mentally compensating for every twist in the catheter, the surgeon simply toggles to the right on the X-ray image, the Remedy system adjusts, and the catheter moves in the correct direction.

This system grew out of ideas that Bell and Sganga were pursuing when they met at Stanford in 2019. Already a physician, Bell was completing an MBA and enrolled in a robotics class in hopes of meeting an engineer who might share his interest in creating a medical robot. The professor connected him to Sganga, a bioengineering doctoral student who was developing pathfinding algorithms for an FDA-approved robotic bronchoscope to navigate the lungs.

Outside the body, a robotic arm advances the catheter while tiny wires tug its leading tip in any direction, as if an inquisitive worm is navigating the narrow branches of a bloodstream.

Sganga’s engineering work had exposed him to surgical robotics companies that failed because they hadn’t chosen a valuable enough problem to solve. He sought a medical problem where a robot could prove its worth well before human trials, and stroke stood out. “It’s an already verified clinical need,” Sganga says, “Time.” When he and Bell met for coffee, they matched each other’s energy right away: “It was like ‘Hey how you doing?’ and then we were looking at medical images of blood vessels together off of his phone,” Sganga says.

About a year after they both left Stanford, Bell and Sganga rented a two-car garage in Southern California and X-ray-proofed it with lead lining. “We called it the bunker because it had exposed lead on all sides, including the ceiling,” Sganga says. “It was just big enough to fit a bed and this rickety old C-arm [X-ray].” There they test-drove a prototype of their steerable catheter through silicone arteries—first controlling the robot on-site from another room, and then from a laptop hundreds of kilometers away. “We were trying to get an initial sign of life,” Sganga says. “And it was that moment that we realized that this could work.”

Dreams of remote surgery predate modern stroke care. In the 1980s and 1990s, the companies Computer Motion and Intuitive developed bedside robots to assist surgeons. Then, in 2001, French surgeon Jacques Marescaux and Canadian surgeon Michel Gagner removed a patient’s gallbladder from more than 6,000 km away. In New York City, Marescaux used a computer connected via high-speed fiber optics to control a Computer Motion robot in Strasbourg, France. The milestone, known as the Lindbergh Operation, was completed safely with no complications.

But telesurgery did not take off after Lindbergh. Instead, companies invested in robots operated by surgeons in the same room. Computer Motion and Intuitive merged in 2003, more companies sprang up, and robotic surgery steadily entered the mainstream. Today thousands of surgical robots operate in hospitals around the country, assisting in roughly 22 percent of surgeries. In 2023 alone, more than 2 million surgeries were performed with da Vinci, Intuitive’s flagship platform.

Remedy mechanical engineer Chris Hapstack [left] and software engineer Campbell Crowley adjust the N1 robot. Christie Hemm Klok

In the summer of 2025, telesurgery appeared to regain momentum when surgeons near Orlando, Fla., removed the prostate from a man 11,000 km away in Luanda, Angola. Around the same time, Intuitive demonstrated what it called “telecollaboration,” in which two surgeons on different continents operated together on a tissue model. Meanwhile, India-based SS Innovations has been testing cardiac telesurgery; in Panama, the Texas-based medical robotics company XCath has tested a steerable guide wire for thrombectomies. These companies are building on advances in computer vision and machine learning, yet remote robotics is hardly a sure bet.

“The first procedures are going to be those procedures where time is critical,” says Brad Nelson, who develops surgical robots at ETH Zurich and is not affiliated with Remedy. Last year, Nelson coauthored a report in Science Robotics arguing that telesurgery’s future success hinges on finding emergency operations where patients can’t always reach specialists in time, including stroke, heart attack, and fetal operations.

Surgeries that occur within blood vessels seem an attractive proving ground for teleoperation in emergencies. “If you have a hiccup, the nice thing about vascular procedures is nothing bad can happen other than the thing stops moving,” Nelson says. There’s neither a large open cavity to tend to, nor the urgent choreography one might need in organ transplants. If the surgeon loses connection to the robot while the catheter is inside a blood vessel, the operation can pause in place without damage.

Nelson’s lab is also working on a stroke solution. He has partnered with the Mayo Clinic in Arizona to build microscopic robots—the size of a coffee grain—steered with magnets to dissolve a clot.

After preliminary success in the garage, Sganga and Bell turned their focus to the environment where the Remedy N1 would live. Doctors and nurses advised them to improve the live audio-video feed, as any surgery is a coordinated team effort requiring constant communication. They were told to improve setup time, maintenance, cleaning, and began a series of conversations about secure communication and cybersecurity.

In 2021, CEO David Bell naps next to Remedy’s first X-ray machine in a lead-lined garage in Venice, Calif. Remedy Robotics

Absent a cyberattack, the elephant in the room for any telesurgery hopeful is latency. Experts speak about latency, or lag, in terms of how many thousandths of a second it takes for a small packet of data to reach a destination then ping back to its original source. In a major city with strong 5G or fiber-optic internet, latency might measure in the tens of milliseconds. In rural areas, even in the United States, lag can drag above 100.

Noticeable lag may not be a dealbreaker. When researchers in Japan analyzed five years of surgical simulations and demonstrations, they reported surgeons adapting to the connection speed. They paused. They moved more slowly. Remedy has noticed similar behavior in test runs. “We’ve actually found that operators are quite resilient to latency,” Sganga says.

Still, Remedy targets a round-trip latency of no more than 150 milliseconds, below the average human reaction time of 200 milliseconds. Whenever latency sneaks above that threshold, the system pauses all surgical action. Bell and Sganga say they’ve tailored their system to work with the slower internet speeds common in rural areas that would benefit from better access to stroke care, claiming they recently operated their system from across the Pacific using a mobile hotspot.

But sorting out the engineering details raises more questions about how telesurgery might change surgical practice. Bell told me he worries about what a telesurgical future could bring. What if surgeons’ skills erode? What if trainees become dependent on specific platforms? What if two patients need care from the same remote surgeon at the same time? “Is the person suffering a stroke in America necessarily more important than the person suffering a stroke in India? No,” Bell says. “So how do you figure that out? That’s something I think about a lot.”

During a stroke, a blockage in the brain triggers symptoms within seconds or minutes. The following hour is the so-called golden period for saving the brain before the risk of permanent damage grows. “Every minute wasted or delayed, 2 million brain cells are going to die,” says neurologist Archit Bhatt of Providence Medical Group in Portland, Oregon. “You really need to act fast.” Yet decades after the advent of thrombectomies, one in five Americans lives more than an hour from a hospital that offers the procedure.

Medium and small hospitals often lack the 24-hour surgical team, experience, or equipment for thrombectomies, so they must transfer stroke patients to large hospitals. As a result, standard stroke care is concentrated in urban areas. For example, Alaska’s only two thrombectomy centers serving the 739,000 people who live or work in the state are both in Anchorage, leaving more than half of residents out of range.

But the places most in need of telesurgery may also be the hardest places to deploy it. For starters, they may not have the high-quality network connections that remote surgery requires. Last June, experts from five major robotic corporations coauthored a list of technical standards for what they called “surgical-grade networks.” Mike Teodorescu, an information systems researcher with the University of Washington, says experts usually consider 100 milliseconds a safe threshold, but his team recently reported that many rural communities—and even most countries—struggle to meet it.

Neuroradiologist Hal Rice of the Australian Stroke Alliance remotely operates Remedy’s N1 System.Remedy Robotics

And connectivity is only part of the problem. The smallest and most remote hospitals may lack other support needed for thrombectomy, including neurologists, catheterization teams, CT scanners, and specialized intensive care units. “It’s an infrastructure problem,” Teodorescu says.

Medium-size regional hospitals may be a better target. Although they rarely offer thrombectomies, many already have the right support, experience, and patient volume. “There is a window for a thrombectomy center in a reasonably sized town where there is a stable economy,” says neurologist Bhatt.

“Every minute wasted or delayed, 2 million brain cells are going to die.”–neurologist Archit Bhatt

Telesurgery could do more than bring a distant specialist into the operating room. Jasdeep Bahra, an emergency medicine physician and lecturer in Kilifi, Kenya, worries that telerobotics could concentrate expertise in cities—widening the skill gap between rich cities and poor towns. The thrombectomy access problem is real, Bahra says, but lower income communities might benefit more if a system like Remedy’s could both treat patients and help train clinicians on-site. Sganga says Bahra’s idea fits Remedy’s mission.

“Digital operating rooms where you have surgeons that are over your shoulder as a mentor,” Bahra says. “If that’s what we’re talking about in telesurgery, that is the future for me.”

If smoothness and precision aren’t clinical outcomes, as Bell told me, what would count as success? One target is safety. In more than 1 percent of thrombectomy operations, surgeons unintentionally slice open a blood vessel, a feared and sometimes fatal occurrence that Bell believes robots can prevent.

In September 2025, Bell flew to Toronto for Remedy’s first test in human patients. Ten patients had consented to nonemergency procedures with Remedy’s robot. A neurosurgeon with a laptop would operate on six patients in an adjoining room; two elsewhere in the hospital; and two at an entirely different hospital across town. The Remedy team had experimented for years on silicone models, like the one I test-drove. Tests on lab animals suggested that, compared with a human, their robot collided less often with blood vessels and finished procedures faster.

Neurosurgeon Vitor Mendes Pereira pilots the N1 system in 2024 for its first in-person robotic procedure, in Toronto. Remedy Robotics

In the run-up to the Toronto procedures, the team measured internet latencies meticulously. Now they could only hope that their results would translate to human patients. “You’re never sure of how that leap is going to look, and it’s actually really hard to test,” Bell says. The night before the first operation, Bell barely slept.

The procedures—recording images called angiograms from within patients’ blood vessels—were a success, and were completed nearly twice as quickly as the current standard. “I cannot explain the relief,” Bell says. Remedy considers speed one measure of success because it can allow doctors to treat more people.

In 2025, neurosurgeon Vitor Mendes Pereira and his team at Unity Health Toronto perform the first fully remote robotic neurointerventional procedures. Remedy Robotics

A few months after my visit, Remedy announced US $62 million in new funding to support upcoming clinical trials. A portion of that investment came from the University of California system, which will host the clinical studies within a year, according to Bell. Remedy’s first trials will be on-site elective procedures, such as treating unruptured aneurysms, before expanding to remote surgeries in Australia or within the University of California system, near the end of 2027.

Sganga emphasizes that the on-site trials are not just a stepping stone. He’s come to believe that Remedy’s success depends on improving operations even when the surgeon is in the room. “The remote solution—it’s very flashy, it’s very obvious what that patient need is—but in order to get there, we believe you have to solve a meaningful problem on-premise,” he says. “Otherwise, doctors simply won’t use the system, and if they don’t use the system, they’re not going to gain the expertise required to operate remotely.”

The steerable catheter and computer-vision algorithm are two features he claims will improve thrombectomies, remote or not. And as trials ramp up, Sganga says they will look at factors beyond safety and surgical speed. “How quickly are doctors picking up on this new technique? How smoothly are the bedside interactions going? How quickly are folks able to set up the draping and interact with the tools?” he says. Bell has wondered whether to add a photo or video of the patient’s face to the surgeon’s display to preserve the emotional stakes of surgery.

These ambitions draw Bell and Sganga’s 25-person company into uncharted waters. Beyond one-time demonstrations, no robotics company has earned full regulatory approval for telesurgery, and no patient has been operated on remotely in the United States. Remedy hopes to change that. Decades after stroke research conquered the “therapeutic nihilism” that once defined the field, Remedy hopes telesurgery can bring thrombectomy to everyone who needs it, no matter where they might be.

Max G. Levy is an independent science journalist based in Los Angeles. His work has appeared in Wired, Quanta Magazine, and MIT Technology Review.

This is a tantalizing, multidisciplinary technology, but the latency issue seems really important. It seems like once they're through the medical hoops national telecoms regulators will have to figure out whether the necessary connections as emergency or critical infrastructure that deserve special spectrum allocation or similar, especially since this seems to have the most promise in more rural or remote settings.

#3201. Halide camera app just got even better for iPhone Duo

Halide 3.4 is out today as the latest update to the pro camera app. The update adds several new features, including a larger viewfinder for iPhone Duo and more.

The new Halide update also lets you use the outer screen on iPhone Duo as a live preview or a fill flash. It brings back a few camera tools from Halide Mark II as well.

Lux Optics first added iPhone Duo support in October with Halide 3.3. With the phone fully open, the initial iPhone Duo update let you review your most recent photo alongside the live viewfinder.

Today’s new XL mode gives you the option to swap the photo preview for a larger viewfinder. Controls on both sides enable two-handed shooting.

While the Duo is open, the outer screen can mirror Halide’s camera controls or show a full-screen viewfinder without controls. The second option lets the person you’re photographing see how you’ve framed the shot.

In low light, Halide can use the outer screen as a fill flash. That gives you a softer source of light for portraits, and Halide’s developers recommend turning the screen brightness all the way up before taking the photo.

Halide also now places the histogram along the Duo’s crease. The update revises the Photo Lab interface for editing with the Duo half open as well.

On other iPhones, Halide 3.4 restores the color and luminance histograms and the shutter timer from Mark II.

Halide Mark III launched back in May with a redesigned camera and the new Photo Lab editor. Recent updates added RAW-only capture in 3.1 and Aperture Priority for iPhone 18 Pro in 3.2. Halide Mark III version 3.4 is available now on the App Store.

#3200. The Apple executive behind the iPhone’s Camera app has left

He argued photos should show real moments, as rivals lean into AI image editing.

Jon McCormack, Apple’s head of camera and photo software, retired at the end of October after more than eight years, Bloomberg reported. Apple has not named a replacement, and his deputies are taking over his work under other executives.

Jon McCormack, the Apple executive in charge of the iPhone’s Camera and Photos software, has retired, Bloomberg reported on Thursday. He left at the end of October after more than eight years at the company, according to people familiar with the matter.

Apple has not named a new vice president for his role. His former deputies are taking on his work under other executives, Bloomberg said. An Apple spokesperson declined to comment.

McCormack oversaw the software behind how iPhone users take, view and edit photos and videos. His team worked on the redesigned selfie camera in the iPhone 17 and the new camera controls this year, when the iPhone 18 Pro got Apple’s first variable-aperture camera.

He was a strong opponent of using generative AI to create or alter photos, people inside Apple told Bloomberg. Google and Samsung have leaned into AI tools that can make big changes to images.

“A photograph is of something that actually happened,” McCormack told Wired earlier this year.

Unlike its rivals, Apple added a mode that lets the iPhone 18 Pro prove photos are real. Bloomberg’s sources said his retirement was not linked to any clash over Apple’s AI strategy.

McCormack reported to software chief Craig Federighi, whose team is under pressure to speed up AI work. He follows Apple Pay head Jennifer Bailey out the door this autumn, as new CEO John Ternus cuts management layers to move faster.

#3198. iOS 27 gave AirPods Pro a convenient new setting, here’s how to use it

iOS 27 gave AirPods Pro a variety of new features, but there’s another addition that’s easy to miss: a convenient new setting in Control Center for Adaptive Audio.

Several AirPods models offer excellent Active Noise Cancellation and Transparency modes—especially AirPods Pro 3 (now only $179).

But Adaptive Audio is another option you may or may not have tried. The feature aims to blend the strengths of both ANC and Transparency in a single mode.

And in iOS 27, Apple added a new setting to let you conveniently fine-tune Adaptive Audio to your preferences.

While wearing AirPods, open Control Center on your iPhone and tap the volume slider, then hit ‘Listening Mode’ in the bottom-left corner. Here you’ll see the standard listening mode options.

New in iOS 27 though, when ‘Adaptive’ is selected, you can now use a Liquid Glass slider to adjust whether the mode lets in more or less external noise.

Slide it to the left and Adaptive Audio will more closely resemble Transparency, while sliding it to the right makes it cancel out more noise.

You can also move the new slider incrementally to achieve exactly your ideal balance of Transparency and Noise Cancellation. It’s not limited to just a few preset options.

This Control Center slider is available on all AirPods models that support Adaptive Audio.

Do you ever use Adaptive Audio, and if so, have you adjusted it at all? Let us know in the comments.

#3197. Understand How Satellite Links Shape IoT Device Design and Testing

Cellular IoT has extended low-power connectivity to many remote places. Even so, about four-fifths of the earth’s surface remains outside the range of a base station. Non-terrestrial networks (NTN) address this gap by adding satellite access to the 5G standard. One modem can then connect through a satellite when no terrestrial cell is available.

This shift changes how devices are designed. Satellites are in motion. Signals therefore face long propagation delays and changing Doppler shift. Link budgets are tight and device antennas are small. A device can pass static conformance tests and still fail on a real satellite link.

This White Paper explains these challenges. It also outlines the test conditions and measurements needed to evaluate synchronization, signaling, receiver performance, and link reliability.

#3196. Williams-Sonoma (WSM) Q3 2026 Earnings Call Transcript

Margins expanded as e-commerce accelerated, despite rising diesel costs.

By Motley Fool Transcribing – Nov 19, 2026 at 4:23PM EST

Need a quote from a Motley Fool analyst? Email [email protected]

Williams-Sonoma (WSM -15.16%) reported a 5.8% increase in net revenue to $1.99 billion, supported by positive comparable growth across all brands and the acceleration of its e-commerce channel. Management reported that the non-GAAP operating margin expanded to 17.4% as the company prioritized full price selling and reduced promotional activity, particularly within the Pottery Barn brand. The company maintained a strong liquidity position with $992 million in cash and no debt while returning $253 million to shareholders through buybacks and dividends. Strategic focus remains on leveraging an integrated multi-brand platform and proprietary AI technology to drive operational efficiency and customer engagement despite macroeconomic challenges in the housing market and rising transportation costs.

Operator: Welcome to the Williams Sonoma Inc third quarter Fiscal 26 Earnings Conference Call. At this time, all participants are in a listen-only mode. A question and answer session will follow the conclusion of the prepared remarks. I would now like to turn the call over to Jeremy Brooks, chief accounting officer and head of investor relations. Please go ahead.

Digital experience personalization is also driving stronger results. Unlike generic AI design tools that may place furniture, without exact product specifications, our platform uses the actual products a customer selects with their real dimensions so they can see precisely how those pieces fit and work together in their own room.

By combining our assortment, with the customer's own space, we bring the entire design to life giving customers a clear view of how their choices work together, and greater confidence in their finished project. Across our corporate teams, AI is helping associates work more efficiently and amplify the impact of their expertise. Our in house AI tools enable creative teams to showcase our products in a wider range of inspiring settings, scaling our brand's distinctive design perspective. AI is also giving business teams faster access to insights and automating repetitive analysis and reporting freeing associates to focus on decisions and work that moves the business forward. This focus on marketing efficiency contributed to our strong e commerce revenue growth. On the bottom line, operating income was $347 million up 9% year over year.

With operating margin at 17.4%, up 40 basis points. Diluted earnings per share grew 12% to $2.19 this year from $1.96 last year. Turning now to the balance sheet. We ended the quarter with $992 million in cash, and no debt. Merchandise inventories were $1.6 billion up 7% year over year. Essentially in line with total revenue growth of nearly 6%. We continue to chase bestsellers across both core and newness, and we are working to mitigate the delays in overseas shipments. To be clear, our guidance is non GAAP. And excludes the IEEPA refunds and related interest recognized in Q2 and Q3. We do not anticipate any additional IEEPA refunds in Q4. Next, oil. Higher oil prices continue to pressure transportation and raw material costs. Our guidance embeds oil prices at today's levels. We are proud to say this marks our 17th consecutive year of increased dividend payouts. Regarding share repurchases, we have approximately $900 million remaining under our authorization and we will continue to repurchase shares opportunistically. And we will provide guidance for fiscal 27 in March. Per our usual cadence. Wrapping up, the 5 reasons we are confident we will continue to outperform our peers remain the same. And Q3 added another proof point to each. 1, our ability to gain share in the fragmented industry. Full price selling expanded merchandise margin, while we grew our top line. 3, the advantage of our digital first but not digital only channel strategy. E commerce accelerated to a 6.8% comp and retail comp 1.5% for a 10% 2-year stack.

Over $990 million in cash, no debt, inventory in line with sales, and approximately $900 million of share repurchase capacity in reserve When you put those 5 reasons together, it is clear how the power of 10 brands on 1 integrated platform produces compounding results. #3195. Apple’s head of camera and Photos software has retired, per report

According to a new report from Bloomberg, Apple’s head of camera and photo software retired last month. Jon McCormack spent eight years at Apple and “oversaw the Camera and Photos apps and the underlying technology that determines how users capture, view, and edit their pictures and video.”

9to5Mac is supported by Sony: Score Sony’s ULT Field 1 Bluetooth speaker for 51% off. Powerful bass, room-filling sound, up to 12 hours of battery life, IP67 durability, stereo pairing support, and much more.

Mark Gurman reports that Apple hasn’t named a new vice president to replace McCormack, who reported to software chief Craig Federighi. “Instead, his former deputies are assuming his responsibilities under other executives,” the report says.

In his role, McCormack oversaw “close coordination between software engineers and Apple’s camera hardware and chip teams.” He’s credited with last year’s redesigned selfie camera and other projects:

His work included the redesigned selfie camera introduced with the iPhone 17 lineup last year. This year, Apple added a variable-aperture camera to the iPhone 18 Pro lineup, giving users more control over lighting and depth of field. The company also introduced a customizable Camera app interface with professional controls.

Bloomberg describes McCormack as a “strong opponent of using generative AI to create or alter photographs,” a philosophy that created tension as Apple embraced AI tools in the Photos app. His retirement, however, “wasn’t related to a disagreement or clash with Apple over its AI strategy,” the report says.

McCormack spoke in depth about iOS 27 features like Clean Up, Extend, and Spatial Reframing in an interview with Tyler Stalman in June. He emphasized how the features “preserve the integrity of the moment.”

#3194. Microsoft says MAI Code 2 matches 98% of GPT-6.1 Sol at 40% of the price

MAI Code 2’s price comparisons use a launch discount that ends in May 2027. Microsoft will also let trusted customers license its model weights and customise them with their own data.

Mustafa Suleyman, CEO of Microsoft AI, speaks at Microsoft Ignite 2026 in San Francisco, 17 November 2026.

Microsoft has released MAI Code 2, an in-house coding model. It says the model delivers 98% of the performance of OpenAI’s GPT-6.1 Sol at 40% of the price.

The company presented it at its Ignite conference in San Francisco on Tuesday. New models for security and image editing launched alongside it.

Against Anthropic’s Claude Opus 5.5, Microsoft says MAI Code 2 gives 96% of the performance at 5% of the cost. The figures are averages across four coding benchmarks that Microsoft chose.

Both comparisons use a launch price. A footnote to Microsoft AI’s announcement says the cost is shown at a 50% promotional rate. That rate runs until 17 May 2027, GitHub’s pricing page shows. After that, input tokens rise from $0.50 to $1 per million. Output tokens rise from $2.50 to $5 per million.

MAI Code 2 and a smaller model, MAI Code 2 Flash, are available in GitHub Copilot. Microsoft says Flash matches OpenAI’s GPT-6 Luna at 65% of the price. It matches Anthropic’s Claude Haiku 5.5 at 20%.

Mustafa Suleyman, chief executive of Microsoft AI, led the launch on stage.

“Right now, token spend is going through the roof,” Suleyman said, describing what he hears from CIOs and CFOs.

Microsoft says both coding models are not yet tuned for harder problems. Those include fundamental science research and very long agentic work.

Microsoft is also building a general-purpose frontier model, Suleyman told Axios. He said the company has reached state-of-the-art pre-training results. It is also making strong progress in reinforcement learning. He gave no release date.

“My team is building true superintelligence,” Suleyman told Axios.

He gave no target for how much Copilot traffic will move to Microsoft’s own models. He predicted significant adoption.

MAI Cyber 2 Flash, a security model, beats OpenAI’s GPT-6 Astra, Suleyman said. It does so at less than 2% of the cost per task. A larger MAI Cyber 2 is in preview inside MDASH, Microsoft’s agentic code scanner.

MAI Image 2.7 is now the top image editing model, Suleyman said. It costs a fifth of what its rivals charge.

Microsoft is also launching MAI Licensed Weights. Trusted customers can take a Microsoft AI model and customise it with their own data. They then run it in their own Azure environment, with help from Microsoft’s Frontier Company team.

Suleyman told Axios the approach would “feel like open source” with more security and control.

“No one wants to pour their IQ into somebody else’s model,” Suleyman said on stage.

AT&T built a custom version of Code 2 Flash. It beats GPT-6.1 Sol at standard 5G network analysis and costs 50 times less, according to Suleyman.

Microsoft still sells OpenAI and Anthropic models. Satya Nadella announced OpenAI’s GPT-6.2 for Microsoft Foundry on the same stage. Earlier, Microsoft’s commercial chief pitched Copilot as cheaper than ChatGPT and Claude.

Microsoft cut back Claude Code licences for its own engineers in May over token costs. In September, Suleyman took on Anthropic over how it trains Claude.

#3191. Gemini app for Mac adds computer use to control desktop apps

Google is upgrading the Gemini app on Mac with computer use capabilities that can work across local desktop applications and the web.

The existing Task (previously Gemini Spark) functionality in the Mac app could just access local files in conjunction with Connected Apps, like @Gmail or @Google Calendar.

Computer use lets Gemini for Mac click and type on your behalf to accomplish multi-step tasks in local desktop apps and the web, like navigating menus and filling out forms.

Gemini works in an “isolated background window with a live preview right in your chat,” while your main screen and cursor remain free to use. On the safety front, you can stop Gemini at any time with one click, while you choose what apps Gemini uses. Google will pause for logins and payments, with confirmation needed for sensitive actions.

Many everyday tasks span desktop apps and websites that don’t connect to each other. Computer use handles the tedious steps in the background so you can save time without giving up your screen or cursor.

To use, add @Computer use to your prompt. In Customize > Connectors, you’ll see new “Desktop” apps like Blender and Autodesk Fusion join the existing Git and Obsidian integrations.

#3190. Everful raises $48.5M for AI agents that source products from factories

The two-year-old startup says it ships over 5 million items a month for retailers.

San Francisco startup Everful has raised a $48.5M Series A led by Vertex Ventures Southeast Asia & India and January Capital. Its AI agents find and vet factories and manage orders for retailers and brands, and it says it is on track for $100M in annualised revenue by year-end.

Everful, a San Francisco startup that uses AI agents to source products from factories, has raised a $48.5M Series A, the company announced on Thursday. Vertex Ventures Southeast Asia & India and January Capital led the round, with existing investors Square Peg and Lightspeed taking part.

Retailers and brands usually buy stock through layers of middlemen, long email threads and high minimum orders. Everful’s agents spot trending products, find and vet factories, and handle the messages for each order.

Everful scores each factory on quality using its own inspections, then ships the goods itself. Customers can buy wholesale, dropship or order custom products with low minimums. Quality checks are drawing AI investment too, with Smartex launching AI fabric checks for H&M on Thursday.

“AI lets us turn that team into software,” said co-founder and CEO Sisi Song, referring to the overseas sourcing teams big retailers hire.

Founded in 2024, Everful says it now ships more than 5 million items a month to customers in over 60 countries. It works with more than 30,000 factories and says it is on track for $100M in annualised revenue by year-end. Those figures come from the company and have not been independently confirmed.

Song is a former Alibaba executive and Bessemer Venture Partners investor. Co-founder Kevin Han previously sold his AI startup, Orbeus, to Amazon.

The money will fund growth in the US, its biggest market, and Europe. Investors are betting on AI agents across the supply chain: Freehand raised $75M in July to manage company spending, and Plato raised $14.5M to automate wholesale trade.

Cheap cross-border shopping is also under pressure. Shein, which lost its US tariff exemption, is pitching its IPO at under $30B, far below its 2022 valuation.

#3187. Microsoft puts Word, Excel and PowerPoint inside Copilot at Ignite

Satya Nadella opened the keynote that launched Office in Copilot with an apology for last week’s outage. Afterwards he told reporters he is AGI-pilled, doubts Claude is conscious and leaves Jensen Huang’s fate to Nvidia.

Microsoft Chairman and CEO Satya Nadella speaks at Microsoft Ignite 2026 in San Francisco, 17 November 2026.

Microsoft has built Word, Excel and PowerPoint into Copilot. Chief executive Satya Nadella called Copilot “the new operating system for work” at Ignite in San Francisco on Tuesday.

Office in Copilot is now generally available, according to Microsoft’s Ignite news page. So is Home, which brings Chat and Cowork together in one place.

Code turns plain language into working apps. Autopilot is an agent that keeps working in the background. Both are rolling out to customers in Microsoft’s Frontier programme.

“But time has come for a true multiplayer form factor,” Nadella said.

That product is Copilot Workspaces, shared spaces for teams, their agents and Copilot. Nadella also announced a Salesforce plugin for Copilot and new plugins for Dynamics 365.

Nadella opened the keynote with last week’s Microsoft 365 outage, which took down Outlook and Teams around the world.

“We know the trust you place in our services and take that responsibility extremely seriously. And in that context, I know we have work to do,” Nadella said.

Microsoft IQ is a new platform that gathers a company’s data from Fabric, Foundry and Microsoft 365. It adds more than 350 third-party connectors, so agents can work with the full business context.

Agent 365 already manages 50 million agents. It now gains Business Analytics, which shows what drives AI spend and ties it to outcomes.

“You can simply think of this as an ERP system of AI usage,” Nadella said.

Perception, Microsoft’s security system of red, blue and green team agents, is now generally available. The agents attack, detect and fix.

Microsoft also launched the AI Transparency Initiative with 40 organisations. It will build open standards for checking what AI models do, and expand Microsoft’s work in NIST’s Agent Standards Initiative.

“How can you even trust all this powerful technology? And the reality is, by definition, you can’t,” Nadella said.

Microsoft’s own new models, led by MAI Code 2, were the other big launch of the day. TNW covered them separately, along with Microsoft’s price pitch against Claude.

Nadella took questions at a press roundtable after the keynote. He said he is “AGI-pilled” about how AI could change the economy and politics, he told The Verge.

Asked whether models like Anthropic’s Claude are conscious, he said: “I don’t think so.” He called it a good debate and said he is not dogmatic about it.

“If the Marxist sort of view is that there’s only one firm, then it’s over, right? For all of us,” Nadella said.

Jensen Huang stepped down as Nvidia’s chief executive last week. Nadella called him a singular person but said his return is not his call, Fortune reported. Nvidia’s board has said it does not intend to bring Huang back.

“It’s up to the Nvidia board to decide what happens next,” Nadella said.

Nadella told reporters that AI code and AI deployments did not cause the outage. A bug surfaced under specific traffic conditions during routine testing, he said. Internal AI tools helped engineers fix it faster.

Some communities voted to restrict data centres in the US midterms. Nadella said support has to be earned one community at a time. The results have not changed Microsoft’s building plans, he added.

“I don’t think the public is getting it wrong,” Nadella said.

The Novilla Bliss Memory Foam is an all-foam mattress that’s particularly suited to side sleepers and lightweight back sleepers. I slept on a Full size 10" mattress for a month, along with my husband, and I found it especially comfortable for side sleeping. I was also really impressed with the support it provided, considering its low price. But support at the edges left a lot to be desired and it won't be supportive enough for heavier sleepers, and my hot-sleeping husband found it slept way too warm, too.

Far more supportive than its price would suggest

Not robust enough for stomach sleepers or those over 230lbs

Why you can trust Tom's Guide Our writers and editors spend hours analyzing and reviewing products, services, and apps to help find what's best for you. Find out more about how we test, analyze, and rate.

Insanely popular on Amazon, the Novilla Bliss Memory Foam Mattress is a cheap and cheerful all-foam offering that I freely admit I wasn’t expecting much from. However, there were lots of things about the Novilla Bliss that surprised me in a good way and overall, I was quite impressed by the support considering the mattress’ very reasonable pricing.

Name: Jo PlumridgeAge bracket: 45-55Weight bracket: 100-130lbsPredominant sleep position: Combination sleeper who spends slightly more time on her sideSleep issues: Suffers with back pain which can easily be exacerbated by an unsupportive mattress

It’s not going to rival the very best mattresses on the market but if you’re on a budget, this should definitely be on your radar. With a queen mattress currently priced at $269.99 in the Black Friday mattress deals, I think this is one of the best budget beds currently on the market.

In terms of firmness, I’d suggest that most sleepers will find it at the firmer end of the medium scale. There is sinkage and this is an all-foam mattress, but there’s still some support underneath. I can’t think of any other all-foam mattresses I’ve slept on that are as firm, except for the Nectar Classic Memory Foam. However, I must stress that I’m a lightweight sleeper and my husband, who is lightweight to average weight for a man, found it softer than I did.

Still, we both enjoyed it for side sleeping particularly and, as someone who is ultra fussy about lumbar support, I found it more comfortable for back sleeping than I expected. Motion isolation on the Novilla Bliss is exceptional, and I couldn’t feel my husband moving around at all, but edge support is lacking both when you lie or sit on the edge. I didn’t feel as if I’d actually fall off the bed, but there was some definite tilting.

Type: Memory FoamFirmness: Medium (lighter sleepers will find it medium firm)Height: 10"Trial period: 100 nightsWarranty: 10 yearsPrice: From $179.99 at Novilla

The mattress' one big failing, though, is temperature regulation. I sleep cold so this wasn't an issue, but my husband found it stuffy and, while he didn't wake up sweaty, he didn’t find it massively comfortable either. Hot sleepers on a budget might be happier on the Siena 10" Signature mattress, which kept our testers comfortably cool. But value for money is the Novilla Bliss' big selling point and considering its price, I was really impressed overall with the mattress.

Read on for my full assessment of the Novilla Bliss Memory Foam mattress so you can decide if it’s worth investing in.

A queen size Novilla Bliss is listed at $269.99 with a 20% discount from $337.99 on the brand’s own website, while Amazon currently has the price at $269.99. This sale price seems to be fairly set, so here are the MSRPs for each size, plus the usual sale price you can expect to pay:

Get instant access to breaking news, the hottest reviews, great deals and helpful tips.

Of course, November is one of the best times of the year for mattress sales and we’re seeing some Black Friday deals — a twin size Novilla 8" hybrid mattress is down to $90, for example, and on Amazon the queen size 10" Novilla Bliss has dropped below $210 a couple of times in 2026. So, it’s definitely worth keeping an eye on prices but do remember that, at $269.99 for a queen, the Novilla Bliss is already incredibly well priced.

Benefits differ very slightly depending on where you buy the mattress. On the brand’s own site, you’ll bet a 100-night trial, 10-year warranty and free shipping and returns. Amazon, on the other hand, offers a 90-night easy returns system, manufacturer’s warranty and free shipping and returns.

An extremely affordable all-foam mattress that offers far more support than you’d expect for its price tag, a queen size Novilla Bliss is currently priced at $269.99 on both the brand’s own website and on Amazon. Keep an eye on prices as Black Friday approaches.

I tested the 10" version, but as detailed above, you can buy the Novilla Bliss in a variety of heights. But for this review, I’m concentrating on the middle ground of the 10” version. Starting at the top, there’s a breathable cover with OEKO-TEX certified fabric. This is helpfully removeable and washable — mattress covers that can’t be removed for freshening up are a real bugbear of mine, although I’d obviously recommend that you use a mattress protector anyway.

Underneath this is a layer of cooling memory foam that’s CertiPUR-US certified and contains the brand’s NanoGEL cooling particles, which Novilla says are designed to ‘capture and redirect excess body heat away from the surface’.

Next up is a layer of adaptive cushioning foam that provides comfort and a transition layer to the high-density support foam layer underneath it. This layer provides most of the support and prevents the mattress from sagging.

Underneath this you’ll find the zip to remove the top cover, plus a non-slip fabric to stop the mattress from sliding about on your bed base. Somewhat annoyingly, the mattress doesn’t have handles to help move it about but as it’s all-foam, it’s not impossible to rotate it without them.

As a lightweight sleeper, I rated the Novilla Bliss as a medium-firm mattress but my husband (and additional testers of a heavier build that I asked to try out the mattress) felt it was a medium, albeit a firmer medium. Averaging out scores, I’d probably place the mattress at a 6 out of 10 on the firmness scale.

There’s definitely some ‘squidge’ when you first lie on the mattress, but this is backed up by a decent amount of support from the lower levels. This combination makes it particularly suited for side sleepers. My husband in particular found the mattress instantly comfortable in this sleeping position, but it did take a couple of days for the foams to soften up a little at the shoulders for me — after this, it was extremely comfortable.

Pressure relief around the pressure points was also really good and I didn’t wake up with any symptoms of a dead hip (something that I can be prone to if the mattress is too unyielding).

I wasn’t expecting great things from this mattress when it came to sleeping on my back, as I’ve historically found all-foam mattresses can lack the firmer lumbar support that I find essential. And, when I first lay down on the bed, I did notice a tiny amount of pulling through my lower back. However, this eased quickly and as a lightweight sleeper, I actually found the mattress supportive enough to keep my spine aligned.

My husband, who boarders the lightweight and average weight category also found it pretty supportive. It’s not going to rival the very best mattresses for back pain but, overall, I thought it did an excellent job on pressure relief for both side and back sleeping.

If you’re of a heavier weight though, I don’t think you’ll find the Novilla Bliss supportive enough and even average weight sleepers towards the higher end of that weight bracket may find it lacks support for back sleeping. I asked a couple of friends who are larger than my husband and I to try the mattress out and while they both thought they could just about get away with it for side sleeping, they felt that support was lacking for both back and stomach sleeping.

In fact, strict stomach sleepers of any weight probably won’t get on with the Novilla Bliss as it’s just lacking in enough support to keep the hips lifted, leading to the spine sinking out of alignment. If you’re a stomach sleeper, have a look at our recommended mattresses for stomach sleepers instead.

I’m in the UK so the mattress was shipped over the Atlantic and, despite its long journey, it arrived none the worse for its voyage. Order on the Novilla website and you’ll receive a tracking number within two business days, with delivery within three to seven business days. Novilla uses FedEx, UPS and GOFO Express for delivery. If you order through Amazon, you can expect delivery in around five days and there’s also the option to pay for the delivery drivers to unpack the mattress and take away packaging.

I recruited my long-suffering husband to help get the mattress upstairs although, being all-foam, it was considerably lighter than the hybrid and pocket sprung mattresses I’ve tested in the past.

Once released from its vacuum seal, the Novilla Bliss did take longer than a hybrid mattress to inflate and I left it for a good 10 hours before sleeping on it. It did definitely continue to expand minutely over the next few days, so I’d say it was around 48 hours before it was fully expanded. The brand suggests that it will take 24-72 hours to fully expand, so this was bang on the money. Some Amazon customers have reported issues with the mattress not expanding fully but in fairness, I didn’t have any issues on this front.

Like most foam mattresses, there was some off-gassing from the Novilla Bliss. It wasn’t the worst I’ve come across but it did last for a couple of days.

My husband and I slept on the mattress for four weeks to get a clear overview of how it performed in key areas. In addition, I carried out some objective tests in an approximation of our comprehensive sleep lab testing methodology.

Through both objective and subjective testing, I’ve assessed the mattress in three key areas. I’ve looked at motion isolation (will a partner moving about at night disturb you?), temperature regulation (does the mattress keep a hot sleeper comfortable through the night?) and edge support (how solid does the edge of the bed feel when you lie right on it or sit on the mattress?). These are the results.

If you share your bed with a restless partner or are a light sleeper, a mattress with good motion isolation is a must. Good motion isolation stops movement from one side of the bed travelling over and waking up another sleeper. I can report back that the Novilla Bliss is particularly strong in this department.

My husband does tend to flail about in bed when he’s rolling over, channeling a walrus trying to leave the ocean and I’m a pretty light sleeper, so even a little motion transfer can be enough to wake me up. I’m pleased to report that I wasn’t disturbed by him at all during our testing period, which was an unusual and pleasing thing.

This was backed up by my objective tests. Firstly, I performed a series of drop tests. I placed a wine glass on the left-hand side of the mattress and dropped a weight from 24" above the bed surface on the right-hand side. This is a similar sensation to a person getting into bed.

I dropped the weight five times consecutively 30" away from the wine glass. Each time, the wine glass gave a very slight wobble but otherwise stayed upright, which was impressive. Next up, I got my husband to perform some subjective tests, starting with low force movements and then increasing to moderate and high force movements. I rated the mattress 10 out of 10 at low force and nine out of 10 at both moderate and high force. Overall, the Novilla Bliss really excelled when it came to motion isolation.

When I talk about temperature regulation, I’m looking at how well the mattress manages heat build-up throughout the night and whether it leaves a sleeper feeling stuffy. I’m afraid this was one area where the Novilla Bliss didn’t perform brilliantly, despite claims of a breathable cover and gel-infused memory foam.

My husband sleeps hot and he found the mattress stuffy after only 15 minutes of lying on it. And while he didn’t wake up seriously overheating, he did feel slightly clammy and uncomfortable. It was not a particularly breathable mattress and, on some hotter nights during testing, he did actually decamp to our spare room.

I’m something of a reptile at the best of times but even I noticed some heat building up around my lower back while lying on it. However, thanks to my cold nature, I wasn’t ever uncomfortable on it.

We tested through the tail end of an unusually warm period in the UK and through to some slightly cooler nights, so it gave me a good overall view of the mattress. For context, temperatures in the room ranged from around 75F down to 60F. However, I should point out that I wouldn’t expect an all-foam mattress to perform as well as a hybrid for temperature regulation and, if you are a hot sleeper, you’d be better off investing in one of our best cooling mattress picks.

A mattress with good edge support allows sleepers to use the whole width of the bed, as well as providing a stable surface to sit on while getting in and out of bed. My husband and I foster cats for a local charity and, as any cat servant will tell you, these little furry creatures have the ability to take up 90% of the bed overnight, leaving human subjects very much clinging to the edges.

Unfortunately, the Novilla Bliss wasn’t the strongest candidate when it came to edge support. There was some definite tilting when we lay on the edges, although I didn’t feel as if I’d actually fall off. It was a similar story when sitting on the edge of the bed — there was some definite tilting, but I didn’t feel as if I’d actually slip off.

To back up my experiences, I placed a 53lb weight midway across and 3" in from the foot and sides of the mattress. The weight sunk in by 5" immediately and dropped further to 6.5" after five minutes. And I had to get my husband to hold the weight the whole time (he only took his hands off very briefly for a photograph).

I repeated this test midway down and 3" in from the side of the mattress and got exactly the same results, with the weight needing to be held the whole time. Just for context, the same weight placed in the center of the mattress compressed by 5" immediately but then didn’t drop any further.

The Novilla Bliss receives overwhelmingly positive reviews from sleepers on both Amazon and the brand’s website. There’s lots of praise for the “exceptional” price and many sleepers praise it for its good quality. Sleepers also praise the mattress for pressure relief, with one customer describing it as the “perfect balance of softness and support…I woke up feeling much more rested without the usual aches and stiffness.” Overall, this is a recurrent theme, along with frequent praise for the motion isolation.

There are nearly 45,000 reviews for the mattress on Amazon so, as you might expect, you will find some complaints in there. The most common one seems to be poor expansion of the mattress, so it would seem that this might be something you’ll need to look out for. And, while many people praise the mattress for soothing aches and pains, stomach sleepers and those of a heavier build complain that the mattress is nowhere near supportive enough for their sleeping style or body weight.

✅ You’re a side sleeper of light or average weight: The Novilla Bliss excelled in pressure relief and comfort for side sleepers, easing tension and providing enough support for a really comfortable night’s sleep.

✅ You share your bed with a restless partner: There really wasn’t any motion transfer to speak of with the Novilla Bliss and I never felt disturbed by my husband moving about.✅ You’re on a budget: At $269.99 for a queen size, the Novilla Bliss is exceptionally good value for money and holds its own against some more expensive options.

❌You sleep on your stomach or are of a heavier build: The all-foam construction of the Novilla Bliss simply isn’t supportive enough for stomach sleepers or those who weigh over 230lbs. Try the Siena Signature mattress instead if you’re on a budget and fall into these categories.❌You’re a hot sleeper: The Novilla Bliss left my hot-sleeping husband feeling pretty stuffy and uncomfortable and its all-foam construction does trap heat a little too easily. The SweetNight CoolNest Memory Foam mattress offers excellent temperature regulation and is another budget option. ❌You need excellent edge support: The Novilla Bliss suffered with some sinkage at its edges and didn’t feel like the most secure surface to lie on the edge of or sit on. If you need an affordable mattress with decent edge support, check out the EGOHOME Black 12” Memory Foam mattress instead.

There are plenty of positives about the Novilla Bliss, but the price is the overwhelming winner. At under $300 for a queen, it’s a bit of a bargain and I was impressed by how well it performed considering that price tag. It certainly beats out quite a few more expensive mattresses when it comes to side sleeping in particular. The soft foams at the top and some decent support underneath mean that this is a great option for side sleepers, except for those of a heavier weight.

It also boasts some of the best motion isolation I’ve come across, and it will be a winner for co-sleepers thanks to this. But, as mentioned, I don’t think it’s a great fit for hot sleepers and I would like to see better edge support.

But overall, I was hugely impressed with this mattress, and I think that most lightweight and average side and back sleepers will be comfortable on this mattress.

This plush pillow is available in two sizes and two different firmness options. In our SquishPillow review, our tester found it best suited to side sleepers, which will match well with the Novilla Bliss. It's also only $29.99, so a bit of a bargain.

Rated the best bed sheets for hot sleepers by our bedding testers, these sheets are silky-soft and cool-to-touch — so they could help to make the Novilla Bliss a bit cooler to sleep on. And there are over a dozen colors/patterns to choose from.

Another way to help make a mattress cooler is to add a cooling mattress topper. The Lucid Gel Memory Foam mattress topper did a great job of keeping our tester cool and it's reasonably priced for such a nice thick topper. A thinner and cheaper 2" version could also save you some money.

When natural light isn't available, the best sunrise alarm clocks are the next best thing. You won't get a better gadget than the Hatch Restore 3 for this and, although it's not the cheapest purchase, it could really help to keep you happy through the winter months.

The best cheap option in our best weighted blankets round up, the YNM Original Cotton Weighted Blanket has a big choice of weights and lots of different colours to choose from - many of which are often dramatically reduced on Amazon.

Jo Plumridge is an experienced mattress reviewer with several years' experience covering all things mattresses and sleep, and who tests memory foam, hybrid and organic mattresses. What Jo doesn't know about a boxed mattress isn't worth knowing, so naturally we tasked her with producing a series of features for Tom's Guide looking at all aspects of mattresses, from how to pick between latex and memory foam (it's a tricky one), to the seven mistakes people make when buying a mattress for the first time. When testing the DreamCloud Luxury Hybrid for Tom's Guide, Jo said: "I loved the back support and pressure relief it offered. Plus, it looks far more expensive than it is." When she isn’t writing about sleep, Jo also writes extensively on interior design, home products and photography.

#3184. Google Quantum AI tests quantum contextuality on up to 105 qubits

Its qubits won a coordination game 98.3% of the time, beating the 88.9% classical limit.

A smartphone displaying the Google search start screen.

Google Quantum AI says it has shown contextuality, a quantum property thought to power some algorithms, on up to 105 qubits, in a paper on the cover of Science. The tests also expose subtle hardware errors, but the paper does not claim an unconditional advantage over classical computers.

Google Quantum AI says a quantum property thought to power some algorithms still holds on up to 105 qubits. The research, published on Thursday on the cover of Science, tested the property on Google’s superconducting quantum processors.

The property is called contextuality. It means a measurement’s result is not fixed in advance, but depends on which other measurements are made alongside it. Until now, it had mostly been shown in systems of just a few particles.

In one test, Google’s qubits won a two-player game, the Mermin-Peres magic square, 98.3% of the time. The best possible classical strategy wins only 88.9% of the time. A larger task using 105 qubits also beat classical strategies with limited resources.

Google says the tests double as a sensitive way to catch subtle hardware errors that other benchmarks miss. It says this could help pave the way for uses in chemistry and materials science, though the experiments did not simulate either.

The paper is careful about its limits. It says there is no unconditional proof that quantum computers beat classical ones in general, and its quantum edge in one game shrank as more qubits joined. The work first appeared as a preprint in December 2025.

Error-free hardware remains the industry’s big goal. Google has said it wants a useful, error-corrected quantum computer by 2029, and Microsoft, which unveiled its Majorana 2 chip in June, has set the same target.

IBM agreed to buy HRL as it showed a chip that corrects its own errors, and Nvidia has simulated a 104-qubit error-corrected machine. Investors are piling in too, with Quantinuum raising $1.68B in its IPO in June.

#3183. "The Big Short's" Michael Burry Issued a Blunt Warning about Anthropic

Burry has made some pretty impressive short bets over the past two decades.

By Bram Berkowitz – Nov 19, 2026 at 4:28PM EST

10 stocks we like better than Anthropic ›

Dr. Michael Burry made a name for himself during the Great Recession in 2008, when, prior to the collapse of the housing bubble, he bet against mortgage-backed securities that would eventually fail, earning hundreds of millions of dollars in profits for him and the investors in his hedge fund.

Due to Burry's track record, the market still pays close attention to his investment calls. In recent weeks, he has issued a blunt warning about Anthropic (ANT +17.07%), which just went public Thursday.

Michael Burry. Image source: Getty Images.

Since the emergence of artificial intelligence and large language models (LLMs), Burry has largely been bearish on the AI revolution. At this point, he believes a bubble has formed in the industry, and that the market has gotten far too exuberant about the values of the companies involved in it.

As part of its IPO process, Anthropic had to disclose many details about the company's inner workings, including its financials. In the second quarter, it generated spectacular revenue growth of 144% sequentially to nearly $11.6 billion. The company even managed to generate an operating profit.

However, in the third quarter, revenue was nearly $17 billion. That nearly 47% sequential growth disappointed some onlookers because it slowed quarter over quarter, although it was still incredibly strong. Anthropic is a frontier AI lab, and its models have found strong resonance with enterprises. But there are now more open-weight models that are reportedly much cheaper to use.

"Not only is the company priced for optimism... it is betting its entire existence on that optimism," Burry wrote in a Substack post, according to Business Insider.

But Burry's even bigger concern has to do with the magnitude of the spending Anthropic has committed to on compute to power and train its models. Vast quantities of compute will really be required in perpetuity to support its business model. Anthropic said in its registration statement that it had already committed to spend roughly $895 billion on compute, a significant portion of which is projected to be spent by the end of 2030. This also doesn't include an additional $125 billion to $150 billion of compute the company plans to purchase between 2028 and 2031.

Burry noted that these commitments are equivalent to roughly 12 times the more bullish revenue estimates for Anthropic of about $100 billion over the next year. He also noted that while the market is not blind to what's going on, he doesn't believe investors are concerned enough, and he has no plans to invest in the stock.

"Under take-or-pay, Anthropic could end up effectively paying more for compute at a time when it is not needed, which would increase its costs and reduce competitiveness with other language model providers," he added.

Burry’s warning hits the question sitting at the crux of the debate over the AI trade: Is spending hundreds of billions of dollars annually — and soon-to-be trillions — going to yield adequate returns on investment?

Certainly, no one can scoff at Anthropic's product or its revenue growth, but its third-quarter results highlighted that its growth may not be linear, and it may slow from here.

Anthropic priced its IPO at $1.5 trillion. Annualizing Anthropic's third-quarter revenue of nearly $17 billion would give it an implied annual recurring revenue (ARR) run rate of $68 billion and a price-to-ARR multiple of about 220.

Bullish investors, of course, can be tempted to assume that revenue will keep growing like a weed, but we still don't fully know how competition from open-weight models will impact its business, nor how future innovations in the rapidly-evolving AI segment could potentially erode Anthropic's moat.

Burry's warning is that the company will have to spend hundreds of billions of dollars on data center compute, even as its growth trajectory remains uncertain. Furthermore, the cost it is paying for compute now may look high in several years.

That's why I think investors should remain on the sidelines in the coming months and gather more intel on Anthropic's business before deciding whether to buy the stock.

#3182. Apple fires back at Epic over claims it withheld 122,000 documents

Apple has responded to Epic Games’ filing from last Friday, pushing back against accusations that it improperly withheld more than 122,000 documents related to its proposed App Store commissions. Here are the details.

While the Supreme Court is set to review whether the civil contempt designation against Apple should be upheld in its lawsuit against Epic Games, the two companies have also been battling in the district court over what commission, if any, Apple should be allowed to charge on purchases made through external payment systems.

Apple submitted its proposal to the district court on August 13, calling for commissions ranging from 5% to 15%, but Epic is disputing not just the basis for those proposed rates, but also Apple’s handling of document production in the proceedings.

As part of the proceedings, Epic had submitted 16 categories of documents it wanted Apple to produce (including “internal analyses of the financial or business impact” of its proposed commissions and “communications relating to any strategies to dissuade developers from offering link-outs”), along with a list of current and former Apple employees whose records should be searched.

Apple agreed to use Epic’s proposed search terms and include all employees, and began producing documents it determined were responsive to Epic’s requests.

Epic, however, said last Friday that Apple was improperly withholding more than 122,000 documents matching those search terms from the records of the seven initial employees, and asked the court to order Apple to produce all matching non-privileged documents, regardless of its relevance assessments.

Which brings us to Apple’s newest filing.

In its filing, Apple argues that contrary to Epic’s claim that its proposed search terms were “tailored” to the proceedings over link-out fees, they were actually “overbroad,” capturing large numbers of unrelated documents.

For instance, Apple notes that while intended to identify documents related to its proposed commission rates, Epic’s “commission*” search term also “captures documents that refer to government and private commissions, as well as documents hitting on the totally irrelevant term ‘commissioner,’ such as documents discussing the NFL Commissioner.”

“[…] the use of a wildcard in a search string is designated by the asterisk symbol, which means that the search string will hit on any term that includes the prefix before the asterisk.

In the same vein, Apple notes that “Epic’s use of ‘fee*’ in its search strings related to litigation and Apple’s link-out-related projects pulled in documents containing words like ‘feel,’ ‘feed,’ ‘feedback,’ ‘feet,’ and ‘feeble’ without the word ‘fee’ or ‘fees’ appearing at all.”

Apple’s overall argument is that these unrelated matches account for the vast majority of documents identified by Epic’s searches, and it cites legal precedent to argue that it should only be required to produce documents responsive to Epic’s requests, rather than every document matching the agreed-upon search terms:

In fact, at least 95% of the Initial Custodian Document Population hit on generic terms like these and did not include any reference to the term “link-out” or its variations, despite that concept being central to the Proffer and related discovery. These sweeping terms do not just increase the total volume of the Initial Custodian Document Population, they also captured highly sensitive and irrelevant documents, such as Apple employees’ personal tax or financial records, medical records, documents discussing unannounced products, documents containing passwords, investor-relations materials, and privileged or protected legal communications.

The law is clear: parties are only required to produce responsive documents, not every document returned by a search string. […] (“The Court will not compel defendants to produce any document simply because it contains a search term whether or not it is responsive to the discovery request.”). Epic has not shown, and cannot show, why the regular discovery process should be disrupted here. Speculation based on hit counts, particularly where the producing party can explain low responsiveness rates, does not justify the extraordinary and unprecedented remedy Epic seeks.

Apple goes on to argue that complying with Epic’s demands would require extensive additional work, including reviewing documents for privileged or sensitive information and redacting protected material, making it impossible to meet Epic’s proposed December 2 deadline.

Finally, Apple asks the court to reject Epic’s motion but proposes that, should the court decide that some intervention is warranted, a randomized, statistically significant sample of the documents it deems nonresponsive be submitted to a Special Master for independent review, rather than producing all of them to Epic directly.
