#3171. Apple releases iOS 27.3 public beta 2, new developer beta 2 build

Apple has released iOS 27.3 public beta 2 for iPhone. Today’s release also includes a new build for iOS 27.3 beta 2 for developers. The update brings new Calendar controls, more Siri AI capabilities, and new features for iPhone Duo. It also includes the redesigned Health app and other changes introduced earlier this month.

The update follows yesterday’s second developer beta and the first public beta on November 5.

Apple has also detailed higher daily usage limits for Siri AI and other Apple Intelligence features through eligible iCloud+ plans. Plans with 200GB or more include extra capacity; the 50GB plan keeps standard limits.

See our full iOS 27.3 beta 2 roundup for more on the latest discoveries.

The first public beta brought back the redesigned Health app after its earlier preview during iOS 27.2 testing. On iPhones with Apple Intelligence support, Insights collects trends across your health data, while Longevity includes a Health Age comparison based on Apple Watch measurements.

If you’re already testing the public beta, open Settings > General > Software Update to check for the new version.

Joining for the first time? Make a backup, then enroll in the free Apple Beta Software Program using your iPhone’s Apple Account. In Settings > General > Software Update > Beta Updates, choose iOS 27 Public Beta. Go back to Software Update to download and install it.

What are you trying first in iOS 27.3 public beta 2? Let us know in the comments.

#3170. Community-Focused Academic Brings AI Tools to Colorado Farmers

This senior member’s chatbot helps them start agritourism businesses

Willie Jones covers transportation for IEEE Spectrum and the history of technology for The Institute.

Alice Dong has created an AI chatbot website that helps Colorado farmers plan and operate agribusinesses that draw visitors to their properties.

Many farmers and ranchers in eastern Colorado are curious about artificial intelligence, but they don’t have a local tech-savvy person to show them how to use it. Xue “Alice” Dong has made that her job.

Dong, an IEEE senior member, is an extension regional specialist with the Colorado State University Extension, CSU’s outreach arm. She works in Logan County and serves a 10-county farming area in Colorado’s northeast corner. Her job is to turn university research into practical help for the people who live there.

Xue “Alice” Dong Employer Colorado State University Extension in Logan CountyTitle Extension regional specialistMember grade Senior memberAlma maters Inner Mongolia Normal University, in Hohhot; Beijing Normal University; State University of New York College of Environmental Science and Forestry, in Syracuse; Colorado State University Global

Colorado State University Extension in Logan County

Inner Mongolia Normal University, in Hohhot; Beijing Normal University; State University of New York College of Environmental Science and Forestry, in Syracuse; Colorado State University Global

She built the AI-Powered Agritourism Chatbot (AgriTourismAI.com), which helps farmers and ranchers launch and run “agritourism” businesses. Agritourism is when farmers open their property to visitors for fun, education, or shopping events. Familiar examples include pick-your-own fruit orchards, lessons on how to grow vegetables, and sales of handmade products.

Dong also teaches workshops where she shows farmers and ranchers how they can use AI tools to help grow and manage their business.

She says she sees herself as a link between the university and the countryside.

“We [extension specialists] act as a bridge,” she says. “We bridge our campus to the rural communities we serve.”

Many farmers and ranchers are older, and they typically have no technical training. Often their children and grandchildren have left the farm to work in a city or otherwise aren’t around to teach them about new tools. Without help, the benefits of AI could pass the farmers by. Dong’s workshops give them a way in.

Dong was named a finalist in the 2026 GenAI for Good Challenge for her AgriPivot AI Agent. The challenge was organized by IEEE Humanitarian Technologies and theU.N.’s International Telecommunication Union, and her project was selected from 318 teams across 79 countries. She also won the 2026 Award for Innovation from the National Extension Technology Community (NETC), and both the 2025 national and Western regional Educational Technology Awards from the National Association of Community Development Extension Professionals (NACDEP).

She has secured seven competitive grants totaling more than US $250,000 as principal investigator or co-principal investigator, including funding supported by the Department of Agriculture’s National Institute of Food and Agriculture.

Dong was born in Beijing. Both her parents are doctors.

As a child, she liked drawing new and inventive things. Sketching, she says, lets her picture solutions to problems in her head and put them on paper as practical designs.

That habit grew into a way of relating to her surroundings.

“I’ve always had a passion to create something tangible that can solve problems in the real world,” she says.

She doesn’t credit a single mentor for the direction her life has taken. Instead, she says all her teachers helped lay the groundwork for her career.

She attended the Inner Mongolia Normal University, in Hohhot, an institution that trains teachers. She earned two bachelor’s degrees there in 2013—one in geographical science and one in education.

She then earned a master’s degree in curriculum and instruction from Beijing Normal University in 2016.

That year, she moved to the United States to continue her graduate studies at the State University of New York College of Environmental Science and Forestry, in Syracuse. She earned a master’s degree in environmental biology in 2020.

After earning her second master’s degree, she joined Paul Smith’s College, in Paul Smiths, N.Y., as an education and outreach coordinator.

She managed several national watershed projects to protect rivers, lakes, and aquifers. Watersheds are areas of land from which water drains into bodies of water.

She also undertook invasive-species-prevention projects, wrote grants to secure project funding, and designed two educational websites and several outreach publications. One website, Maintain the Chain, helps lake residents, boaters, and visitors from around the world keep invasive species out of the Fulton Chain of Lakes in New York’s Adirondack Park.

In 2022, she joined Stewards of the Coast and Redwoods as program manager. The nonprofit, based in Guerneville, Calif., works with California State Parks to protect, restore, and educate the public about the parks along Sonoma County’s coast and the Russian River area. The region is known for its redwood forests, wineries, and resort towns.

She left in 2023 to join the CSU Extension as a regional specialist, a title she still holds.

Her employer is part of the Cooperative Extension System, a nationwide network run by land-grant universities, schools founded with federal grants to teach farming and other practical subjects. Extension faculty and staff share what researchers at their universities learn with the citizens of those states.

The cooperative system operates on three levels. It is overseen federally by the Department of Agriculture’s National Institute of Food and Agriculture, managed statewide through land-grant universities, and delivered locally by county offices and Extension agents across more than 3,000 counties.

The work goes well beyond farming, Dong says, also covering community and economic development, health initiatives, and the 4-H program, which teaches children hands-on skills in agriculture, science, leadership, and citizenship.

Extension faculty members’ performance is judged on their research, teaching, and service to the community, Dong says—similar to the way professors in academia are evaluated. The difference, she says, is the audience: Professors teach students; most extension specialists teach adults, including farmers, ranchers, and community leaders. The setting is different, too. Dong doesn’t commute from the campus to the countryside; she lives and works in it. Her office is in Sterling, a small rural town. But her projects serve the whole state, and many of the people she helps live one to four hours’ drive away. So, most of her work with farmers and ranchers happens by email, phone, and virtual meetings. County fairs, farmers markets, and agricultural events give her chances to meet large groups of them in person.

She can’t just hand Colorado residents research findings and expect them to figure out the information they need, she says.

“We need to translate that research into something more practical, and easier to use, that farmers and ranchers can understand immediately,” she says.

Dong also focuses not on only on whether people use AI, but also on how they use it. In 2026, she and Paul Hill from Utah State University Extension published “From Access to Governance: Generative AI Literacy for Extension Professionals and Small Businesses, and a Governance-Aware Design Framework” in the journal AI. The paper offers a framework for helping Extension professionals and small businesses adopt generative AI responsibly.

In 2025, Dong earned a third master’s degree, in artificial intelligence and machine learning, from CSU Global.

She immediately put those skills to work on agritourism, she says. She built the chatbot in Python, a popular programming language. It answers typed questions, and its user interface looks much like ChatGPT’s, but it works differently. Under the hood, it uses retrieval-augmented generation, a technique that has the AI look up information in a set of trusted documents before it answers. Dong curated that collection from Extension publications, so the chatbot’s answers rest on authoritative sources and are less likely to be made up. She presented the project at NeurIPS 2025 (Conference on Neural Information Processing Systems). The code is openly available on GitHub, so other Extension offices can adapt it.

The bot runs in a web browser rather than as a phone app. Many farmers she works with don’t own a smartphone, Dong says, but nearly all have a computer, tablet, or other gadget that can connect to a website. The bot works on any of them, with no app to download.

Extension specialists “act as a bridge. We bridge our campus to the rural communities we serve.”

Farmers often ask the bot how to attract visitors and how to write a business plan. A farmer thinking about opening a corn maze, for example, can ask how to price admission, what kind of insurance to carry, and which permits to get. The bot also gives advice on managing risk.

One of her test sites was Prairie Ridge Buffalo Ranch, in eastern Colorado. Dong documented how the ranch put AI to work in a peer-reviewed case study, “Revolutionizing Agritourism with AI and Machine Learning: A Case Study of Prairie Ridge Buffalo Ranch in Colorado,” published in 2025 in CABI Tourism Cases.

Surveys and interviews she conducted with other users showed that people find it’s easy to use the bot, learn from it, and act on its advice, she says. She is preparing the full results for publication.

Her work extends beyond agritourism. In 2026, she contributed an AI assistant to Project Pythia, an open-science program funded by the U.S. National Science Foundation and led by the National Center for Atmospheric Research (NCAR). The AI assistant turns raw airport weather report data into plain-language guidance for farmers and other non-technical users, and it tells users when data is missing rather than guessing.

She also teaches workshops on AI tools such as ChatGPT, Claude, and Gemini. She has taught her workshop 20 times to more than 200 entrepreneurs and business owners, who came from 32 Colorado counties. In follow-up surveys, 90 percent of participants reported trying at least one new AI task in their business. Some of the workshops take place at a community center run by the Logan County Economic Development Corp., in Sterling. She has also co-hosted the workshops with the Rural Community Assistance Corp., Colorado Startup Week, and Boulder Startup Week. And she occasionally presents them as webinars, so people don’t have to travel.

Her outreach has taught her that many farmers are eager to try new tools, she says. She shows them how simple her chatbot is to use.

She also offers advice to high school students drawn to the field. Extension specialists each have a specialty, such as livestock, natural resources, food systems, or 4-H. Students should pick one based on their passion, she says.

Land-grant universities offer related programs at the bachelor’s and master’s levels. For graduate students, she adds, Extension offers a third career path beyond academia and industry: “You apply advanced skills directly to the communities that need them.”

Dong joined IEEE in 2025 and soon was elevated to senior member. Her professional home is the IEEE Society on Social Implications of Technology. She also serves as vice treasurer of the IEEE Denver Section’s Young Professionals group.

IEEE supports all three parts of her job, she says. For research, she presented “Entrepreneur AI Agent: Empowering Small Businesses and Bridging the Digital Divide through Context-Aware Generative AI” at the 2026 IEEE Global Humanitarian Technology Conference (GHTC). For teaching, she has offered to bring her AI workshop to Denver Section members and local entrepreneurs. For service, she reviews papers for IEEE conferences.

IEEE conferences matter most to her, she says: “Through them, I can present my research and network with other researchers in the field.”

She attended the IEEE World Forum on Public Safety Technology in Boulder, Colo., in September 2026. The event, she says, opened her eyes to many new projects underway across IEEE.

Still, she says, her work always points back to the farms and ranches of eastern Colorado. Its people are curious, she says, but they can’t make the leap to new technology alone.

“They really need this kind of a bridge,” she says.

Willie Jones is an associate editor at IEEE Spectrum. In addition to editing and planning daily coverage, he manages several of Spectrum's newsletters and contributes regularly to the monthly Big Picture section that appears in the print edition.

#3169. The Crypto Bear Market Could Be Back. Here’s What I’m Doing About It.

With Bitcoin's spectacular breakdown over the last weeks, a lot of questions about the crypto market's short-term prospects are being raised.

By Alex Carchidi – Nov 19, 2026 at 4:33PM EST

The crypto bear market may not be as completely finished as investors had hoped. After a weak October, between Nov. 5 and Nov. 17, Bitcoin (BTC -2.14%) fell about 19%, putting its price near $65,000 -- not too far from the $58,000 level it hit during the depths of the summer's doldrums. Other crypto market leaders like Ethereum (ETH -3.28%), Hyperliquid (HYPE -3.45%), Solana (SOL -2.50%), and Zcash (ZEC -9.31%) have been falling quickly too.

This pullback wasn't something I expected, but here's how I'm planning to make the most of it.

First, let's unpack a few headwinds blowing strongly at the moment.

October's hot inflation readout increased the odds of the Federal Reserve hiking interest rates at its December meeting, making bonds more tempting and assets that pay no interest, like most of crypto, less appealing to investors. Separately, the Democrats' incoming takeover of Congress is making the market more volatile due to a widespread (and not entirely accurate) expectation that Democrats are bad for asset prices.

As if that weren't enough, there's an ongoing sell-off in artificial intelligence (AI) stocks, which is depressing marketwide sentiment and has just gone into overdrive as a result of the Nvidia drama.

Then there's the collection of crypto-specific problems, most of which would be digested by the market as fairly routine if they weren't happening at the same time as the above.

Hackers stole $6.3 billion in funds from Binance in October. Then, as part of the ongoing sell-off, investors withdrew $1.3 billion from U.S. Bitcoin exchange-traded funds (ETFs) in the week ending Nov. 6, with additional withdrawals in the subsequent week.

Finally, as marketwide selling accelerated on Nov. 15, about $2 billion in leveraged crypto positions were liquidated, sending the market lower.

One particularly concerning aspect of the ongoing downtrend is that positive news and good financial performance are not leading to consistent increases in the prices of leading assets.

For example, Hyperliquid runs a blockchain exchange for perpetual futures (perps), price-tracking contracts that never expire, and on Oct. 29, the New York Stock Exchange's parent company, Intercontinental Exchange, inked a deal to run new U.S. perps markets designed by TradeXYZ and built on Hyperliquid's technology, pending regulatory approval. As far as upside catalysts go, it's hard to imagine a better one for Hyperliquid than that.

Hyperliquid brought in $71.7 million in revenue in the 30-day period ending on Nov. 17. Yet the coin is now 29.2% below its all-time high set earlier this year. And the three Hyperliquid ETFs have had six straight weeks of net capital outflows through Nov. 13.

When investors sell a project that's making money and teeing up future income, it signals very low confidence, suggesting the crypto bear market never ended despite some excitement in the late summer.

I am taking this signal as an opportunity to reassess my read on the crypto market.

My prior analysis was that the bear market was over, due to the now-erased rebound in Bitcoin's price, the continued uptrends in Zcash, Hyperliquid, and Solana, and an explosion of new projects hosted on Solana and elsewhere. I calculated that their strong performance, both in their fundamentals and in price, would enable them to muddle through the uncertainty and headwinds I knew they were facing. That could still happen, but it's now less probable.

Instead, I'm now assessing that I should look for opportunities to slowly buy the dip in these assets with small amounts of capital, with the intention of holding whatever I buy for at least a handful of years. After all, the market could keep falling from here if the bear market really is back.

Even if it doesn't, the arrival of a new crypto bull market looks a lot further away than it did just a few months ago.

#3165. 22nd Century (XXII) Q3 2026 Earnings Call Transcript

Consumer pack sales for Pinnacle VLN surged as the branded pivot took hold.

By Motley Fool Transcribing – Nov 19, 2026 at 4:40PM EST

Need a quote from a Motley Fool analyst? Email [email protected]

22nd Century (XXII +7.54%) reported a transition toward a branded-product strategy, emphasizing its FDA-authorized low-nicotine offerings. Management indicated that the company is shifting its manufacturing focus away from low-margin contract work to prioritize higher-tier branded products like Pinnacle VLN and Pinnacle Pure. The company completed a restructuring of its capital table to remove warrant overhang and facilitate future growth financing. Strategic initiatives include expanding direct-to-consumer reach through digital platforms and increasing the retail footprint across authorized states.

Operator: Welcome to the 22nd Century Group's third quarter 2026 conference call and webcast. At this time, all participants are in a listen-only mode. It is now my pleasure to turn the call over to Daniel Otto, Chief Financial Officer of 22nd Century Group. Please go ahead.

Daniel Otto: Good morning, everyone, and welcome to 22nd Century Group's third quarter 2026 earnings conference call. Thank you for joining us. With me on the call today is Lawrence Firestone, Chief Executive Officer. Before we begin, please note that today's remarks include forward-looking statements that are subject to risks and uncertainties that could cause actual results to differ materially from those described in these statements. Please refer to the company's earnings release and SEC filings, including our most recent annual report on Form 10-K and quarterly reports on Form 10-Q, for a discussion of these risks and other factors. In addition, during today's call, management may refer to certain non-GAAP financial measures.

Reconciliations of those measures to the most directly comparable GAAP measures are included in the company's earnings release. With that, I'll go through the financial results first, then turn the call over to Lawrence to discuss broader corporate updates and highlights. Let me start with the P&L headline. Net revenues for the third quarter were $4.8 million, up 66% from $2.9 million in the second quarter 2026, and up 18.6% from $4 million in the third quarter of 2025. For the first nine months of 2026, net revenues were $11.7 million versus $14.1 million in the prior year period. The decline year-over-year is consistent with the planned exit of low and negative margin contract volume.

Sales by product line for the quarter were cigarette revenues of $3.9 million versus $2.3 million in the second quarter on higher cartons sold and better pricing. Filtered cigar revenues were $0.7 million, consistent with the second quarter, as that category continues its planned wind-down. Other tobacco products contributed $0.1 million compared to -$0.2 million in the second quarter, of which the prior quarter had included a one-time write-off of aged inventory discontinued by a customer. VLN cigarette revenues were $0.03 million, consistent with the second quarter, reflecting steady initial orders and reorders of Pinnacle VLN, alongside targeted price promotions that we view as awareness investments. These are promotions that are showing up in point-of-sale results at retail.

Continuing on, gross profit for the third quarter 2026 was +$0.4 million versus a gross loss of $0.3 million last quarter. The drivers are the ones we have described and are integral to our strategy, better mix and better pricing. Operating expenses for the third quarter 2026 were $3 million, flat sequentially. On a year-over-year basis, operating expenses are higher than the $2.2 million we recorded in the third quarter of 2025, which reflects deliberate investment in the commercial organization, including sales coverage, marketing execution, and the infrastructure required to service a larger and more demanding retail footprint. Operating loss for the third quarter 2026 narrowed to $2.6 million from $3.3 million last quarter.

Net loss from continuing operations was $2.6 million versus $3.3 million last quarter. Adjusted EBITDA loss improved to $2.2 million from a loss of $3.5 million last quarter. For the nine-month period, Adjusted EBITDA loss was $8.3 million versus $7.8 million in the prior year period, with the modest unfavorable variance reflecting the commercial investments I just described. On the balance sheet, we ended the quarter with $3.9 million of cash and no debt. Subsequent to quarter end, our at-the-market facility generated approximately $5.8 million of net proceeds, of which $1.2 million was used to redeem an equal amount of Series B convertible preferred shares at par, leaving us with approximately $8 million of cash on a pro forma basis.

One structural change to the cap table worth noting: as of September 30th, 2026, no warrants to purchase common stock remain outstanding. That entire class of dilution overhang is gone. The result is a capital structure that is dramatically simpler than the one we started 2026 with, as we look toward new capital raise going toward the commercial plan rather than toward servicing legacy structures. Looking at the fourth quarter, the financial agenda continues to focus on broadening distribution and increasing rate of sale. We expect to see the legacy CMO wind-down substantially complete by the end of 2026. These two forces will yield a new look in the P&L to our revenue run rate and growth going forward.

With that, I'll turn the call over to Lawrence.

Lawrence Firestone: Thanks, Daniel, and good morning, everyone. Thank you for joining us today and for your continued interest in 22nd Century Group. We continue to make significant progress towards our ultimate objective, becoming a pure-play tobacco company focused on leading the low-nicotine movement, anchored by our FDA-authorized low-nicotine cigarette products, Pinnacle VLN and our flagship VLN. We took an important step towards achieving this objective in the third quarter. Retail same-store sales reported by our retail partners for our Pinnacle Pure branded products, Pinnacle VLN and Pinnacle Pure, increased 166% compared to the previous quarter. More importantly, as our higher-margin branded products gain traction in the marketplace and consumers increasingly seek them out, our gross margin profile is improving significantly.

Pinnacle Pure, Pinnacle VLN, and our flagship VLN are positioned in the higher margin tiers of the tobacco market, where gross margins of 50% or more are achievable at scale. As sales volumes increase and we experience greater absorption of our manufacturing overhead, we believe we can achieve the gross margins, operating margins, and cash flow characteristics traditionally associated with the tobacco industry. We are now firmly in growth mode. With our branded products in the marketplace and generating sales, our primary focus is expanding distribution and increasing retail sales velocity. We now have meaningful in-market sales data that demonstrates consumer demand and provides us with the evidence needed to approach additional retailers and expand our distribution footprint.

Our two brands, Pinnacle and our flagship VLN brand, serve distinct consumer segments. Pinnacle VLN and our flagship VLN appeal to smokers who are actively looking for an alternative that allows them to continue smoking while reducing their nicotine consumption. Consumers who have discovered our low nicotine products are responding positively to the experience and are increasingly seeking out these products. The science supporting our VLN technology is well established, and we continue to hear directly from consumers across the U.S. who contact us through our tryvln.com website to find out where they can purchase our products. Unfortunately, some interested consumers live in states where we have the necessary state-level authorizations, but have not yet established retail distribution.

Our planned expansion through Gopuff is designed to help address this gap. Many of these consumers live in major metropolitan markets where Gopuff's direct-to-consumer platform can provide access to our products before we establish a broader brick-and-mortar retail presence. We also expect the resulting regional sales data to help us demonstrate local consumer demand and support our efforts to secure additional retail distribution in those markets. We believe low nicotine cigarette category is emerging as a meaningful segment of the tobacco market. Consumer interest is growing, and our products are positioned to serve smokers who want to change their nicotine consumption without necessarily switching to vaping products, e-cigarettes, or nicotine pouches.

We conducted a recent study involving more than 1,000 smokers, and over 70% of the respondents indicated they would like to change their smoking habits and reduce their nicotine consumption while continuing to smoke cigarettes. The study also identified similar interest among consumers who currently use vaping products and nicotine pouches. These findings reinforce our belief that there is a substantial consumer population seeking alternatives within the existing nicotine marketplace. We believe our VLN products offer an important option for these consumers. We are not simply introducing another cigarette brand. We are building a brand platform around a specific consumer need.

One recent customer experience illustrates the level of interest that we are beginning to see in our low nicotine products. A smoker for 50 years, after learning about our VLN products online, set out to address her nicotine cravings. In her words exactly, and I quote, "I did not want the nicotine to take over my life again." End quote. She then traveled approximately two hours each way to purchase our VLN cigarettes from one of our retail locations. Following her experience, she took the additional step of submitting a testimonial, including the quote I just read, through the FDA website, describing her satisfaction with the product.

Stories like this and others that are coming in demonstrate the importance of the product accessibility and the potential demand that can develop as consumer awareness increases. Pinnacle Pure serves a different consumer segment. The brand is designed to appeal to value-conscious smokers who are looking for an affordable alternative to traditional lower-priced cigarette brands. By offering a tobacco and water cigarette formulation in both regular and menthol varieties, we believe Pinnacle Pure provides consumers with a differentiated value proposition. Rather than relying exclusively on temporary discounts or coupons, we are offering a competitively priced product that consumers can choose as their regular brand.

In the approximately three and a half months since its market introduction, Pinnacle Pure has generated encouraging consumer response. Early retail performance indicates that consumers are willing to try the brand and that repeat interest is growing the brand. Our satisfied customer base is growing month-over-month, and we believe Pinnacle Pure has the potential to become a meaningful contributor to both revenue and gross margin as distribution expands. At this stage, our growth strategy is increasingly about execution. We currently have retail presence in 23 states through the nation's third-largest cigarette retailer. Our products are available in every store within that retailer's network, where we have the necessary state authorization. Establishing this relationship was an important proof of concept.

Successfully entering the distribution network of a major national retailer required considerable effort, but we have accomplished that milestone, and we are now positioned to build on it. Our next priority is expanding the distribution through the nation's second-largest cigarette retailer, where we currently have a presence in Illinois. We are actively working to expand into additional territories within this retailer's network. We are also preparing to launch Pinnacle VLN and Pinnacle Pure through the national direct-to-consumer platform, Gopuff, featuring home delivery of our products. We expect this initiative to begin in the fourth quarter, with the objective of establishing a well-developed direct-to-consumer operating model as we enter 2027.

Gopuff offers an important opportunity to reach consumers in markets where we have not yet established brick-and-mortar distribution. We believe this channel can accelerate product availability, generate valuable sales data, and help us demonstrate brand performance with consumer demand metrics to prospective retail partners. Our strategy is straightforward: expand distribution, increase sales velocity, educate the smoking consumer about our low-nicotine VLN products, build brand awareness, and establish a growing base of repeat customers. The U.S. tobacco market represents approximately $70 billion in annual sales, with cigarettes accounting for roughly $50 billion. Based on the reported research and industry reports over the past several years, more than 70% of smokers are interested in changing their habits.

Therefore, we believe the serviceable addressable market, or what I call SAM, we are targeting for our products is approximately $35 billion annually. Our ability to capture a meaningful share of that SAM will depend on consumer adoption and continued execution. We believe our VLN products are well-positioned within this opportunity. We have developed the only FDA-authorized low-nicotine combustible cigarette currently available in the United States, and consumer feedback regarding taste and the overall smoking experience has been all positive. Our objective is to make these products available in every state where they are authorized and available in as many of the more than 272,000 U.S. retail locations that sell cigarettes as possible.

We believe there is a sustainable place for low-nicotine cigarettes in this marketplace. The opportunity now is to accelerate retailer adoption, increase consumer awareness, and expand availability. As awareness of our VLN products continues to grow, we are receiving an increasing number of inquiries from prospective customers across the country, as well as from consumers outside the United States. Our marketing team, under new leadership, is developing programs designed to educate consumers, strengthen brand awareness, and support continued retail expansion. Importantly, the retail sales data that we have accumulated over the past year provides us with valuable insight into customer behavior and purchasing patterns.

With continued access to point-of-sale information, we can better understand the demographics and preferences of the markets we serve, and this allows us to tailor our marketing strategies to individual markets rather than relying on a one-size-fits-all approach. Our research and development team also continues to advance new tobacco technologies and product concepts. We are evaluating additional branded products designed to fit within the applicable regulatory framework, including cigarette predicate requirements established under the 2007 legislation and our existing MRTP and PMTA regulatory strategies. We believe our continued investment in product development, particularly in the low-nicotine combustible category, differentiates 22nd Century within the U.S. tobacco industry. Consumers interested in locating our VLN products can visit our store locator at tryvln.com.

We have also made substantial progress on the capital structure and financial fronts. The increased trading activity in our stock during October provided an opportunity to complete an important cleanup of our capitalization table. With the exception of one remaining preferred stockholder holding Series B preferred shares, our capital structure consists of only common stock now. We have also eliminated the outstanding warrant overhang, which significantly simplifies our capitalization structure. Additionally, we have addressed the applicable baby shelf limitations, making our $250 million shelf registration statement available for use without restrictions. These actions provide greater financial flexibility as we pursue our growth strategy.

We currently have sufficient cash on the balance sheet to fund operations well into 2027 based on management's current outlook, and our focus is on achieving cash flow breakeven before the additional capital becomes needed. Our priorities are clear: grow revenue, improve gross margins, manage operating expenses, and strengthen the balance sheet. Every pack and carton sold represents an opportunity to gain market share from established competitors and build a lasting relationship with a consumer seeking an alternative in their comfort zone with a cigarette. Our sights are set on the substantial market opportunity represented by consumers who are looking for solutions addressing nicotine and tobacco products.

Consumer preferences continue to evolve, and we believe many traditional cigarette smokers will consider VLN products as an alternative to switching to vaping products, e-cigarettes, or nicotine pouches. We are building our business around the idea that consumers want choices. An interesting example of this strategy can be found in the beer industry, particularly at Heineken. Heineken has successfully developed a portfolio of premium brands, and while introducing Heineken 0.0 to provide consumers with an additional choice, offering a zero-alcohol product within its flagship brand family. We see a similar opportunity with the Pinnacle brand platform and our flagship VLN products. Pinnacle Pure offers a differentiated tobacco and water product, while Pinnacle VLN provides a low-nicotine alternative.

Together, these products allow us to serve distinct consumer preferences within the combustible cigarette category. We believe the U.S. market presents a significant opportunity for this approach. The potential $35 billion SAM is substantial, and particularly when compared with the existing markets for vaping and smokeless nicotine tobacco products. Consumer migration towards alternative products is already underway. While adoption of low-nicotine cigarettes is still developing, we believe awareness is increasing and the opportunity to expand distribution is significant. Our competitive position is supported by our VLN technology, our FDA authorization, our established manufacturing capabilities, and our growing retail relationships.

The next phase is about execution and getting our products into more stores, making them easier for consumers to find, and building the sales momentum necessary to support sustainable growth. As we look towards the end of 2026 and into 2027, we believe 22nd Century Group is entering a new chapter. The restructuring work is substantially behind us. Our capital structure is simplified, our branded products are established in the marketplace, and we've begun building the retail relationships necessary to support national expansion. We now have a clear path forward with a focus on growing distribution, increasing sales, improving margins, and ultimately achieving cash flow breakeven.

Our goal is to establish 22nd Century as the leading company in the emerging low-nicotine cigarette category while continuing to develop innovative tobacco products that respond to changing consumer preferences. We believe Pinnacle Pure and Pinnacle VLN have meaningful opportunities within the approximately $50 billion U.S. cigarette market. We're excited about the progress we've made and the opportunities that lie ahead, and the potential to build a profitable, cash-positive, sustainable business in a mature industry. I would like to thank our employees, our management team, board of directors, retail partners, and shareholders for their continued commitment and support. We appreciate your interest in 22nd Century Group. Thank you for joining us today, and have a nice day.

#3162. 2 Reasons to Buy SpaceX (SPCX) Stock -- and 1 Reason to Wait

The aerospace and AI company remains a polarizing investment.

10 stocks we like better than Space Exploration Technologies ›

SpaceX (SPCX -3.53%) has been a divisive stock since its IPO on June 12. The aerospace and AI company went public at $135 per share, closed at an all-time high of $201.80 four days later, but now trades at about $138 per share. Investors were initially impressed by its explosive growth, but its luster faded as rising interest rates and Treasury yields chilled the market.

Should investors buy SpaceX's stock as the bulls look the other way? Let's review two reasons to buy SpaceX -- as well as one reason to sell it -- to see if it's a contrarian investment.

Starlink also acquired Grain Management's nationwide 800 MHz low-band spectrum, which previously belonged to T-Mobile (TMUS -0.91%), for $8 billion in October. That acquisition, which adds terrestrial cellular towers to its networks, could make it a formidable challenger to AT&T (T -0.46%), Verizon (T -0.46%), and other telco giants in the wireless carrier market.

SpaceX's Connectivity segment, which houses Starlink, is the company's only profitable business by generally accepted accounting principles (GAAP). Its ongoing growth should subsidize the expansion of its lower-margin space and SI ("super intelligence") businesses.

SpaceX has launched Starship, its largest rocket ever built, in 15 test flights since April 2023. It isn't a major revenue source for the Space segment yet, but it plans to launch 50-100 Starship rockets in 2027. That acceleration would likely widen its moat, dilute its expenses, and boost its adjusted earnings before interest, taxes, depreciation, and amortization (EBITDA) -- which remained negative in the first nine months of 2026 -- into positive territory.

Elon Musk believes the combined growth of Starlink, Starship, and its SI business will boost SpaceX's revenue from an estimated $49 billion this year to $1 trillion by 2030. With a market cap of $1.95 trillion, it trades at 40 times this year's sales but less than two times its 2030 target.

SpaceX's Starlink and space segments have clear long-term catalysts, but the SI segment -- which houses X, xAI, Grok, Cursor, and its other AI assets -- faces a murkier future. The SI business generated $10.9 billion in revenue (40% of SpaceX's total revenue of $27.1 billion) in the first nine months of 2026, but it racked up an operating loss of $3.8 billion.

That loss -- along with the Space segment's $1.2 billion operating loss -- nearly erased the Connectivity segment's operating profit of $5.21 billion. SpaceX still squeezed out a total operating profit of $705 million in the first nine months of the year, but that balancing act could falter as SpaceX ramps up its AI investments over the next few quarters.

SpaceX already plans to roughly double its capex sequentially, from $19.6 billion in the third quarter to $35-$40 billion in the fourth quarter, with most of that spending earmarked for Nvidia's (NVDA -3.30%) data center GPUs. That spending spree will continue to weigh down SpaceX's stock, especially if interest rates remain elevated.

With Anthropic's (ANT +17.07%) IPO sucking the oxygen out of the market and Nvidia dominating the headlines, it seems like fewer investors are paying attention to SpaceX. So if you can look past its near-term challenges and ride out the volatility, it might be a great time to accumulate the stock as it hovers near its IPO price. Over the long term, its three core growth engines -- space, Starlink, and SI -- could catapult its stock to fresh all-time highs.

#3161. Report: Apple job listings detail plans for autonomous AI agents

Bloomberg reports that Apple is hiring engineers to develop an autonomous AI agent capable of browsing the web, writing code, and controlling apps on behalf of users. Here are the details.

In a report published today, Bloomberg notes that new job listings on Apple’s website indicate the company’s efforts to develop an autonomous AI agent capable of performing complex tasks on the user’s behalf.

Since the breakout success of OpenClaw, autonomous AI agents have become increasingly popular, with companies such as OpenAI, Anthropic, Meta, and SpaceXSI among those offering their own solutions.

The increasing popularity of these agents has put Apple under pressure to catch up, while the company has also introduced new restrictions on how third-party AI agents can access and control Macs.

Over at the App Store, Meta’s Muse has become one of the fastest-growing apps in US history, surpassing 10 million downloads in just 40 days, according to Sensor Tower, and spending weeks at the top of the charts. As of today, it sits at No. 2 among free apps, behind TikTok.

And while there are differences in how phone-based and computer-based agents operate, these systems can usually work together, coordinating tasks across devices and apps to accomplish increasingly complex goals.

Back to Bloomberg’s report, it notes Apple recently posted new job listings that offer a closer look at its plans to develop autonomous AI agents:

In one, Apple said it’s seeking a senior engineering manager for a proactive, agentic AI assistant. The system will write code, browse the web, control apps and navigate devices on a user’s behalf, according to the post.

One job listing, which is for “Senior Engineering Manager, Agentic AI – Proactive,” features the following summary:

“Imagine an AI agent that can use a computer the way a capable person does. It browses the web, works across apps, runs commands, writes and debugs code, and calls services, and it chooses the right tool for each step. It does all this privately and with the polish people expect from Apple. Our team is building the foundation for that future, and we’re looking for a senior engineering leader to make it real.”

The listing also notes that Apple is building agents that can “plan and carry out multi-step tasks across apps, browsers, command lines, code, and APIs, and they can coordinate specialized sub-agents along the way,” much like existing solutions from frontier AI labs.

Today’s report on the new job listings comes just days after Bloomberg reported that Apple wants to make Siri more like an autonomous AI agent, with the ability to proactively carry out tasks without requiring users to initiate every step. According to Mark Gurman, the company could introduce these capabilities as soon as next year.

With the new job listings, Apple has offered a more detailed look at its plans for autonomous AI agents, although the language suggests that development is still in its early stages.

Of course, given how quickly the technology is evolving, the landscape could look very different by the time Apple is ready to introduce its own solution next year, much like how the industry had already moved toward autonomous agents by the time Apple finally launched its long-awaited Siri AI overhaul.

#3160. Critical Java Flaw Leaves Systems Open to Hackers

Our gifting experts are obsessively searching for holiday gifts that are unique, thoughtful and suitable for any budget.

Our expert, award-winning staff selects the products we cover and rigorously researches and tests our top picks. If you buy through our links, we may earn a commission.

Tech > Services & Software > Cybersecurity

The Java4Shell vulnerability could allow hackers to take over systems without a password.

A newly identified vulnerability in Oracle Java could give hackers unauthorized access to major applications and allow them to run code without logging in. The flaw could affect a sweeping array of big businesses, including tech companies like Google, Amazon, Microsoft, Apple and Netflix, which rely heavily on Java’s server-side software and core products.

“Roughly 90% of Fortune 500 companies run on Java,” Thai Duong, CEO of cybersecurity firm Calif, said.

The flaw, tracked as CVE-2026-114938 (and dubbed Java4Shell), corrupts memory when Java decodes Base64, a standard format used to transmit login credentials and file uploads.

Duong told CNET that his company identified the critical software vulnerability in October and notified Oracle, which has since patched the vulnerability. This week, the US Cybersecurity and Infrastructure Security Agency issued guidance urging organizations to do the same immediately. CISA recommends identifying affected Java installations, reviewing software inventory for JDKs and Java runtimes, and applying vendor patches as soon as they’re available.

Oracle rated the flaw a serious 8.1 out of 10 on the standard vulnerability scale. It can lead to an unauthenticated remote code execution vulnerability in Java, allowing hackers to run their own malicious commands or code over the internet without requiring a username, password or prior access.

Federico Kirschbaum, head of Security Lab, the research arm at cybersecurity company XBOW, told CNET that Java is primarily used at the enterprise level. As a result, the vulnerability could trickle across different sectors, including finance, government, transportation and large corporations.

“Java is a great language for creating solutions, but this vulnerability — it’s a reminder that maybe the languages that we’re using have flaws, and everything built on those might inherit that problem,” Kirschbaum said.

Amid recent technological disruptions, he suggested leaning on AI solutions to address vulnerabilities in AI.

“That new normal is that most of the technology we rely on has flaws, and now that we have resources using LLMs, we can find those problems,” Kirschbaum said.

He pointed out that bad actors and hackers can also find these vulnerabilities.

“We are in a race to find the problems first and help the industry by guiding them on what’s urgent so they patch it,” Kirschbaum said.

#3157. iPhone Duo 2 prototypes suggest Face ID, Action Button, other potential 2027 features

Our gifting experts are obsessively searching for holiday gifts that are unique, thoughtful and suitable for any budget.

With manufacturing deadlines looming, it's unclear which of several feature upgrades may have to wait until the foldable's third generation.

Although the iPhone Duo was released just this fall, Apple is finalizing the foldable’s second generation. According to a Bloomberg report, Apple has already created prototypes for the second iPhone Duo, codenamed V78, and some include a sought-after feature: Face ID.

Apple reportedly wants to bring Face ID to the foldable, potentially integrating it into the outer display. However, Bloomberg’s Mark Gurman notes that Apple appears to be running out of time to finalize its plans for the Duo ahead of a fall 2027 launch.

Also: iPhone Duo review: Hard to recommend, even harder to put down

iPhone launch events typically take place in early September, when Apple releases its new smartphone lineups. To have the iPhones ready for sale on the heels of their announcement, Apple must manufacture the new models well before the launch event.

Because of this timeline concern, Face ID isn’t guaranteed for the iPhone Duo 2, though it could come to a third generation instead.

Other planned uogrades — including an Action Button, a telephoto camera, and a thinner, lighter construction — are also noted in the report.

Apple reportedly wants to add an Action Button, the customizable button that performs an action when pressed. The iPhone Duo 2 may combine the Action Button and the Camera Control buttons into a single button, providing a useful physical shortcut instead of adding a new button.

The report indicates that many users don’t use the camera control button as often as Apple expected. Combining the camera and action buttons gives Apple the real estate necessary to add both options in an already constrained space.

Apple also wants to incorporate a telephoto camera into the iPhone Duo, though this is likely to happen in one of the next couple of generations. A telephoto camera would give users greater flexibility to zoom in and capture clear photos of distant objects, which would be an upgrade to the Duo’s photography features.

Technically, equipping the Duo with a telephoto camera is feasible, but the biggest obstacle is space constraints. A telephoto camera needs more room than a wide-angle one, since it requires additional optical elements to magnify distant objects.

Apple already uses a tetraprism design in its Pro iPhones, which allows a longer optical path without too much physical depth.

Apple also wants to reduce the weight and thickness of the iPhone Duo, which is legitimately clunky and cumbersome. To do this, Apple needs to balance the large internal and outer displays, battery capacity, camera array, and the hinge mechanism.

Also: The iPhone Action Button you’re hardly using has a superpower

For many users, reducing the weight and thickness of a passport-sized foldable could matter more in buying decisions than adding another button or camera.

Gurman’s latest report doesn’t mention any planned changes for the iPhone Duo’s hinge mechanism, even after concerns with the first generation’s durability. With manufacturing deadlines fast approaching, however, it’s unlikely that Apple will be able to make changes to the Duo 2 based on consumer feedback. More than likely, these changes would come with the third-generation model.

CNET tested the iPhone Duo’s hinge mechanism and found that, after around 440,000 cycles, the hinge stopped opening flat on its own. Loosening and other signs of wear were evident after 390,000 folds.

Also: The best iPhone Duo cases: Expert recommended

Given the thinner, lighter construction of a future Duo model, one could assume that changes to the hinge and the foldable’s internal structure are imminent, but this has not been confirmed.

Because Apple will not have enough time to gather feedback on the iPhone Duo before the manufacturing deadlines for the iPhone Duo 2, I don’t expect the second-generation iPhone Duo to be significantly different from its predecessor. We do expect a thinner iPhone Duo 2 and a way to incorporate the Action and Camera buttons.

For a meaningful recovery to materialize, investors should look for improving market breadth, stabilizing Treasury yields, and the S&P 500 reclaiming its 200-day moving average. Until then, investors should be cautious about interpreting isolated rallies as signs of a broader market recovery.

#3155. Voyager 1 Becomes the First Spacecraft to Travel a Full Light-Day From Earth

Our gifting experts are obsessively searching for holiday gifts that are unique, thoughtful and suitable for any budget.

Our expert, award-winning staff selects the products we cover and rigorously researches and tests our top picks. If you buy through our links, we may earn a commission.

Voyager 1 has been flying at about 38,000 mph since 1980. That steady pace carried it a full light-day from home.

NASA’s Voyager 1 left Earth on Sept. 5, 1977, carrying a camera, a set of science instruments and a gold-plated record of sounds and images from home. Forty-nine years later, it’s reached a distance no spacecraft has attained before: one light-day, or roughly 16.1 billion miles, from Earth. At that range, light needs a full 24 hours to make the trip between Earth and the probe.

At 5:16:07 a.m. ET on Wednesday, Voyager 1 became the first human-made object to reach that light-day milestone. From that point on, a radio signal between the spacecraft and NASA’s Deep Space Network takes more than a day to travel in either direction.

NASA puts the journey at 49 years, two months and 11 days, counting from Voyager 1’s launch in September 1977. The probe still sends data home, though at a rate slower than dial-up, and NASA plans a live discussion with the Voyager team on Thursday to mark the occasion.

It’s quite an accomplishment for a spacecraft built in the mid-1970s. One light-day is the distance that light travels in a single day at the speed of light, which is approximately 186,282 miles per second. That translates to 25.9 billion kilometers or about 16.1 billion miles in a single day. At an average human walking speed of 3 mph, it would take a human 612,015 years to travel that distance on foot.

Fortunately, Voyager 1 has been traveling a bit faster. It currently zips through the cosmos at a steady 37,763 mph, a speed it achieved in 1980 after a gravity-assisted Saturn flyby. It has been flying at that speed ever since.

The milestone comes 14 years after Voyager 1 crossed the heliopause, the point where the sun’s heliosphere ends, and entered interstellar space. It’s also 28 years after the spacecraft passed Pioneer 10 to become the human-made object that has traveled the farthest into space.

NASA marked the milestone with a global Shine Bright for Voyager’s Light-Day event on Tuesday evening. Just after sunset, the agency wanted people to head outside and point their smartphone or tablet lights skyward to spark a planet-wide wave of light as Earth rotates, much like fans doing the wave at a stadium.

The space agency also made a website for the occasion. The website is simple. It flashes Voyager’s VGR call sign in Morse code. If you want to try it, click the link, hit begin, and then point your phone or tablet screen at the sky. The website does all the work for you.

NASA’s Jet Propulsion Laboratory will follow up on Thursday at noon ET with a moderated discussion on the milestone, featuring status updates on both Voyager probes and a live Q&A with reporters and audience members.

The historic milestone isn’t without its drama. Voyager 1 has been in space for nearly half a century, and in that time, the Jet Propulsion Laboratory has done everything it can to extend the spacecraft’s life. That includes troubleshooting issues, performing maintenance, and shutting down various systems to save power and extend the spacecraft’s lifespan.

Several of those efforts took place in 2026. The team running Voyager 1 spent weeks shutting down three devices and powering on three low-power alternatives to reduce overall power usage. This initiative, which was internally called the Big Bang, was also performed on Voyager 2. The transition was completed in early September, giving Voyager 1 more time with its dwindling power supply while also keeping it warm enough to continue operating in the frigid conditions of interstellar space.

It was a tricky maneuver that required the team to simultaneously turn multiple instruments on and off. The difficulty of the maneuver was amplified by the fact that it took almost a full day for a signal to reach Voyager and another full day for Voyager to send a signal back, with hours of downtime while the spacecraft performed the operations.

All of this took place several months after Voyager 1 experienced a sudden drop in power, which necessitated shutting off one of its three instruments still in operation. Voyager 1 now has only two operational instruments.

Making it a whole light-day away from Earth is likely going to be Voyager 1’s final milestone while it still has enough power to communicate with Earth. Voyager 1 is powered by three radioisotope thermoelectric generators. They are essentially nuclear-powered batteries that generate energy by converting the steady heat from decaying plutonium-238.

When Voyager 1 first launched, its radioisotope thermoelectric generators produced about 470 watts of power. But plutonium-238 doesn’t last forever, and after 50 years in space, those generators now produce about 215 watts of power, with an average loss of about 4 watts per year. Most of that power is used to keep Voyager 1 up and running, which is why NASA has shut down eight of the 10 instruments that Voyager had when it launched.

At its current rate of usage and decay, Voyager 1 is expected to shut down its final science instrument in the 2030s and will eventually lose communication with Earth in 2036 due to insufficient power to send back a radio signal.

The same fate is expected for Voyager 2, Voyager 1’s twin, which has also spent half a century in space. While it is labeled the sequel, Voyager 2 actually launched 16 days before Voyager 1, and the two have spent nearly identical amounts of time traversing the cosmos. Thanks to its slower speed and trajectory, it likely won’t reach the one light-day distance until after its instruments shut down.

Voyager 1 will lose all of its power before it hits its next milestone, which is the beginning of the Oort Cloud, a vast, icy shell of comets at the edge of our solar system. It’ll take about 300 years for Voyager 1 to make it there.

Thanks to the near-perfect vacuum of outer space, Voyager 1 will continue to fly at its current speed even after it shuts down entirely. So it’ll still hit that milestone; it just won’t be able to phone home to tell us about it.

#3153. 5 ways AI will change how you defend your business in 2027

Our gifting experts are obsessively searching for holiday gifts that are unique, thoughtful and suitable for any budget.

Security leaders reveal the future consequences of AI outpacing human defenders.

At the beginning of the year, few organizations were utilizing large language models (LLMs) and AI agents in their cybersecurity workflows, including for discovering and patching vulnerabilities. According to Google, this is now happening at scale.

Also: Rogue AI incidents hit ‘tens of thousands’: Can businesses trust these tools?

The capabilities of agentic AI are fast outstripping the speed and scale at which traditional security operations centers (SOCs) can operate. Like it or not, AI has an integral role in the new reality — for the defenders and threat actors.

Speed and scale are the main reasons enterprises consider adopting AI in SOCs and for security more broadly, and these factors underpin Google’s new security forecast for 2027 — Cloud CISO Perspectives. However, without the right precautions, AI security adopters could inadvertently increase their attack surface rather than shrink it.

With this in mind, these are five ways AI will change the security industry over the next year and what CISOs need to consider going into 2027.

Alert fatigue is well-known across SOC teams. Alert after alert needs to be trawled through; many are irrelevant or false positives, tying up skilled staff with the mundane, tedious, time-consuming task of triaging them.

Now that autonomous, AI-driven threats can probe a network, gain entry, and move laterally across it in minutes, chasing threat data and security alerts from multiple systems logged days or weeks ago can’t help a business mitigate them — and certainly not at the speed of the threat.

According to Google’s forecast, AI will mean the alert queue quietly disappears. Ramya Chitrakar, VP of engineering at Google Cloud Security, believes that “2027 is the year analysts stop chasing alerts and start shaping outcomes.”

Also: AI is both a cyber weapon and a massive target

How? CISOs must change the alert model itself. Instead of human defenders triaging alerts at the start of a cybersecurity incident, the alert becomes final output, with autonomous agents handling “data enrichment, correlation, and triage automatically, surfacing a verified conclusion rather than a raw ticket,” according to Google.

This means cybersecurity experts can oversee alert handling and verify automated actions, potentially freeing them to focus on other tasks.

Custom agentic AI is often designed — or at least intended — to work autonomously, with human oversight. However, having thousands of individual agents working across multiple environments can create high-value entry points into corporate networks that cyberattackers target.

We need to think of agentic AI as more than a tool: each one needs its own identity, like a human employee, to operate within a zero-trust architecture, retain control, and reduce the risk of compromise.

Also: Your enterprise AI access can be sold for pennies – beware ‘LLM Mixers’

However, Heather Adkins, VP of security engineering at Google, thinks this needs to go further and suggests the zero-trust concept shouldn’t stop at the network layer. Instead, Adkins believes it needs to reach the transaction layer.

A paper trail for each agent needs to be established, which is impossible to handle manually, and even within a zero-trust framework, AI agents could be given too much scope. Instead, implement verification for each transaction and for every authorization, and assign each AI agent its own least-privilege set of credentials that can be revoked if there is a security incident or the agent is no longer required.

“When backed by real-time autonomous reasoning, we can dynamically allow a transaction on Tuesday and block the exact same request on Wednesday if conditions look anomalous,” the report notes.

AI is being used to speed up the development and deployment of new software, and in 2027, security will have to become a continuous system embedded in the software delivery pipeline, according to Google.

Threat actors have carried out software supply chain attacks over the years, one of the most notable being the SolarWinds incident of 2020. Sandra Joyce, VP of Google Threat Intelligence, says cybercriminals are now poisoning everything from open-source code to software libraries, which AI coding assistants often pull automatically into codebases.

Also: How AI security failures are endangering your supply chain

Bug-fix tickets that take days to respond to and security appearing at the end of a software development cycle no longer work. Instead, writing and securing code must happen simultaneously, with the help of agentic AI, so speed doesn’t compromise security.

“It’s also crucial that we link live production environments directly back to source code so that defenders can trace a real-world exposure to the exact line of code, validate whether it is genuinely exploitable, and deliver a pre-tested fix at machine speed without breaking production,” Google added.

As organizations rush to implement AI into their applications and services to appear “AI-first,” innovative, and modern, security may be ignored or treated as an afterthought.

As a result, we may face a new, broader attack surface than we realize, as AI introduces new security issues, including software vulnerabilities, misconfiguration, bypasses, and indirect prompt injection attacks. Now that AI is also in the hands of all cyberattackers — from script kiddies to state-sponsored groups — auditing corporate networks and infrastructure is crucial.

Also: Who’s responsible for catching rogue AI agents? You are

Penetration testing and red team exercises now need to cover agentic AI. This wasn’t in scope for many red teams only a few years ago, but now that businesses have run with the idea of implementing AI in their workflows, processes, and products, organizations need to identify and fix security issues introduced by AI before threat actors take advantage of them.

CISOs should task pen testers with auditing before an autonomous workflow hits production, then combine the results with threat intelligence to ensure defenders have the information they need to bolster network defenses and harden classifiers against new and novel attacks.

The final significant trend we are likely to see in 2027 is tackling agent sprawl to create coordinated teams of AI agents that can rapidly handle security tasks at scale.

Single AI agents given general instructions won’t cut it when AI-assisted attackers can compromise endpoint devices, enter networks, move laterally, or start stealing data in a far shorter timeframe than before. Instead, CISOs should replace these “generalist” AI agents with specialized, orchestrated teams of AI agents that can meet the demands of defending against AI-driven attacks by employing specialist tooling and skill sets.

Also: AI agent kill switch urged by Okta-led alliance

CISOs also need to ensure that each agent has its own domain training and understanding, memory, and dedicated tools, and can act on its own within set limits, with a central coordinator that knows when to hand a decision to a human. This requires oversight, but in return, organizations will avoid agent sprawl, which the tech giant believes is the next iteration of shadow IT and its associated threats.

#3151. iFixit Says Apple’s HomeView Breaks Easily. Here’s Why I’m Not Worried

Our gifting experts are obsessively searching for holiday gifts that are unique, thoughtful and suitable for any budget.

Our expert, award-winning staff selects the products we cover and rigorously researches and tests our top picks. If you buy through our links, we may earn a commission.

iFixit found the HomeView nearly impossible to repair yourself, but smart displays don't face the same daily risks as iPhones.

Senior Editor / Home Security and Smart Home

Senior Editor / Home Security and Smart Home

For the past few years, Apple was looking almost DIY-friendly. The company had been moving toward smart speakers that you could take apart without damaging and iPads with accessible batteries. But the new HomeView smart display broke apart when iFixit tried to access components in Tuesday’s full analysis.

The good news? I don’t think it really matters, at least not for this particular Apple device. Here’s why.

DIY repairs are a big deal for Apple products, not just because they’re difficult, but because many people believe they have a right to repair their own phones or computers.

Making repairs more accessible also sustains a secondary market of iPhone and Mac repair services that Apple would rather tightly control — or squash entirely. That’s one reason the EU has required Apple to make iPhone batteries replaceable in 2027.

The HomeView moves sharply in the opposite direction, held together by the toughest adhesive iFixit has ever encountered in an Apple product. The glue is so stubborn that the team accidentally snapped a speaker in half during disassembly, and the logic board was bound too dangerously tight to the aluminum chassis to remove.

“Obviously, when you buy a product you don’t anticipate the accidents, and there’s no way of knowing when wear and tear will become a problem,” iFixit said in its report. “But you can be sure of one thing: The HomeView will not be an easy or pleasant repair when that time comes.”

A representative from Apple did not immediately respond to a request for comment.

iFixit also pointed out that if a HomeView device falls out of warranty, the repair typically costs as much as the $299 smart display itself.

I’m just not sure any potential HomeView users need to worry about the device’s repairability the way they would about an iPhone or Mac.

Smart displays don’t have the same DIY repair needs as the phone in your pocket. There’s no battery to replace, which is one of the most common reasons to open up an iPhone or MacBook. And while a shattered iPhone screen can easily be swapped out for a third-party replacement, no aftermarket alternatives exist for the HomeView’s custom 7-inch display. Since you can only get a replacement screen through Apple anyway, making the device easier to open wouldn’t actually help you fix it yourself.

Plus, smart displays don’t face the same environmental risks as phones and laptops, which are constantly on the move, encounter dust in pockets, accidentally dropped and exposed to potential heat and rain. The HomeView is designed to remain stationary in your home. The need for DIY repairs is simply far less of a concern.

I don’t mean to say iFixit’s teardown was unnecessary. We learned valuable information, including how the speakers and their connectors broke in several ways when iFixit tried to remove them. (The speaker assembly is actually one HomeView component I worry people may need to replace.)

“Embedded speakers are a relatively common source of failure. The under-screen speakers inside the HomeView in particular, more closely resemble laptop speakers than HomePod tweeters,” the iFixit report notes. “As far as laptop and MacBook speakers go, we’ve seen plenty of examples of damage caused by accidents and wear and tear.”

I’ve been testing smart displays and smart speakers since they first hit the market, and none of the devices I’ve tested have developed a blown or faulty speaker. In the HomePod subreddit, I couldn’t find any reports of speaker failures except from people already Frankensteining their Apple speakers with third-party components.

I wouldn’t let the fear of repair difficulties get in the way of buying a HomeView. A bigger concern is the HomeView’s compact 7-inch screen, which feels cramped for watching video, especially compared with the larger displays Amazon has rolled out across its Echo Show lineup.

Our gifting experts are obsessively searching for holiday gifts that are unique, thoughtful and suitable for any budget.

Apple is leaning into AI-powered health tools with the launch of its Apple Health AI Usage Study.

Apple is exploring how people use AI for their health, presumably to build its own AI health coach. On Sunday, it launched the Apple Health AI Usage Study, which could contribute to the next AI health experience Apple builds by measuring the quality of AI health responses, comprehension, and everyday health behaviors, according to a press release.

Apple is conducting the study in collaboration with OpenEvidence, a clinical AI platform widely used by healthcare professionals. The study examines the relationship between conversational AI tools, like chatbots, and the people who use them.

“Insights from this study will help advance the broader scientific conversation and ensure that as technology evolves, we continue building trusted tools that genuinely support people wherever they are on their health journey,” Sumbul Desai, M.D., Apple’s vice president of Health and Fitness, said in the press release.

Also: Apple Watch Series 12 review: Finally, the health tracker I’ve been waiting for

Participants are encouraged to share their HealthKit data and query the health app with questions. The study will also explore how AI tools can best prepare patients ahead of clinical visits. Apple will monitor the AI’s clarity and approachability when providing medical information, and each response or recommendation will be linked to peer-reviewed clinical citations. Responses could be unclear or incomplete, which is why Apple is rolling this out as a study to explore a responsibly designed AI health assistant.

Apple often launches studies for features it would like to develop in the future. For example, many of the hearing health features launched on the AirPods were a direct result of the findings from Apple’s Hearing Study.

Also: Athenahealth patients can ask Claude about their medical records now

The AI usage study comes on the heels of the revamped Health app’s debut, which launches officially next month. It also arrives amid a bevy of AI health coaches, popping up alongside companion health devices. Google launched its AI Health Coach in Google Health Premium last year, and Oura launched a proprietary AI model for women trained on medical standards and research from Oura’s in-house team of board-certified clinicians.

A growing number of Americans are relying on AI for medical advice. A recent survey from Pew Research Center found that 34% of US adults have talked with a chatbot for medical advice. As AI proliferates, that percentage will only increase.

“Patients and clinicians are both turning to AI, but the tools they use are being built and tested in separate worlds,” said Robert M. Wachter, M.D., UCSF’s professor and chair of the Department of Medicine, in the press release.

Apple and other tech companies are building for this new health normal, and the AI usage study indicates that Apple isn’t taking the responsibility lightly.

If you’re interested in participating in Apple’s study, it’s open to 200,000 eligible participants age 21 and older in the US. You’ll need a phone with Apple Intelligence enabled (the iPhone 15 Pro or later), running iOS 26 or later. You can download the study app to learn more and enroll.
