#3146. Scout Motors Is Using AI Earpieces to Train Factory Workers

Our gifting experts are obsessively searching for holiday gifts that are unique, thoughtful and suitable for any budget.

Our expert, award-winning staff selects the products we cover and rigorously researches and tests our top picks. If you buy through our links, we may earn a commission.

The automaker is replacing the instructional binder with an AI voice that walks new hires through hands-on tasks, and it sees the same approach reaching service centers and, eventually, owners' garages.

“AI training” usually refers to instilling artificial intelligence with human knowledge. Scout Motors says it’s been doing the opposite: using AI tools to help hire, onboard and train factory workers, including an AI assistant in an earpiece that guides trainees through tasks as they perform them.

CEO Scott Keogh spoke with CNET during a reporters roundtable at Scout’s still-under-construction factory in Blythewood, South Carolina. Keogh said that rather than “sitting new hires down with an instructional binder and a test,” workers are getting AI-driven, hands-on experience early in a push to make the training more efficient and effective. Meanwhile, the automaker can collect and feed training data back into the system to fine-tune its hiring, training and placement processes.

Keogh described the approach as starting from the work itself. Manufacturing, he said, can be broken down into a handful of fundamental tasks, and the AI system is built to teach each one. He offered parts picking as the simplest example: A worker walks to 12 boxes, pulls 12 parts, confirms they’re in the right sequence and checks them for defects. The AI in the earpiece can guide the worker through that sequence, providing real-time, adaptable instructions.

“We can train that within minutes,” Keogh said. “A worker repeats the cycle about 15 times, getting faster and better each pass, and then moves down the task line to the next skill.”

To my ears, that doesn’t sound like the sort of task you’d need an AI system to help with and, to some extent, Scout’s executives agreed.

However, the automaker’s representatives argued that the new method is far more productive than traditional classroom training — with increasing benefits as the trained tasks and concepts become more complex. Keogh also linked the speed at which the company has seen its newest factory hires become productive with how quickly Scout can ramp up the factory itself.

Scout execs say AI also plays a role in the hiring and onboarding before training begins. Todd Johnson, vice president of manufacturing, said the team feeds new hires’ backgrounds into an AI system, which suggests where each person might fit best: A former forklift driver might be steered toward logistics, someone with no final assembly experience might do better in the body shop and a person with paint shop experience could be placed as a painter.

Again, that sounded a lot like common sense to me. Isn’t that how people were hired before AI? According to Scout Motors’ leadership, the algorithm can potentially identify less obvious connections between skills and tasks that a human might miss, expanding access to jobs for applicants who may not have received traditional manufacturing training, which is important because Scout’s new plant is located in an area that doesn’t have a large pool of local dyed-in-the-wool traditional automotive workers.

To fill the over 4,000 roles that factory will need to reach full speed ahead by 2028, the automaker says it’s hiring from a national pool of applicants. However, executives told me that using AI to consider nontraditional factory workers — citing one hire who worked at the DMV — will allow Scout to identify and place more local applicants and bring fresh ideas to the factory floor.

Ryan Decker, vice president of strategy and brand, called Scout’s AI-forward approach to placement and training “a passion project for the company.” Decker told CNET that Scout’s training AI can tailor instruction to each person rather than delivering the same material to a room of 10 people over 10 days. People learn differently, he said, with different language skills and levels of technical depth.

Decker also said the system is bidirectional. The AI can learn from how each group responds to the training and use that information to modify instruction for the next cohort. Decker thinks that each subsequent batch of workers will be “1% better,” and that after 1,000 repetitions, he expects the AI to be “dialed in and know how to provide information to the people in the most productive way possible.”

Scout says it’s also exploring vision-based AI training, in which the trainee is guided via augmented reality glasses, as the next evolution of the technology. The automaker is also looking to eventually expand the tech for do-it-yourself use by owners at home. I imagine a future where owners can use an Apple Vision Pro or similar device — which would be a pricey investment — to guide themselves through installing a roof rack or performing routine maintenance.

In practice, the next step, according to Scout’s execs, is to scale its AI learning tools beyond the training room and into the actual factory and service centers, where the automaker believes the tech can continue to improve on-the-floor productivity and guide its workers as they advance through their careers.

Decker says the AI can ingest and organize decades of institutional knowledge, making it accessible to workers during and beyond the training process. Scout has been feeding the AI equipment manuals and manufacturing documentation spanning multiple decades, disciplines and countries — what Decker called “hundreds of years of accumulated enterprise know-how” — which the AI earpiece can surface in real time, something he said was near impossible to do before in a world of binders and PDFs.

Scout’s AI-fueled “passion project” arrives amid broader tensions across industries affected by artificial intelligence. Companies are eager for the efficiencies AI promises, while workers worry the same technology could eventually cost them their jobs. Scout’s executives didn’t address that concern directly in this exchange. Keogh framed the payoff in terms of speed — how quickly a new hire can be made productive — leaving the wider workforce conversation for another time.

The latest in a string of bad days for Nvidia

When you purchase through links on our site, we may earn an affiliate commission. Here’s how it works.

If you haven't updated your Nvidia drivers recently, you may want to hold off. A newly discovered bug apparently can damage your PC by writing excessive amounts of data to solid-state drives (SSDs).

The bug was found in the two most recent Nvidia GPU driver updates — specifically 621.14 and 621.24 — for the Nvidia GeForce Game Ready Driver. The 621.24 update was released on November 12.

The bug was discovered by TroubleGrid who reported that the bug causes the NVDisplay.Container.exe to write (save data) far too much information to an Nvidia log file that can degrade the SSD. It can result in as much as 30GB per hour.

The executable already wrote log files before the updates but not that much. SSDs typically take years to degrade, but the excessive data written by this bug can speed up the process causing stuttering and mouse lag.

On Reddit, I've seen a few posts about the bug with users complaining that this is why you never update. "By principle I never ever update my drivers unless there are feature inclusions for let's say a new game I bought," one Redditor said.

Plenty of others agreed with that sentiment, and I'm inclined to say they're correct here.

The other half of the comments split between blaming AI-written code. Before his ouster, CEO Jensen Huang was pushing for Nvidia engineers to use more AI-generated code via chatbots and agents.

Get instant access to breaking news, the hottest reviews, great deals and helpful tips.

Or they were of the belief that Nvidia is purposely killing drives to force customers to pay more for new ones. Several called out Sam Altman and his recent claim that laptop RAM is a "terrible" allocation of a scarce resource.

"I honestly would not be surprised if they are doing this on purpose to kill our NVMe's," wrote a poster.

If we were to put blame on something, at this point, I'd say its AI-fueled incompetence, not AI-fueled greed, though that has led to said stupidity.

The easiest fix is to rollback your graphics card driver to version 621.01, which is the last known patch to lack this bug.

TroubleGrid listed a manual fix that requires you to set the Nvidia Display Container LS service to manual. Though it'll cost you. Basically, this can disable the Nvidia Control Panel and Nvidia App, meaning G-Sync color settings, display scaling, resolution overrides and more will not rock. "Do not disable the service outright if you use G-SYNC or a custom colour profile," the report warns.

If you need a temporary fix, you can stop the service, delete the log file and start again. However, the file will return and continue to grow in size.

If Android Fast Switch works like iPhone Handoff, one eSIM can be quickly switched between two phones.

In iOS 27, Apple announced iPhone Handoff, a networking feature that allows users to switch cell service between two eSIM-enabled iPhones. Text strings in Google’s SIM Manager app suggest the company is preparing a similar feature for compatible Android phones, according to Android Authority.

Code strings include “Use a SIM on two phones,” and note that the feature will be called Fast Switch. Little information is currently available about the feature’s limitations, including which phones or mobile carriers may not be compatible.

Also: Why your USB-C cables look alike, but work differently – and how to tell them apart

On Apple’s side, any iPhone in the US running iOS 27 with a T-Mobile or Verizon-provided eSIM can use iPhone Handoff. AT&T does not currently support iPhone Handoff.

However, the code strings uncovered by Android Authority show that Android’s Fast Switch will work similarly to iPhone Handoff, in that users must be signed in to both devices under the same Google account for the feature to work.

Strings in Google’s SIM Manager app also point to no sharing between two users, so this feature isn’t a way to circumvent carrier fees by adding service to someone else’s phone for the price of one.

If Fast Switch works anything like iPhone Handoff, which it appears it will, one eSIM can be switched between two phones. So, calls, messages, location services, and other information synced to your Apple ID can remain consistent between two devices.

Some third-party apps, like banking, communications, or social media, may also remain consistent across the two phones, depending on the app’s syncing behavior.

Features like Apple’s iPhone Handoff and Google’s Fast Switch are ideal for people who regularly use two phones. Business owners and digital creators may want one phone strictly for business purposes and the other for personal use.

In that case, one person can keep up with two phones without paying for two phone service lines through their carrier. Still, users will incur a fee, as T-Mobile charges $5/month for iPhone Handoff, while Verizon charges $10/month.

#3142. At Scout Motors’ New Plant, Validation of Terra and Traveler EVs Has Begun

Our gifting experts are obsessively searching for holiday gifts that are unique, thoughtful and suitable for any budget.

Our expert, award-winning staff selects the products we cover and rigorously researches and tests our top picks. If you buy through our links, we may earn a commission.

Early preproduction Terra trucks and Traveler SUVs are coming together at the Blythewood Production Center. I got an inside look.

At Scout Motors’ South Carolina Production Center, the automaker’s very first electrified trucks and SUVs are being welded, painted and assembled. The revived American automaker has begun the first validation builds of its upcoming Terra pickup truck and Traveler SUV at the Blythewood plant, but hold your electric horses — final production and customer deliveries are still a little over a year away.

After a period of slow sales, American interest in electric vehicles and hybrids is on the rise, driven by high fuel costs and the steady growth of EV charging infrastructure in 2026. Scout, with its battery-electric and gasoline range-extended powertrains, could have both of those bases covered when it arrives to compete in America’s most popular vehicle classes (trucks and SUVs) in 2028. It’s worth keeping an eye on Scout as it inches toward production.

I donned my hardhat, steel-toe caps and high-vis vest to get an early look inside the plant.

The Volkswagen Group revived the Scout Motors brand (formerly International Scout) in 2022, and in 2024, the public got its first look at the Terra and Traveler concepts. The two were initially revealed as full-electric models with the option to add Scout’s Harvester onboard gasoline generator to boost the range.

However, demand for the extended-range EV configuration was overwhelming — roughly 87% of the 160,000-plus reservation holders selected the Harvester spec over the all-electric version — and Scout pivoted to delivering the EREV first, then following up with the pure battery-electric model later in production.

Both models are expected to start under $60,000, though Scout has not yet confirmed the exact price difference between the Harvester and pure BEV trims.

In early 2024, the automaker broke ground on the Blythewood Production Center, pledging to invest more than $2 billion in the plant and create more than 4,000 local jobs. A year later, Scout announced plans to add a $300 million supplier park to the complex, supporting around 1,000 on-site jobs at parts suppliers.

Today, construction is mostly complete. (Executives told me it’s about 80% to 95% done, depending on how you measure it.) The walls are up, much of the equipment is in place, and the first movement toward full production of the brand’s extended-range EV and, eventually, battery electric trucks and SUVs has begun.

Scout’s manufacturing and production teams have begun building the first validation builds — early-stage preproduction vehicles that allow factory planners to dial in vehicle quality, confirm the accuracy of the engineering and hone the efficiency of the manufacturing and assembly lines.

These aren’t complete vehicles by any stretch, being pulled from the line at various points to check and double-check that the new factory equipment functions properly and that the right parts arrive when and where they’re needed. Executives warned me that, at this point, there would still be inconsistencies as they dial in panel gaps, welds and the application of various coatings, but that Scout expects the process to be dialed in by the time full production starts in late 2027.

I was able to get up close to these validation vehicles, checking out a body-in-white bare chassis in the body shop, seeing various stages of coatings applied to bare metal, and watching workers complete calibration and alignment of lights and sensors in the final assembly area.

Along the way, Scout told me that more than 160 individual parts must come together to form the vehicle’s chassis, a process supported by more than 750 robots and 5,000 weld points. Once up to speed, the factory body shop is designed to produce around 40 vehicles per hour, with pickups and SUVs sharing the same line.

However, while I saw the robotic welding arms and paint sprayers performing their motions to apply color, no vehicles were actually moving through the assembly line. This early in the process, the automaker doesn’t need a continuous flow of validation vehicles, and many of the factory areas — such as the supplier park that will provide the batteries, electric motors and modified VW Group four-cylinder engines for Harvester models — are still under construction.

Additionally, the validation process gives workers hands-on experience, rather than having them learn from mistakes on cars that will reach customers or being confined to a classroom.

As more parts of the factory complete construction and come online, the validation process will encompass more of the vehicle’s construction until the automaker is ready to start building full customer vehicles. Todd Johnson, Scout’s vice president of manufacturing, tells me that validation will continue into 2027 through multiple preproduction phases starting with the Traveler SUV.

The automaker expects the first customer deliveries of the Traveler Harvester to begin in early 2028, followed by the Terra Harvester and, eventually, fully electric versions of both.

#3141. The Peloton Turnaround Story: Here's the Good News, the Bad News, and Where Its Stock Could Go Next

Peloton's revenue has declined significantly over the last five years, led by shrinking exercise equipment sales.

By Anthony Di Pizio – Nov 19, 2026 at 5:00PM EST

10 stocks we like better than Peloton Interactive ›

Peloton Interactive (PTON -5.23%) stock peaked at around $163 in late 2020, which was a whopping 462% increase from its initial public offering (IPO) price of $29. Consumers were buying the company's stationary exercise bikes, treadmills, and other equipment hand over fist at the height of the COVID-19 pandemic to maintain their fitness levels at home while gyms were closed.

But as lockdowns and social restrictions were gradually lifted in 2022, demand for Peloton's equipment crashed. The company quickly found itself in a fight for survival as its losses ballooned into the billions of dollars.

Peloton stock has since plummeted 96% from its peak. However, although equipment sales remain weak, management has made a series of changes to bring the company back from the brink of failure. Here's the good news, the bad news, and whether this might be a buying opportunity for investors.

Peloton's annual revenue peaked at $4 billion in fiscal 2021 (ended June 30, 2021), with equipment sales accounting for $3.1 billion of that total. However, the company's revenue has since declined for five straight years, coming in at $2.4 billion in fiscal 2026 (ended June 30). Equipment sales represented just $770.1 million -- or less than one third -- of the total.

Even partnering with third-party retailers like Amazon, Dick's Sporting Goods, and Costco hasn't been enough to revive Peloton's slumping equipment sales. Simply put, the pandemic triggered a unique, one-off spike in demand that the company hasn't been able to replicate, despite its best efforts.

The bulk of Peloton's revenue now comes from digital subscriptions. There is the connected fitness subscription, which gives equipment owners access to virtual classes and performance tracking tools. Then there is a separate subscription for the company's mobile application, which can be used by fitness enthusiasts who don't own Peloton's equipment. It helps them build workout plans and provides access to certain virtual classes.

Unfortunately, both the connected fitness subscription and the mobile app subscription saw a decline in paying members during the recent fiscal 2027 first quarter (ended Sept. 30), so Peloton is now experiencing a deterioration in sales across both hardware and software.

As a result, Peloton's business is likely to shrink for the seventh straight year, because management is forecasting a 4% decline in revenue during fiscal 2027 overall.

Following Peloton's excellent operating results in fiscal 2021, management positioned the company for more growth by increasing costs. But when that growth failed to arrive in fiscal 2022, Peloton suffered a whopping $2.8 billion net loss at the bottom line, and available cash was quickly running out.

Management proceeded to slash operating costs by 68% between fiscal 2022 and fiscal 2026, and Peloton is now profitable again. It generated a net income of $63.2 million in fiscal 2026, followed by a further $96.2 million in profit during the first quarter of fiscal 2027, after additional cost cuts.

After excluding one-off and noncash expenses like stock-based compensation, Peloton has delivered adjusted (non-GAAP) earnings before interest, taxes, depreciation, and amortization (EBITDA) of $517.7 million over the last four quarters. Simply put, the company is no longer at risk of going under.

If Peloton's revenue continues to decline year after year, the only way it can maintain profitability is by slashing costs even further. But, unfortunately, it will eventually run out of ways to do that -- and every time it pulls money away from areas like marketing, it becomes even harder to generate sales growth. As a result, the company could find itself in a downward spiral in the next few years that will be very challenging to reverse.

Peloton was sitting on over $1.3 billion in cash and cash equivalents as of Sept. 30, so it has some runway to continue testing different strategies to reignite equipment and subscription sales. However, the company is also carrying over $900 million in long-term debt, so it doesn't have an indefinite amount of time to deliver results.

Shrinking businesses tend to destroy shareholder value over time, so I don't think it's a good idea to buy Peloton stock right now, even after its 96% decline. It might be better to wait until the company proves it can deliver consistent revenue growth on an annual basis, because that's the big missing piece in the turnaround story. Until then, more downside in the stock could be ahead.

#3138. Ford Designed Its Fathom EV Battery Pack to Bend in a Crash, for Safety

Our gifting experts are obsessively searching for holiday gifts that are unique, thoughtful and suitable for any budget.

Our expert, award-winning staff selects the products we cover and rigorously researches and tests our top picks. If you buy through our links, we may earn a commission.

Ford is designing the Fathom’s LFP battery to bend in a crash, not be shielded from one — and says the resulting EV will be safer and lighter for it.

Ford’s new LFP battery pack isn’t a fragile electric car component that needs protection. During my visit this week to the automaker’s newly operational battery plant, engineers proudly showed me a video of the battery being crash-tested, the shell and the prismatic cells within bending violently under the force. My jaw practically hit the floor.

Conventional wisdom views an EV battery as a potentially explosive component that, if damaged, can cause catastrophic failure and hours-long fires that are difficult to extinguish. Years of lithium-ion batteries in phones, tablets and laptops taught us that and it’s largely held true for electric cars as well.

So the anxiety is well founded, even if, statistically, EVs are generally as safe as (if not safer than) internal combustion engine vehicles in crash testing and far less likely to catch fire.

Ford dropped that bombshell of a video on me at the end of my tour of its Blue Oval Battery Park outside Marshall, Michigan. However, I was barred from recording or photographing the footage.

The design team’s mantra was “don’t assume a cell must never deform.” For the upcoming Fathom and Ford’s Universal EV platform, or UEV, the pack is designed to carry up to 40% of side-impact forces and is treated as part of the vehicle’s crash structure. The company’s leadership and engineers are confident that the EV won’t catch fire or explode despite the bent cells.

“Traditionally the battery is thought of as payload, a fragile jewel you must protect,” said Vladimir Bogachuk, chief engineer for advanced vehicle structure architecture at Ford. That approach, he said, means heavy bracing and protective structures around the pack. “The battery is not a jewel you must protect,” he said.

Bogachuk (along with every other Ford engineer and executive I spoke with that day) takes a less-is-more stance on the new EV platform. “The best part is no part,” he told me, “and if you have to have a part, it’s pretty much got to serve multiple functions.” And so the engineers set out to remove unnecessary armor and build a battery that serves double duty as an energy reservoir and crash structure.

Without that extra protection, the resulting EV can be lighter and more efficient, with improved driving dynamics. The UEV pack is deeply integrated into the vehicle’s structure: Its top lid is the cabin floor, and the seats bolt directly onto it. The bottom of the pack is the EV’s underbody. A service door beneath the Fathom’s rear seats will provide access to the charging and power electronics for service without the need to drop the pack.

The crash videos showed deformation that would scare me on an older EV, but when I stopped to think, it wasn’t much different from what I’ve seen in conventional car side-impact crash tests. Ford says an impact strong enough to deform the battery would also deform the chassis of a conventional vehicle or traditional EV, so the vehicle would likely be totaled anyway. More importantly, the engineers say the driver would be safe from thermal runaway and fire.

When asked, Ford’s engineers said they don’t believe in a “right chemistry” for every electric vehicle. The UEV platform’s LFP — short for lithium iron phosphate — chemistry, prismatic cells and “jelly roll” construction were chosen for low manufacturing cost, resistance to temperature extremes, suitability for bidirectional energy use and the ability to deform while remaining inert under designed loads and forces.

Other automakers have floated solid-state batteries as a potential solution to battery safety and energy density, but the technology isn’t ready for use in production cars — at least not at the scale and price that Ford needs for the reasonably priced Fathom.

Ford hasn’t stated the LFP pack’s energy capacity, the cell capacity or the number of cells the Fathom’s pack will comprise. Based on a cutaway displayed during my tour, I estimate 90 to 108 individual prismatic cells. The aluminum prismatic cans that enclose the cathode-anode “jelly roll” battery provide structural support and aid thermal dissipation throughout the larger pack.

Wes Thibault, chief engineer for global energy storage systems, described the rigorous validation that the cells and packs underwent to reach the point where they can be trusted to bend like a taco. He told me that Ford has “a dedicated abuse-testing team” integrated with battery design and engineering at every level and stage of the manufacturing process, searching for edge cases and probing the limits of what the chemistry, the cells and full production-spec battery packs can take, from withstanding over 150,000 miles of simulated daily driving to remaining safe and inert in a crash. Along the way, CT scans of the cells offered an inside look at the jelly roll and how it was responding.

Ford’s testing covers structural integrity and load-bearing capability, heat soak from minus 40 to 60 degrees Celsius, IP67 water resistance and humidity cycling, and high-charge and high-discharge tests. For multiaxis vibration, the battery, seats and brackets are strapped to what I can describe only as a giant mechanical bull that shakes the hardware through roll, pitch, yaw and multiple harmonic frequencies. Ford can combine multiple factors in a single test, such as a high-humidity heat soak under vibration during high discharge.

Once the first batch of UEV vehicles are on the road, Ford says it’ll be able to capture real-world data from the fleet to further fine-tune its validation methods for future generations of EVs.

Given how well the first model year of Ford’s Mustang Mach-E‘s batteries have held up after six years and thousands of real-world miles, it’s clear the automaker knows a thing or two about building a reliable battery.

That said, the UEV platform’s LFP chemistry and construction are very different from those of the earlier generation, and the automaker is asking much, much more of the pack than just holding and discharging energy. It’s asking the pack to actively protect the souls onboard in the event of a crash. Testing to failure early and learning from those mistakes quickly is something the engineers I spoke to seem to take very seriously.

This bold, out-of-the-box approach to how the automaker thinks about battery fragility — protecting the souls onboard rather than the “jewel” that is the battery from a potential crash at the end of the vehicle’s life — comes with the promise of more range and efficiency, less weight and more driving fun over the vehicle’s lifetime.

I’m ready to believe. I want EV batteries to be safer and less scary. That promise depends heavily on whether the Fathom’s UEV battery pack is as safe as Ford says it is when it reaches driveways and dealerships in late 2027.

Editors’ note: Antuan Goodwin’s travel costs were covered by Ford. The judgments and opinions of CNET are our own.

The Paramount+ hit thriller finally delivers on the survivors’ harrowing return home across its gripping first eight episodes

When you purchase through links on our site, we may earn an affiliate commission. Here’s how it works.

For five years and three seasons, Paramount’s “Yellowjackets” has been at once enthralling and appalling audiences. As someone who is easily squeamish, I’ll admit that when I first tuned in years ago, I almost abandoned the show altogether, too disturbed by watching teenagers hunt their friends like animals and decapitate corpses to continue.

What eventually roped me in and made it impossible to look away were the stellar performances from the massive ensemble cast and the storytelling that — cliché as it sounds — actually left me on the edge of my seat, peeking out in horror from behind my fingers. Adding to that was “Yellowjackets’” knack for unveiling mysteries that left viewers, myself included, desperate for answers.

Heading into the show’s fourth and final season, though, those strengths become double-edged swords. The major questions that kept audiences hooked for years now demand answers before the series finale. Likewise, the interwoven narrative — jumping between the teenage plane crash survivors stranded in the wilderness and their adult counterparts — has always been an effective tool, but before the end, these timelines need to find a satisfying cohesion.

Having watched the first eight of season 4's 10 episodes, I can safely and somewhat unfortunately say that while “Yellowjackets” satisfies in some areas, it falls short in others — and it doesn’t have much time left to course-correct.

Easily the most compelling aspect of these first eight episodes is the exploration of the team’s return home. For three seasons, audiences knew these traumatized kids — the ones who survived, at least — would eventually make it back, with the adult timeline confirming several names (Shauna, Misty, and Melissa among them).

Prior to season 4, however, “Yellowjackets” had yet to reveal that exact moment of return and its immediate fallout: watching characters who hunted, killed, and ate their friends attempt to slip back into their “normal” lives. While the adult timeline already proved the survivors never truly moved past their ordeal, seeing their parent reunions, the jarring shift in high school social dynamics, and the strange fame that comes with surviving a mass tragedy is precisely what audiences have been waiting for.

Sign up to the weekly Tom's Streaming Guide to stay in the loop with the latest releases and top recommendations across your favorite streaming services. We’ve got you covered with a complete guide on what’s worth watching.

With just two episodes to go, a shocking number of questions remain on the table, raising an obvious concern: has “Yellowjackets” saved too much for an epic finale? Of the many shows met with controversy over their endings, the mind-bending sci-fi series “Lost” is among the most notorious and perhaps the closest comparison to “Yellowjackets” in its approach to mystery and suspense.

Like “Lost,” “Yellowjackets” has spent years building complex mysteries whose reveals appear to be crammed into the final two episodes. In the case of “Lost,” that famously backfired, leaving even dedicated fans frustrated by how questions were answered, the breakneck speed with which some were “resolved,” or the fact that certain mysteries went unaddressed forever.

Based on episodes 1 through 8, “Yellowjackets” season 4 seems to be heading down a very similar path. Several of the show’s most captivating questions haven't just gone unanswered by the end of episode 8, they’ve been largely ignored. Hopefully, this doesn't mean answers are never coming, which would undoubtedly trigger a wave of backlash akin to “Lost.” Even if the finale delivers, it would have been far more satisfying to see this final season deeply flesh out the truth of the wilderness — whether it’s a supernatural force or simply a manifestation of the survivors’ trauma — well before the final curtain.

Ultimately, “Yellowjackets” Season 4 is an exciting final entry that showcases the cast at the top of their game and finally gives audiences a real look at how the survivors reacclimated—or failed to—after nearly two years in the wild. Still, for the final chapter of a show that has captivated viewers for five years, the series has left itself too much ground to cover in too little time.

While heavy narrative exposition was always inevitable in Season 4—especially with so much left unresolved in the adult timeline—what audiences really want heading into the finale are answers, not more questions. With the clock very much ticking, “Yellowjackets” still has to prove it can stick the landing.

"Yellowjackets" season 4 episode 1 is streaming now on Paramount+

#3129. iPhone Duo, One Month Later: I’m Not Ready to End the Love Affair

Our gifting experts are obsessively searching for holiday gifts that are unique, thoughtful and suitable for any budget.

Our expert, award-winning staff selects the products we cover and rigorously researches and tests our top picks. If you buy through our links, we may earn a commission.

After making Apple's foldable my daily companion, I've made peace with some shortcomings while resigning myself to others. Mostly, though, there's been a lot to admire.

One month after getting the iPhone Duo, I’ve stuck to my commitment to keep using it even after publishing my review. Well, mostly.

Apple’s debut foldable has proven to be a practical everyday device, whether I’m streaming movies, texting or getting work done. I’ve grown so accustomed to using it that I sometimes forget how much attention it draws when I pull it out of my pocket, especially given its limited availability and lengthy preorder windows – not to mention its sky-high $1,999 starting price.

Still, there have been times when I’ve reached for the iPhone 18 Pro Max instead for its more advanced camera system, as well as its familiar, straightforward design. The Duo’s cameras pull their weight with casual photography, but while filming social content at F1’s US Grand Prix and chatting with filmmakers at an SFFilm screening, I couldn’t resist going for the best cameras at my disposal on the Pro Max. There are times a conventional slab phone just does the trick – without all the frills and novelty of a folding one.

That hasn’t stopped me from keeping the Duo as my primary device. It’s an enjoyable phone to use, with its compact, palm-sized build and spacious inner display. Plus, as CNET’s ongoing folding test demonstrates, it has a durable build that ensures I can fold and unfold it to my heart’s content.

And if I’m being honest, I kind of love how much of a statement piece it’s become.

The Duo’s versatility has really shown its appeal the more I live with it. I find myself using the 5.4-inch cover screen and 7.6-inch inner display pretty equally, demonstrating the practicality of each.

When I’m on the move, the cover screen suffices for sending texts, responding to emails and checking notifications. Lounging around at home, I’m more inclined to use the larger inner display to endlessly scroll through Instagram or binge YouTube videos.

The matte inner display remains one of my favorite elements. It reduces the appearance of the crease as well as glare, making it easier to see content even outdoors. Yes, the coating can dim the vibrant colors in images and videos, even with the screen’s 3,000-nit peak brightness, and smudges become prominent. But I can live with both of those drawbacks, and a microfiber cloth fixes the latter.

Apple’s phone-tablet hybrid came in clutch when I was on a recent flight and didn’t want to pull out my laptop. Instead, I used the Duo’s split-screen mode to place the Notes app on one half of the screen and an informational video on the other so I could quickly jot down the main points. The Duo has also become my gym buddy; I prop it open on the treadmill so I can watch Magpie Murders on a tablet-like display, then fold it up and toss it in my pocket when I’m done.

Apple Pencil support really helps the Duo feel like a mini iPad, and the matte coating on the inner display adds a satisfying resistance that more closely emulates the feel of writing on paper than a glossy surface. It gives jotting down notes, highlighting book passages and marking up documents a more tactile feel. I’m not much of a doodler, but I imagine that’s fun, too.

The Apple Pencil can magnetically attach to the outer surface of the hinge, though it definitely sticks out, so there’s not really a practical, secure way to carry it around with the Duo (at least not that Apple has shared, but case-makers are sure to cook up a solution). I’m glad the stylus also works on the Duo’s cover screen, though the smaller size and glossy display make that experience slightly less satisfying.

The number of apps optimized for the Duo at launch was relatively small, but it’s steadily increased. I gasped aloud on the train platform one morning while sending an email, realizing Gmail had finally been adapted for the Duo. It’s refreshing to see apps that feel intentional and fill the screen, rather than being awkwardly letterboxed.

Apple said in early November that more than 100,000 apps built for the iPhone Duo were live in the App Store. A week later, that number ballooned to over 200,000 apps. So despite a rather slow start, virtually all apps I regularly use now work seamlessly on Apple’s foldable.

One of my favorite apps on the Duo is Instagram’s Edits. When holding the phone open in landscape orientation, I can view the video timeline and make edits on the right side of the screen while seeing a preview of the video on the left. Rotated to portrait orientation, the layout resembles the interface on a traditional smartphone, but on a larger scale, which is helpful especially for making smaller tweaks.

It’s great to see more apps that don’t just expand to the larger screen, but make meaningful use of the Duo’s design.

As I found during my review, the Duo’s battery life has been pretty good. It consistently lasts through the day, even as I hop between displays. I usually charge my phone at night, but even if I don’t, I know I’ll have some remaining battery in the morning.

For instance, one day I started at 6:30 a.m. with a full battery. After my usual routine of checking emails, texting, scrolling through social media and browsing YouTube throughout the day, my battery was at 55% by 9:12 p.m. The next morning, I woke up with 48% battery, and that charge lasted through a similar routine, along with phone calls, texting and music and video streaming, before the battery finally died at 7:30 p.m.

The Duo has yet to give me a reason to stress about its battery life.

I will acknowledge I’m a tad pretentious when it comes to smartphone cameras. But if I’m documenting an event or photographing my fancy tea sets, I want the best cameras I can get. Unlike the Duo, iPhone 18 Pro models have a telephoto camera, more advanced optical zoom capabilities and larger main-camera sensors.

Most of the time, the Duo’s 48-megapixel wide and ultrawide cameras do the trick just fine. Colors are vivid, details are sharp and images are bright. Videos look good, too, though the 18 Pro Max does a noticeably better job with nighttime footage, which can look more muddy on the Duo. Digital video on the Duo also tops out at 6x, versus 24x on the Pros. Most of the time, though, I’m quite content with what I capture with the Duo’s cameras.

As I noted in my review, the under-display FaceTime camera on the inner screen isn’t great, but I never really take selfies using that camera. It feels much more natural to use the 12-megapixel selfie camera on the cover screen, which serves up sharp photos every time.

The cover screen selfie camera plays a critical role in an update that makes using the Duo even more seamless. In its latest iOS 27.3 developer beta, Apple added an option to unlock the iPhone Duo using the front camera.

In the absence of Face ID, which I have felt rather painfully, this has been a solid workaround, even if it’s not as secure as Apple’s biometric facial recognition and authentication system. You’ll still need to use Touch ID or a passcode when using Apple Pay or accessing passwords, and to unlock the phone after leaving it alone for around 45 minutes. But a win is a win. (You can also unlock the Duo using an Apple Watch, but I don’t have one.)

I’ll admit I still feel a little bashful when pulling out the Duo because of how much attention it drums up, despite being far from the first foldable phone. But its limited availability and hype paired with the unique design make it eye-catching, for better or worse. Using the Duo has led to some fun conversations, whether it’s with a sales associate as I pay for a pastry or with Project Hail Mary directors Phil Lord and Chris Miller, who spotted the phone in my hand during an interview and geeked out over it. That’s been a fun side effect of using Apple’s first foldable in my everyday life.

I’ve been living dangerously without a case; I don’t want anything to detract from the phone’s sleek feel. This is one of those “do as I say, not as I do” moments, as I’d recommend slapping a case on a phone that costs nearly $2,000. I did put a tempered glass screen protector on the cover display to guard against scratches. I can feel its edge against the otherwise flush surface of the phone when I hold it open, but aesthetic sacrifices must be made.

The Duo isn’t perfect, even if I love using this phone. After holding Samsung’s Galaxy Z Fold 8, the iPhone Duo can feel slightly chunky. The Z Fold 8 measures 4.5mm thick when open and 9.7mm when closed. Meanwhile, the Duo is 5.2mm thick when open and 11.3mm when closed. It’s not a huge difference, but it makes me look forward to Apple hopefully slimming down the second-generation version, if and when it comes.

The Duo is also slightly heavier than the Z Fold 8, weighing 254 grams (compared to 201 grams for Samsung’s foldable). I’m always surprised when people remark how heavy the Duo is, but I think the reason I don’t share that sentiment is that I’m accustomed to the iPhone 18 Pro Max, which weighs 249 grams.

When the Duo is open in landscape orientation, I’m glad there’s an option to split the keyboard so it’s easier to type across the wider expanse, but I wish the swipe functionality worked in that configuration, too. It’s a little thing that would make a noticeable difference for those of us who rely heavily on swipe-to-text.

One drawback of the Duo’s compact design is that some existing MagSafe wallets and other accessories won’t stick to the back without awkwardly jutting out. So you might have to invest in some new accessories specifically designed for the Duo.

Until the recent addition of face unlock, the Duo’s biggest drawback was the lack of Face ID. It’s a feature I’d expect on such a premium device, especially given that even the budget-focused iPhone 17E supports it.

Touch ID works reliably on the Duo, but it’s slow compared to fingerprint unlock on the Galaxy Z Fold 8 (which also supports facial recognition). And while the new face unlock capability on the Duo isn’t an exact replacement for Face ID, which is more secure, it helps make accessing the phone’s contents more convenient and in line with the Duo’s modern aesthetics.

I’ve finished my homework: My review is done, and now, so is this one-month follow-up. What’s next?

I’m not sure I’m ready to throw in the towel on Apple’s foldable just yet. The novelty of the iPhone Duo hasn’t worn off, and I’ve become quite used to my passport-size companion. It does just about everything I need, despite some slight imperfections, and it’s fun to use. It’s also amusing to see how people react when they see it in my hand.

So for now, it looks like the Duo will remain my daily driver. Whether the honeymoon phase eventually wears off remains to be seen, but I’m not in any hurry to end this love affair.

#3128. Top Wall Street analysts suggest these 3 dividend stocks for steady income

Energy Transfer is a limited partnership that operates 140,000 miles of pipeline and associated energy infrastructure. With a quarterly cash distribution of 33.75 cents per common unit ($1.35 per unit on an annualized basis), ET offers a yield of 6.8%.

#3127. Goodbye, Gemini Gems: How to use Google’s new Skills – and share them

Our gifting experts are obsessively searching for holiday gifts that are unique, thoughtful and suitable for any budget.

Google is retiring Gemini Gems. Here's what to do to access the same tools as Skills.

Google is replacing Gemini Gems with Skills starting Nov. 17, 2026, and it’s carrying over features that let you share Skills and add files from Google products.

Google has announced that it’s turning Gems, a Gemini feature that lets you create customizable AI chatbots, into Skills, which let you create custom instructions for Gemini. Any Gems you have created will automatically convert, but you can transfer them manually if you want to start using them now.

To help with the transition, Google revealed that two Gems features are moving, too: the ability to share creations and to include Drive, Notebook, and Photos files as part of your Skill’s instructions.

While the Gemini Gems feature is technically going away, any Gems you’ve created aren’t.

If you access the Gems portion of Gemini (since the feature is on the way out, you now have to access this through Settings), you’ll see a message that says “Starting November 17, 2026, we’ll automatically begin migrating all of your Gems to Skills.” (The cutoff date for accessing your Gems will be Dec. 16, 2026. Workspace business, enterprise, and non-profit accounts will get cut off in March 2027, and Workspace education accounts will be cut off in June 2027.)

A Gemini Skill functions much the same as a Gem. You describe specific situations when Gemini should use the Skill automatically and tell Gemini what you want the Skill to do (it’s best to give specific examples of output). Google gives the example of a marketing team sharing a brand-voice skill that references their brand guidelines doc in Drive, or a team lead sharing an onboarding skill based on the team handbook.

The biggest difference is that Gems were standalone chats, while Skills are custom instructions that work in any conversation.

You can create as many Skills as you want, but only 100 can be active at a time.

To get users familiar with Skills, Google is bringing over two features from Gems.

First, you can now share any Skill with other users. When you share a Skill, you can choose whether the other person has permission to edit or view only. To share a Skill, go to the three-bar menu in the top left > Customize > Skills. You can view or change permissions from that screen.

Also: I checked Gemini’s new Memory summary to see what it knew about me – how to see and edit yours

When a Skill is added, Gemini can use it automatically, or you can @mention it in chat to trigger it. One small caveat, though: you can only share Skills through the Gemini web app at the moment, not the mobile app.

Additionally, when you’re creating a Gemini Skill, you can choose to include files of up to 100MB from other Google products like Drive, Photos, and Notebook, along with files from your local device. Gemini will reference these files every time the Skill runs and update in real time, Google says. These features existed with Gems; Google is just moving them to Skills to make the new feature more comparable.

#3126. Microsoft says its new AI coding model rivals Claude Opus 5.5 at 5% of the cost

Our gifting experts are obsessively searching for holiday gifts that are unique, thoughtful and suitable for any budget.

Microsoft announced two new AI models at Ignite 2026 that promise impressive performance for much lower cost. They could reshape its relationship with OpenAI and Anthropic for good.

At today’s Microsoft Ignite 2026 keynote, the company introduced two new frontier AI models built for what the company describes as “everyday” coding tasks. But there’s a bigger story: what these models might mean for Microsoft’s AI costs and its dependence on OpenAI.

Microsoft claims its MAI Code 2 model shows 96% of Claude Opus 5.5 performance at 5% of Opus 5.5’s price.

Also: Microsoft wants to put a dollar value on AI’s work – but can you trust the math?

Microsoft says MAI Code 2 offers comparable performance to GPT-6.1 Sol or Opus 5.5 at a fraction of the cost. Microsoft’s Code 2 Flash model is comparable to the lower-end GPT-6 Luna and Claude Haiku 5.5, also at considerably lower cost.

This doesn’t mean that those of us who pay for $100/month subscriptions will suddenly get the equivalent for five bucks. Instead, these are usage-based metrics based on API usage.

It’s also important to understand that the benchmarks are all Microsoft-provided. Performance numbers may well differ once the models undergo independent performance tests.

Throughout Satya Nadella’s keynote, Microsoft showed slides referencing a wide range of foundation models that are intended to work with Copilot and other Microsoft offerings. Microsoft famously has a multi-billion-dollar investment in OpenAI dating back to 2023, and has built many of its products and services around OpenAI intellectual property.

But now, Redmond is benchmarking its internally built models against Anthropic and OpenAI offerings, and also touting that it’s integrating these new models as optional choices for GitHub Copilot, Microsoft 365, and Fabric.

Also: 75% of developers I surveyed prefer Claude Code over Codex

One thing that Nadella made clear in today’s keynote is how central AI is becoming in everything Microsoft does. Nearly all of those AI operations previously involved the company paying some token fees back to the frontier model providers or customers doing the same thing.

But with high-performing models of its own, Microsoft may become substantially less dependent on outside model providers, especially for the incredible volume of fairly basic and routine AI requests that occur across the company’s vast product line.

If you think back over the history of agentic work models like ChatGPT Work and Claude Cowork, you may recall that they originated as agentic coding tools. As users adopted the coding harnesses in Claude Code and OpenAI Codex to off-label productivity applications, the AI companies noticed and packaged work-centric agentic tools that were more non-programmer-friendly.

Also: I let ChatGPT Work and Claude Cowork loose on my files – only one made me nervous

There’s a lot of similarity between a coding agent and a work agent, including understanding a complex environment, using tools to change things, and producing reliable results. Coding turns out to be a very good environment for developing and testing these capabilities, particularly because code output is highly measurable. Coding agents are effective training grounds for non-coding work agents.

This becomes really interesting in today’s announcement. Along with Code 2 and Code 2 Flash, Microsoft announced MAI Work Flash, which it describes as having been derived from Code 2 Flash. Work Flash can help generate formulas in Excel, work with documents and instructions in Word, track decisions and extract useful information from Teams, and more.

Think about the level of intelligence these tasks are demanding from the AI models. Not that much. As long as the models are good enough, they’ll be good enough.

If Microsoft can reduce its expenses and use reliable models at a much lower price, the company itself will be able to save quite a bit of money across its entire software economy, while at the same time maintaining a deeper level of vertical integration and, therefore, control.

Let’s run some hypothetical numbers. Let’s say a company is spending $0.01 per AI request, which, with these new models, can drop down to $0.001 per request.

Also: Want to try ChatGPT Wallet? Read OpenAI’s liability disclaimer very carefully first

A company with a daily inference cost of a million dollars (a company like Microsoft, for example) could drop that daily cost to about $100,000. Add that up across a year, and the change in models could save $325 million annually.

A million here, a million there. Pretty soon, you’re talking real money.

There’s no direct evidence that Microsoft is trying to produce replacement models for the frontier providers’ offerings. But it is an interesting and compelling story if we look at Microsoft developing its own engines for the software it sells.

Microsoft says the numbers it’s reporting at are using a 50% introductory discount. That’s why I measured against $0.001 per request instead of $0.0005 per request above.

Benchmark selection could be cherry-picking. The numbers are impressive. But as we all know, there are lies, damned lies, and benchmark results. I’m fairly sure Microsoft isn’t padding these numbers too much, because it benefits from the new models more than even its own customers, but still. It’s an open issue.

The company also described clearly that these new models are not designed to handle the most challenging agentic and research workloads. You’re probably not going to use them to solve a decades-old mathematics challenge. But you’re very likely to use them to reformat your PowerPoint.

Speaking of reformatting your PowerPoint, Microsoft also emphasized that these new models did unusually well on visualization assignments. That’s a very good fit for not only UI design challenges but also graphics and slide production.

#3125. Grand Theft Auto 6 Is Out. Here’s How to Make Room on Your Console

Our gifting experts are obsessively searching for holiday gifts that are unique, thoughtful and suitable for any budget.

Our expert, award-winning staff selects the products we cover and rigorously researches and tests our top picks. If you buy through our links, we may earn a commission.

You can make space on your console for GTA 6 a few different ways.

The wait is over. Grand Theft Auto 6 is out, and it is massive. The game is 212 GB, which means it takes up about half of the storage space on my Xbox Series S. The company announced that GTA 6 is available to stream via Xbox Cloud Gaming without downloading it to your console. However, cloud streaming GTA 6 might affect the game’s performance and relies heavily on a strong internet connection. To avoid those issues, I plan on downloading the game.

If you’re like me and are excited to play GTA 6 but don’t have much storage space, you have a few options: delete games, upgrade your console’s hard drive and streaming the game. Here’s what you should know about these options.

The simplest and cheapest way to free up space on your console for Grand Theft Auto 6 is to delete files and other games, which is what I’ll be doing. Uninstalling games is a good choice for folks who plan on spending a lot of time with GTA 6 and don’t intend to juggle different games. Rob Nelson, who oversees Rockstar North with Aaron Garbut, told The New York Times that he had an 80-hour playthrough of the game in February, so you can easily stay immersed in Grand Theft Auto’s state of Leonida.

You may not need to delete much – uninstalling a game like Call of Duty alone could free up nearly 315 GB, giving you enough digital storage for GTA 6. Since deleting files is almost instantaneous, you can quickly reclaim hard drive space. Because you don’t need to buy additional storage, you’ll also save a lot of money – storage prices are through the roof at the moment.

Ultimately, deleting games is a great option if you don’t want to spend any additional money or you don’t mind redownloading games later.

If you plan on hopping between GTA 6 and other games, or you don’t want to delete many of your downloaded titles, you can upgrade your console’s storage. Buying storage is more expensive than deleting files from your console, but benefit from being able to seamlessly hop between Grand Theft Auto 6 and Call of Duty or Madden.

You can use internal or external storage for your console, but you might have to move files between your internal and external storage to launch games. An internal hard drive lets you seamlessly play games. Xbox consoles rely on proprietary expansion cards from Seagate or SanDisk that plug into your console for additional storage. The PlayStation 5 uses M.2 solid-state drives, which are installed alongside the PS5’s built-in storage, and CNET’s David Carnoy recommends the Lexar NM 790 as a fast SSD with a straightforward installation process.

There shouldn’t be any performance, quality or load-time differences between running games from installed storage expansion devices versus your console’s internal storage. Both expansion cards and SSDs can be expensive, especially when compared with deleting games.

You could also use an external hard drive to expand your storage, which can be cheaper than buying expansion cards and internal SSD upgrades – you may even have a compatible USB external drive sitting around that you can use. However, there are caveats around what games can and can’t be played directly from external HDDs.

For Xbox consoles, some older Xbox, Xbox 360 and Xbox One titles can be stored and played from external HDDs. But games optimized for Series X/S consoles can only be stored on HDDs and must be moved back to your internal drive to play. Similarly, the PlayStation 5 only lets you store PS5 games on external HDDs, while you can store and run PS4 games from external drives.

Therefore, using an external HDD requires playing digital musical chairs, moving current-gen games back and forth between your external hard drive and internal console storage in order to play them. The LaCie Rugged SSD4 earned a CNET Editors’ Choice Award and could be a good option. If its price tag scares you, the Western Digital P10 offers more storage at a more economical price point.

Rockstar announced that GTA 6 is available to stream on the Xbox consoles – no download required – via Xbox Cloud Gaming, with some quality and time limitations. You’ll need to buy either an Xbox Game Pass plan or Cloud Gaming hours. Folks who don’t want to delete games or upgrade their console storage can stream GTA 6, but you’ll need an Xbox One or Series X/S console, you won’t get the highest visual quality and you will have to pay for more playtime hours if they run out. Streaming GTA 6 could help budget-conscious gamers who don’t want to upgrade from Xbox One consoles or who don’t have the allotted storage space on their devices.

Normally, you can stream many games on PCs, mobile devices and TVs or streaming devices using Xbox Cloud Gaming or Game Pass, but Grand Theft Auto 6 is limited to the Xbox One, Series S and Series X. Additionally, GTA 6 streaming quality is capped at Series S graphical settings. So if you have a Series X, consider deleting games or upgrading your storage to run the game locally with better graphics.

While you’ll need to install the full game on your console first, remote play for Xbox and PlayStation consoles lets you stream GTA 6 to other devices, like your phone, tablet, streaming device or TV.

If you’re willing to pay a little more for the convenience of having multiple games ready to play at a moment’s notice, Xbox expansion cards or an internal SSD for a PS5 are your best options. If you want a cheaper option and don’t mind moving game files around, an external hard drive could be for you. If you have Xbox Game Pass or Xbox Cloud Gaming, you could stream the game to your console without needing more storage space. However, the cheapest option is to delete games from your internal storage and redownload them later, which can be time-consuming.

I chose the cheapest option and deleted a few games from my Xbox. I’m not planning on leaving GTA 6 any time soon.

Most of the conversation around iOS 27 was centered on Apple’s upgraded, AI-powered Siri, which brings deeper on-screen awareness and smarter multi-step actions. The catch is that Apple Intelligence requires an iPhone 15 Pro or newer, leaving anyone holding onto an older compatible handset locked out of the headline feature.

Scammers frequently rely on high-pressure calls and spoofed texts to trick you into wiring funds or surrendering credentials. Introduced in iOS 27, Impersonation Risk Detection serves as Apple’s built-in defense against this social engineering, and it works without requiring Apple Intelligence.

The system monitors on-device interaction patterns and behavioral cues during high-stakes actions without reading your personal messages, emails, or photos. If you attempt a large transfer or sensitive account change under signs of coercion, your iPhone flags the event and directs supported banking apps to require secondary verification before funds can leave your account.

Launch the Camera app, tap the six-dot icon and hit Edit in the top-left corner. From there, tap any highlighted tools you want kept within thumb’s reach, remove shortcuts you rarely touch using the minus badge, and tap Done.

Even better, iOS 27 saves separate pinned layouts per shooting mode, allowing you to tailor your quick-access toolbar individually for Photo, Portrait, Video, Cinematic, Slow-Mo, and Time-Lapse.

Apple’s translucent Liquid Glass design has remained one of iOS’s most polarizing visual shifts since its debut, particularly when semi-transparent menus sit over bright or busy wallpapers. Rather than forcing a one-size-fits-all look, iOS 27 introduces a dedicated precision slider so you can tailor how much transparency appears across your system interface.

Open Settings, tap Appearance, and select Liquid Glass to find the new control. Sliding the toggle to the left preserves the full see-through glass aesthetic, while moving it to the right applies a heavier, tinted backdrop that makes buttons and text significantly easier to read at a glance.

A live preview window sits directly above the slider so you can test the contrast before locking in your preferred look.

#3123. Anthropic Jumped 17% on its Opening Day. Here's How That Ranks Among Big Tech IPOs

Anthropic's first day is in the books. Did investors learn anything?

By Jeremy Bowman – Nov 19, 2026 at 5:23PM EST

10 stocks we like better than Anthropic ›

Anthropic's (ANT +17.07%) IPO is in the books.

The AI lab sold a record $81.3 billion worth of stock in the offering and finished its first trading day up 17%. A whopping 840 million shares changed hands, equal to roughly $80 billion dollars.

But are the first-day results meaningful? Let's take a look at how the Anthropic debut compares to other prominent tech IPOs.

Of the five most memorable tech IPOs of the last five years, Anthropic ranks third in the biggest gain, closely behind SpaceX, and its 17% gain is in line with the 2026 average first-day IPO gain of 15%-19%.

Anthropic's IPO closely resembles SpaceX's in terms of capital raised and total valuation, and SpaceX received perhaps even more hype.

Of the group, SpaceX seems like the best analog here, as that stock has also evolved into an AI champion and claims a similarly massive market.

Since its initial pop, SpaceX has been volatile, but now trades roughly equal to its IPO price of $135.

Dario Amodei. Image source: Getty Images.

Of the stocks on the list above, Meta has had the best long-term performance, up close to 2,000% since its IPO, though the stock initially struggled. Meta stock, then Facebook, did not get the usual opening-day pop, and the stock was even down by roughly 50% after its first month, as investors worried about its transition to mobile.

Uber struggled through its first few years, and is still underperforming the S&P 500. Its initial sell-off and decline in the subsequent weeks showed that investors thought it was overvalued and worried about its business model, which was deeply unprofitable at the time.

Alibaba has also struggled since its IPO, despite its initial pop, due to a regulatory crackdown, broader investor skepticism toward China, and weak consumer spending.

Based on the group above, there's no correlation between first-day performance in an IPO and longer-term performance, as the initial hype around the opening-day pop often fades.

The good news for Anthropic investors is that the general underperformance of IPOs over the first few years doesn't tend to apply to large companies, as the average performance is weighed down by more speculative listings.

The stock is likely to be volatile in the coming days and weeks as investors better assess the company's prospects and react to new developments in AI, which is changing with concerns about funding, political pressure on data centers, the resignation of Nvidia's Jensen Huang, and falling token prices, which have led to some bearishness around Anthropic.

The next milestone for an IPO is typically the lock-up expiration, which allows insiders to sell their shares. Anthropic’s will come in 180 days and will allow 3.7 billion shares to be sold. In the meantime, we're likely to get the company's fourth-quarter earnings report sometime in February.

From here, Anthropic could replace Nvidia as the avatar for AI, and the stock is likely to move with broader AI sentiment. At a time when that sentiment seems to be rapidly deteriorating, Anthropic's performance will be the biggest test yet for the AI sector.

#3122. Microsoft wants to put a dollar value on AI’s work – but can you trust the math?

Our gifting experts are obsessively searching for holiday gifts that are unique, thoughtful and suitable for any budget.

With Agent 365 Business Analytics, Microsoft could reshape enterprise spending, but there's a critical difference between estimated value and money saved.

We all know AI can get expensive. But does that expense result in real business value? That’s the trillion-dollar question Microsoft aims to answer with today’s introduction of Agent 365 Business Analytics.

Also: Microsoft says its new AI coding model rivals Claude Opus 5.5 at 5% of the cost

Earlier this year, Microsoft introduced Agent 365, its tool for tracking agents the way an HR department would normally track human employees. With Agent 365 Business Analytics, Microsoft is attempting to build an accounting system for AI labor. The system attempts to calculate the economic value of the work performed by agents compared with what the agents cost, and then provide a return on investment estimate.

If it works, this is some very cool stuff. Microsoft is trying to map labor-market economics onto AI usage data to create value estimates.

Also: Work IQ is Microsoft’s big bet on agent-first enterprise IT, and I have questions

To do so, it uses real labor-costing information, including data from the US Bureau of Labor Statistics, the O*NET database from the US Department of Labor, and its own LinkedIn Occupational Graph.

This data, along with data gathered from Agent 365, is aggregated into analysis intended to answer:

The goal is to provide a comprehensive picture of AI spend against value produced.

Software accounting is long established and straightforward. We measure subscription fees, cost per seat, compute costs, burden costs (like floor space and other infrastructure), and more. But AI work doesn’t fit that model, making it very hard to quantify value.

Instead, Agent 365 Business Analytics measures cost both relative to human labor and in terms of technological expense. For example, it might look at a task and determine how much human effort that task would normally take, and then price that effort based on prevailing common labor rates.

Then, it might factor in how much of the task was actually done by a human vs. how much was contributed by an AI, along with the estimated value of the AI’s contribution. Then it mixes in the actual AI processing cost (whether in subscriptions, tokens, on-premises infrastructure, and cloud support).

Also: These Claude Enterprise features let you track AI ROI – what’s new

What comes out is a hybrid labor estimate that combines human contribution, human-replacement savings, AI costs, and then potentially AI savings over human costs. It sounds positively Orwellian. But the bottom line is that companies really haven’t been able to understand the AI bottom line.

There’s a catch. All these numbers are estimates. In its blog post, Redmond specifically says, “Assisted hours are a directional estimate of work AI helped complete, not measured time saved or financial return.”

In other words, what Agent 365 Business Analytics estimates might not actually line up with real-world experience or expenses. It’s also possible that AI work might have been assigned because there was AI to do the work, not that the AI was saving company labor costs with every token processed.

In other words, Microsoft may be able to tell you the economic value of AI-assisted work, but it can’t demonstrate definitively that the company saved any real money.

Also: 5 reasons your company needs a chief AI officer in 2026

I find it particularly telling that this is from the company that makes PowerPoint. Because now, with Agent 365 Business Analytics, it’s entirely possible that you could produce economic dashboards that look really, really impressive, but are entirely irrelevant to real life.

That’s not to say the product is useless. But it does go to the idea that you will have to be quite disciplined in how you interpret the results and how much stock you put in them for decision-making. It is one source of possible truth, not the source of absolute truth.

Microsoft has been investing for decades to build out the core infrastructure of enterprise computing. AI isn’t any different when it comes to the company’s overall mission.

With Agent 365 and the company’s related offerings, Microsoft wants to help you:

This means the company doesn’t necessarily have to provide you with the AI model to help you run your enterprise. With integration with offerings from OpenAI, Anthropic, Salesforce, Google, Databricks, Snowflake, and others, the company doesn’t even have to provide the apps or SaaS capabilities.

But if it can get in there and manage your plumbing, help you control costs, and be the HR operation for your AI workforce, Microsoft could own a central piece of your business’s operations.
