#3121. Black Friday Sales Are Days Away, but Most US Adults Aren’t Waiting, CNET Finds

Our gifting experts are obsessively searching for holiday gifts that are unique, thoughtful and suitable for any budget.

Our expert, award-winning staff selects the products we cover and rigorously researches and tests our top picks. If you buy through our links, we may earn a commission.

Over one-third have already started holiday shopping, but November's sales could yield big savings.

Even though early holiday sales started months ago, shopping your wish lists during Black Friday and Cyber Monday sales may be worth the wait if you’re one of the few planning to shop November sales. It’s the time to save money on most tech devices. But holiday shopping could look different for US adults juggling smaller budgets and shopping frustrations.

CNET’s annual holiday shopping survey shows that 27% of US adults plan to start holiday shopping in November and 17% plan to shop during sales. However, US adults will be juggling a smaller tech budget of $808. That’s $123 less than CNET’s survey findings last year.

Finding savings is paramount to staying within your price range this year, but how can you spot a good deal when nearly every retailer is having a sale? CNET experts weighed in on US adults’ holiday shopping plans and shared expert advice to score the best Black Friday and Cyber Monday deals on must-haves.

CNET found that 27% will plan or start their holiday shopping this month, with 17% of November shoppers planning to shop holiday sales, like Black Friday and Cyber Monday.

The big question is whether the sales are worthwhile. CNET’s director of commerce content, Russell Holly, says it comes down to when you find a deal on a must-have item.

“The best time to buy is the moment you see something you want on an actual discount, because increased prices can come at any time,” Holly said.

Holly says even steep discounts aren’t lowering prices as much as before, but the right deals may make you reconsider. You just have to know where and when to shop for tech devices.

For example, Black Friday is usually the best time to buy electronics, including TVs and robot vacuums, with the biggest deals lasting from Black Friday to Cyber Monday.

CNET’s senior laptops editor, Matt Elliott, says if you’re planning to buy a new laptop during holiday sales, look for discounts at Amazon, Best Buy and vendor sites like Dell, HP and Lenovo.

“These retailers and companies are constantly rotating discounts on laptops, and these sales can save you hundreds of dollars. So, it’s worth tracking the price of a laptop you want and buying it when it dips,” said Elliott.

Black Friday and Cyber Monday are also a good time to buy the latest wearables, said CNET’s wearable expert, Vanessa Hand Orellana.

“For Black Friday, all the heavy wearable hitters tend to go on sale: Google, Samsung, Oura, Garmin and Apple,” said Orellana. However, if you don’t need the latest tech, you can find some of the best deals on last year’s tech at third-party retailers, like Best Buy and Walmart. And many of the previous-gen models share the same features as the newest ones, said Orellana.

CNET’s deals team spends hours making sure sales are legitimate — not just a fake price drop. And in the coming weeks, they’ll track deals on devices like laptops, headphones, wearable devices and smart home gadgets, plus alternatives to more costly tech, to help you determine what’s worth buying now or later.

You can also check an item’s price history to see if you’re getting the best deal by using price trackers like CamelCamelCamel and comparing prices across retailers before buying. But as Holly noted, if you want to upgrade your personal devices, don’t wait. Look for the best price you can find and buy it right away. Otherwise, prices may go up while you wait.

Last year, CNET found that US adults planned to spend an average of $931 on holiday shopping. This year, shoppers are planning to spend less.

On average, they expect to spend $808 on holiday shopping. That’s $123 less than last year. Some generations plan to spend more, such as millennials, who anticipate an average holiday shopping outlay of $1,074. Boomers will spend around half that amount — $582.

Higher everyday living costs could explain why holiday budgets are lower.“Everything else being more expensive means less left over for gifts,” said Holly. “There’s very little indication that component prices are going to come back down anytime soon, so if you’re hoping for the kinds of prices you saw even two years ago, I would say you’re going to be waiting quite a while.”

Balancing holiday gifts and everyday basics on your usual income can be a lot to handle. Now’s the time to set holiday expectations, including a budget and a list of must-haves, along with more affordable options that still meet your needs.

Then keep checking prices and deals from your trusted retailers and be prepared to buy when you spot good savings. Most importantly, try to avoid using credit cards and buy-now, pay-later plans that can lead to debt. The Federal Reserve’s recent rate hike held rates elevated, which means borrowing costs will remain high and make debt more expensive through higher credit card and loan interest rates.

CNET found that 73% of shoppers plan to buy tech products or services this season, but what most US adults plan to buy and how much they plan to spend may surprise you.

Thirty percent of shoppers plan to purchase toys, and 25% plan to buy kitchen items, such as air fryers and cookware. But shoppers don’t plan to buy as many personal electronics and home entertainment products. Only 20% plan to buy headphones or earbuds, and even fewer plan to buy video games for consoles (18%) or laptops and TVs (11%). More shocking is that only 13% plan to buy phones. We’ve seen prices increase across popular tech devices and brands due to the RAM shortage, which has led to low supply and high demand for memory chips.

Some of the latest releases cost way more than the average $808 most US adults plan to spend. For instance, the $2,000 iPhone Duo alone costs even more than the average $1,704 that millennials plan to spend on tech this holiday season. And less costly phones are still beyond holiday budgets, like the $1,200 iPhone 18 Pro Max, and even the iPhone 18 Pro is $1,200. Trade-in offers and sales can help lower that cost if you’re planning to upgrade, but shop around and compare deals before buying.

Increased prices may make you reconsider whether to stick with your current model or upgrade, but remember, you have options.

“If the current laptop works well enough, upgrading can either be viewed as a luxury purchase for later or shifted to buying used or refurbished models to save extra,” Holly said.

You may also consider a slightly older model of the device you’re looking for. It could still have all of the features you need, but cost less. Another money-saving option is to consider refurbished tech that’s in excellent or good condition from a certified refurbished retailer. You may still notice some price increases due to demand, but it could still cost less than the newest models.

Most US shoppers (84%) expect the holiday shopping season to come with a few hurdles this year. Forty-three percent are concerned about deceptive pricing practices, such as retailers raising original prices before discounting them for a sale. Others are concerned about deals selling out immediately because of low stock or automated buying bots (39%).

But if you’re more worried about fake deals or sales being a money grab by retailers, Holly said that historically, there have been some great sales ahead of the holidays. It’s still best to do your research before buying to make sure you’re getting a deal by comparing retailer prices before and after announced sales and using price tracking tools, like CamelCamelCamel. Heads up that many retailers, like Amazon, have flash sales with specific times of deeper discounts, and you’ll need to act fast, so it’s best to plan your holiday shopping now.

“The best thing anyone can do ahead of a shopping event is prepare,” said Holly. “Find your favorite price tracker tool before the event starts, have a general idea of what you’re looking to buy and be sure to keep an eye out for bigger discounts when you bundle things together.”

CNET commissioned YouGov Plc to conduct the survey. All figures, unless otherwise stated, are from YouGov Plc. The total sample size was 2,615 adults, of whom 1,552 were interested in purchasing consumer tech products or services this winter holiday season. Fieldwork was undertaken Sept. 3-6, 2026. The survey was carried out online. The figures have been weighted and are representative of all US adults (aged 18 and older).

#3120. This Beaten-Down Semiconductor Stock Could Soar in 2027

Broadcom’s custom AI chip business is booming, but the market is pricing the stock as if it isn’t.

By Prosper Junior Bakiny – Nov 19, 2026 at 5:25PM EST

The semiconductor industry has been at the center of the ongoing artificial intelligence (AI) revolution, but several market leaders have underperformed this year. One of them is Broadcom (AVGO -2.09%), a semiconductor specialist whose shares have declined by 4% year to date, while the S&P 500 is up by 10%. Broadcom has encountered some issues, but in my view, the market is severely underestimating the company's prospects. Here's why Broadcom could be a winner in 2027.

First, let's review Broadcom's role in the AI value chain. The company designs application-specific integrated circuits (ASICs), which, as their name suggests, are custom AI chips tailored to handle specific workloads, such as training or running AI models. Specialization can improve these custom chips' performance per watt and reduce computing costs, sometimes making them more cost-efficient than market-leading GPUs (graphics processing units).

Broadcom is one of the leaders in the ASIC market and has attracted business from several of the most prominent AI companies. The list includes Anthropic (ANT +17.07%), Alphabet (GOOG -2.93%) (GOOGL -3.46%), and Meta Platforms (META -3.27%). The company's financial results have been strong. However, the company's guidance has been somewhat disappointing in recent quarters, weighing on its stock price.

Further, Broadcom's AI semiconductor business is growing much faster than its higher-margin infrastructure software segments, which could lead to lower gross margins in the medium term. Add that to the fact that investors are still worried about the cyclicality of the semiconductor industry, and it's not too difficult to understand why Broadcom's shares haven't performed well this year. But the stock could bounce back in 2027.

Broadcom's guidance for the next two fiscal years looks strong. During fiscal year 2027, the company expects $115 billion in AI semiconductor revenue. Note that the tech leader has generated $89.1 billion in revenue over the trailing-12-month period across the entire business. For its fiscal year 2028, it expects AI semiconductor revenue to reach $230 billion.

The market has already factored that in, but Broadcom could surprise Wall Street. Several ongoing projects may reinforce Broadcom's position in the custom AI chips industry, potentially helping the company sign more long-term agreements. For instance, Broadcom is on track to deliver three generations of Meta's MTIA custom chips by the end of 2027.

Meta is pouring small fortunes into its AI ambitions and may extend its agreement with Broadcom as their current partnership continues to bring value to both companies. We can also point to the Anthropic (ANT +17.07%) IPO as another boost to Broadcom's business.

The company behind the Claude LLM (large language model) has contracted for billions in AI chips from Broadcom, and its agreement is mostly non-cancellable.

We may also see an expanding relationship between Broadcom and Anthropic, as the latter is planning a massive AI infrastructure build-out, and access to additional capital from its IPO will help fund some of it. Broadcom also has an agreement with OpenAI, the company behind ChatGPT, which arguably started the ongoing AI revolution. We don't know when OpenAI will go public, but it may well happen next year, according to reports.

An OpenAI IPO may also boost Broadcom's business for the same reasons that the Anthropic IPO might. Broadcom's AI semiconductor revenue guidance isn't set in stone, and, provided it signs more deals, which is likely in my view, the company could increase it. And beyond 2027, Broadcom's outlook appears strong if the AI industry continues to expand rapidly, as some projections suggest.

Meanwhile, Broadcom is trading at reasonable levels. The company's shares are trading at 18.5x forward earnings, versus an average of 17.6x for information technology stocks. Given Broadcom's position in the custom AI chips market, its shares look attractive right now. It might be a good idea to buy the stock before 2027.

Speaking of trust, however, Microsoft noted that “Autopilot runs on the identity, security, and compliance foundation IT already uses,” and that “each Autopilot has its own Microsoft Entra Agent ID and a named manager,” meaning IT can block it as needed.

“Its sign-ins and actions are logged under its own name, so security teams have a clear audit trail. Powered by Work IQ, it understands how your organization works within existing permissions,” Microsoft said.

The company added that employees will soon “be able to bring their personal Autopilot into Workspaces” as well. The feature is also available in Frontier.

Nadella also announced a few other productivity features, including a “command center” called Today that spans email, calendar, meetings, tasks, and threads in Teams. Currently in private preview in Outlook and the Copilot app, it includes a personalized briefing and a feed of priorities that updates throughout the day.

“The draft is written and ready for you to edit; the schedule change is already proposed; and the forgotten follow-up is waiting for you to send it, complete with context so you can catch up quickly,” Microsoft said of the feature, which sounds like an agentic briefing-cum-morning-assistant.

Also: Nearly 70% of workers use AI regularly now – but many get no time to upskill

Microsoft also announced that Home, now generally available, unifies Chat and Cowork into a singular starting point. That’s similar to Anthropic’s recent consolidation of its chat and agentic Cowork offerings, demonstrating an overall trend toward simplification in workplace AI.

While more companies are finally starting to see a return on their AI investment, agents are still expensive and can quickly rack up costs when unsupervised.

Microsoft announced a few tools to track this at Ignite: Agent 365 Business Analytics and Agent 365 Cost Management.

Also: Microsoft wants to put a dollar value on AI’s work – but can you trust the math?

Agent 365, which Microsoft announced last year, is the company’s observability platform. Microsoft said Business Analytics, in Frontier Public today, provides insights on what a company is spending on AI and why, and where it’s paying off, as well as forecasts future costs. In a demo during the keynote, Microsoft showed how admins can see when specific agents’ costs have spiked recently and what (human) employee to notify as a result.

“It starts with a new way to measure your investment: in work completed, not simply tokens,” Microsoft said. “It analyzes the tasks, how long that work typically takes a person, and the share Cowork performed, providing a sophisticated view of the hours your intelligence supports and what the work is worth.”

Cost Management lets IT see where teams are using AI down to the model.

“Leaders can set spending policies, limits, and proactive alerts and control which models are available,” Microsoft said. Anthropic released a similar tool last month, though it was focused more on making seats as efficient as possible on Teams and Enterprise plans.

As temperatures drop, our lawns often show signs of wear and tear from battling the elements. Whether dealing with patchy growth, damaged areas, or waterlogged soil, we still need to give our yards extra lawn care for the harsh winter months ahead.

Perhaps one of the most important gardening tasks for healthy lawn growth is applying fertilizer. However, given the cooler conditions, is it too late to fertilize my lawn before winter?

To answer my question, I called on the gardening experts to answer this question — and offer their top tips and tricks. So before you prep your lawn fertilizer, here’s what you need to know.

According to experts, you can fertilize your lawn before winter — as long as it’s completed by mid-November at the latest.

“If you are looking to fertilize your lawn before winter, I would recommend you do this no later than the middle of November, as your grass is becoming dormant and growth is slowing around this time, so it is best to fertilize beforehand,” advises Craig Wilson, co-founder and gardening expert at Gardeners Dream.

While fertilizing is commonly associated with warmer weather, cold-weather lawn care relies on specialized formulas.

“Make sure to use a low-nitrogen fertiliser that features high-potassium levels, as this will help to protect your lawn better in the cold weather,” adds Wilson.

Get instant access to breaking news, the hottest reviews, great deals and helpful tips.

Fall fertilization supports stronger root systems, thicker turf, and lends better resistance to harsh conditions throughout the winter months.

Furthermore, choose a fertilizer designed to specifically help your lawn withstand and handle colder weather conditions.

“Fall fertilization supports stronger root systems, thicker turf, and lends better resistance to harsh conditions throughout the winter months,” states Brian Feldman, Senior Director of Operations and Agronomy at TruGreen.

“Make sure to select a fertilizer that’s formulated specifically for fall and apply it about 3-4 weeks before your area’s first expected frost, and while soil temperatures are still above 50 degrees F.”

Of course, prepping your lawn for winter requires a few extra steps, including clearing away weeds, clearing fallen leaves, and debris to stop them from smothering the soil underneath.

“I would also advise continuing to keep your lawn clear of fallen leaves to avoid any dead patches of grass,” agrees Wilson.

“They needn’t go to waste though — you can spread them over your borders as a nutritious mulch for your plants, which will help improve the soil quality!”

While adding excess fertilizer seems like a good way to protect your lawn through the winter, it can actually do more harm than good. Avoid over-fertilizing if you don’t want to damage your lawn.

“Be careful not to over-fertilize, as too much can lead to nutrient runoff and weak, fast-growing grass that’s more prone to damage. The goal is strong, sustained growth from the roots up,” adds Feldman.

Other top tips include aerating your lawn and knowing when to plant grass seed in November.

#3115. Crypto Market Today, Nov. 19: Bitcoin Approaches $60,000 as ETF Outflows Surpass $2.5 Billion in 2026

Investors are continuing to reduce their exposure to digital assets as the cryptocurrency bear market drags on.

By RJ Fulton – Nov 19, 2026 at 5:25PM EST

Cryptocurrency markets extended their losses on Thursday, November 19, as a broad-based sell-off on Wall Street, mounting concerns over further Federal Reserve interest rate hikes, and weakening ETF demand continued to weigh on digital assets.

As of early evening, Bitcoin (BTC -2.41%) was down 2.15% to $61,635.18, moving dangerously close to the psychologically important $60,000 level. Meanwhile, Ethereum (ETH -3.28%) fell 1.64% to $1,745.57, and Solana (SOL -2.73%) declined 1.56% to $72.47.

Pressure on cryptocurrency markets continued on Thursday as yesterday's Federal Reserve meeting minutes reinforced expectations of further interest rate hikes. With inflation remaining stubbornly elevated, the prospect of tighter monetary policy is weighing heavily on speculative assets and diminishing expectations for improved liquidity conditions heading into 2027.

These concerns were compounded by a sharp sell-off on Wall Street, with all three major stock market indexes declining by at least 2%. Gold also fell more than 2%, highlighting the extent of selling pressure across asset classes.

Spot Bitcoin ETFs remained under pressure on Thursday, with the iShares Bitcoin Trust ETF (IBIT -0.79%) falling 0.79% and the Fidelity Wise Origin Bitcoin Fund (FBTC -0.83%) declining 0.83%. Meanwhile, the iShares Ethereum Trust ETF (ETHA +0.40%) bucked the trend, gaining 0.40%.

According to CoinDesk, U.S. spot Bitcoin ETFs recorded more than $300 million in net outflows on Wednesday, bringing cumulative net outflows for 2026 to more than $2.5 billion. Total assets held by these funds have also fallen to a three-month low.

Perhaps the biggest challenge facing cryptocurrency markets is the absence of sustained buying pressure. Both Bitcoin and Ethereum continue to experience substantial ETF outflows, while Solana's recent return to positive ETF flows has yet to establish a meaningful trend. The persistence of these outflows highlights deteriorating investor demand and the challenges facing the cryptocurrency market as it attempts to establish a bottom.

With Bitcoin approaching $60,000, investors should be particularly mindful of how the market responds at this level. A decisive break below $60,000 could put additional pressure on the broader cryptocurrency market, particularly as Ethereum and Solana are already struggling to regain lost ground.

Looking ahead, the prospect of further interest rate hikes and mounting weakness in equity markets make it increasingly difficult to identify a convincing catalyst for a cryptocurrency recovery before year-end. Rather than attempting to anticipate a bottom, investors should look for evidence that capital is returning to the market, selling pressure is subsiding, and major cryptocurrencies are beginning to reclaim key price levels.

#3114. Microsoft’s new Licensed Weights lets businesses customize AI models with their own data

Our gifting experts are obsessively searching for holiday gifts that are unique, thoughtful and suitable for any budget.

Microsoft is bridging the gap between proprietary and open-weight AI while targeting data-conscious businesses.

During the keynote at its Ignite conference on Tuesday, Microsoft CEO Satya Nadella announced several new models from Microsoft AI (MAI), its lab within the company. But new model releases are almost a dime a dozen these days, and accelerating fast — what really stood out was how Microsoft will let its customers access those models.

Also: Microsoft says its new AI coding model rivals Claude Opus 5.5

MAI said it would allow its customers to customize its frontier models with their own data and run them securely in Azure through an initiative called Licensed Weights. It’s essentially a selective approach to open-weight AI: more so than proprietary models from OpenAI and Anthropic, but not fully downloadable on Hugging Face like Mistral’s Le Chonk. Interested companies will need to go through their Microsoft account reps to get started.

“You control who can access it. Your data and adaptations stay entirely yours. And we’ll work with you through Frontier Company to deliver the custom model and embed it in your own products and agents,” Mustafa Suleyman, CEO of MAI, said during the keynote.

The approach should stand out to businesses looking for affordable AI that lets them retain control over their IP. Microsoft said it would only use customers’ information to train its models if they agreed.

“No one wants to pour their IQ into someone else’s model,” Suleyman said during the keynote, a nod to an argument Palantir CEO Alex Karp has made repeatedly.

The dominant, if simplified, narrative in AI has been that proprietary, expensive models boast peak capabilities but aren’t customizable, while open, cheaper models are customizable but less capable. Microsoft’s AI models don’t necessarily compete with OpenAI and Anthropic yet, but the company has legacy sway with countless businesses. By offering a customizable AI option, it could strike a balance among major tech companies.

Western labs, including Thinking Machines and Mistral, are releasing more competitive open-weight models, but Anthropic and OpenAI still have the overwhelming majority of the enterprise AI market. Though Licensed Weights isn’t an open-weight family of models, it does diversify the open-versus-closed debate a bit and differentiate Microsoft’s offering from OpenAI’s and Anthropic’s. It’s also a smart pairing with Microsoft’s goal to balance price and performance, if businesses find it impressive enough.

Also: Microsoft unveiled Copilot Workspaces at Ignite 2026

“Averaged over four widely used benchmarks that target the everyday enterprise coding tasks we see in GitHub Copilot, MAI Code 2 gives you 98% of the performance of GPT 6.1 Sol at just 40% of the cost, and against Opus 5.5 it’s an incredible 5% of that cost,” Suleyman said of the new coding model the company announced at Ignite.

The company also released its new image editing model, MAI Image 2.7, on Tuesday, which now leads the category on Artificial Analysis while beating Nano Banana Pro and several GPT image models on price and quality. With Licensed Weights, Microsoft has positioned itself for organizations seeking a reliable blend of ROI tools, customization, security controls, and capability.

Tech > Services & Software > Operating Systems > Linux

I've been using Ubuntu 27.04, and the speed boost is noticeable. Here's what else is coming.

Ubuntu 27.04, Tenacious T-Rex, is set for an April 22, 2027 release. Although that seems a long way off, it’s sooner than you think. As is implied by the release number, 27.04 is not an LTS release, so it only receives support for nine months (until January 2028). The good news is that you can migrate from 27.04 to 27.10, and then to the LTS release, 28.04. The entire upgrade path ensures that you don’t have to miss a single release.

But what’s coming in Ubuntu 27.04? Given that it’s an interim release, you’re probably assuming that there’ll be nothing exciting to be found. Although there won’t be any game-changing additions, there will be plenty of refinements and bug fixes.

Also: I’ve used Ubuntu for 22 years – and 26.10 might be its best release yet

I’ve been using the daily release of Ubuntu 27.04 for a bit. Let’s take a look at what is currently expected in Tenacious T-Rex.

This is probably the biggest addition to the next release of Ubuntu. And although you won’t find any major changes in GNOME, there are some important ones. First off, there will be editable quick settings, which allow for customizing, adding, removing, and rearranging toggles and widgets. GNOME 52 will also enjoy a revamped calendar popover, which streamlines the feature to focus primarily on events, time, and weather.

Also: Over Ubuntu? Fedora is the Linux distro I’d hop to next – here’s why

There will also be several improvements to window management, such as a spatial overview and a mosaic/tiling system for auto-resizing and organizing windows, a refined full-screen Alt+Tab app switcher, which will be capable of grouping older windows by application while showing newer ones individually, and finally, the ability to remember window sizing, placement, and workspace.

Desktop search is also getting a bit of polish by way of a redesigned popover and an improved results overlay that includes file previews, multiple actions, and search filters. And, as usual, there will be plenty of bug fixes and performance enhancements. The bump in speed is noticeable, too, in my testing.

Ubuntu 27.04 will ship with the Linux 7.6 kernel, which includes better VRAM management for gaming and expanded support for modern hardware, such as early enablement for AMD Zen 6, stable support for Intel Xe3P, mainline boot capabilities for Apple M3 Pro/Max/Ultra, and initial support for the 2026 Steam Controller.

There will also be performance gains for both the Btrfs and Ext4 file systems, which (along with the improvements in GNOME 52) will make Ubuntu 27.04 one of the best-performing releases in some time.

Once installed, you can use it as expected.

It could make your Pixel Watch or Samsung Galaxy Watch more power efficient.

Some of the most popular Android smartwatches just got a battery-saving update. Google released an updated version of Google Play Services on Tuesday that can help extend the battery life of a Wear OS smartwatch.

The v26.45 update concerns location tracking during outdoor workouts. Wear OS smartwatch users can now use their phone’s Global Navigation Satellite System to track their location during an outdoor workout, which can conserve battery life by outsourcing the smartwatch’s energy to the smartphone when it isn’t in Battery Saver mode.

Constantly communicating with satellites during an outdoor workout can be a battery drain, and every minute of battery life counts when you use your smartwatch for communication, workout tracking, and health monitoring. GPS services, a bright, always-on display, and continuous health sensors like SpO2 can squeeze the most juice out of your smartwatch.

Wear OS software is used by many of the most popular smartwatch brands, including Google, Samsung, and OnePlus. Both the Google Pixel Watch and Samsung Galaxy Watch’s largest batteries last approximately 40 hours. That’s nearly two days of use from two top Android smartwatches, but you’d be surprised how quickly it can drain.

The update improves battery life without users having to take any action or change any settings — the Google Play Services version 26.45 works quietly under the hood.

#3106. Here's What $1,000 Invested at Anthropic's IPO Price Is Worth Now

It was a rough day for Anthropic shares, but not for its IPO investors.

By John Bromels – Nov 19, 2026 at 6:12PM EST

10 stocks we like better than Anthropic ›

As the trading day neared its end, all eyes were on Anthropic (ANT +17.07%)stock. Would the market's newest IPO (not to mention the largest IPO in history) stage a late rally and finish the day above $100/share?

At 3:30 p.m., it didn't look promising. A midafternoon rally that brought the stock price to $99.62/share fizzled, sending it tumbling back down below $95/share again. But then, at about 3:45 p.m., just 15 minutes before the closing bell, things started moving.

Anthropic's share price climbed back above $95... then to $96... and $97...

But then time ran out. The AI heavyweight's shares finished their IPO day at a closing price of $97.17/share, after opening at $111.50/share.

Here's what that means for investors who bought $1,000 of the company's IPO shares and for those who waited.

Although Anthropic announced its official IPO price of $83/share last night, we didn't know what its market debut price would be. That's because the IPO price only applies to designated IPO shares, which are allocated to specific individuals and institutions before public trading ever begins.

If demand is high -- which, of course, was the case for the highly anticipated Anthropic debut -- shares will begin trading at a higher price than the IPO price. This is exactly what happened with SpaceX's (SPCX -3.53%)recent IPO, which was priced at $135/share, but debuted on the NASDAQ at $150/share.

In Anthropic's case, it looks as though that debut price of $111.50/share (a 34.3% premium to its IPO price) might have been a bit too optimistic. Immediately after shares started trading at 11:51 a.m., the price dropped sharply. By noon, it had already tumbled below $106/share. Within the first hour, it fell below $100/share, and stayed there for the rest of the day.

But although it closed well below its debut market price, it was above its IPO price.

$1,000 would have bought you about 12 shares of Anthropic stock at the $83 IPO price (you'd've had $4 left over).

At a closing price of $97.17, you'd have made a one-day profit of $14.17/share, or $170.04 for 12 shares, meaning you'd have $1,170.04 (or, if you bought a fractional share with that last $4, you'd have $1,170.72). That's a 17% gain in one day: not too shabby!

On the other hand, if you missed out on the IPO, but instead bought $1,000 worth of shares right when they debuted at $111.50/share, you'd have been able to afford about 9 shares (8.97 shares, to be exact).

At a closing price of $97.17, you'd've lost $14.33/share today, or about $129 in total ($128.54, if you'd bought exactly 8.97 shares).

So, of your $1,000, you'd have $871.46 remaining, a 14.3% loss.

Meanwhile, if you'd waited to buy shares on the open market until after 1:00 p.m. today, when the worst of the sell-off was already over, you would have bought at a price somewhere between $92.72/share and $99.62/share, meaning you'd have between a 2.5% loss and a 4.8% gain. That translates to a median gain of 1.15% on your $1,000, giving you $1,011.50.

That's not much, but on a day when all the major indexes were down more than 2%, it's not a terrible return for a few hours' investment.

Of course, smart investors don't just calculate their gains after a few hours, or even a few days. Instead, they keep their money invested over the long term, measuring success in years, if not decades.

Given the lack of public information we have about Anthropic's operations and financials, there's no way to know where its share price will end up in three to five years.

So, while IPO investors can pat themselves on the back for their early win, they should pay attention to Anthropic's news releases and quarterly earnings reports to get a fuller picture of how their investment is playing out over time.

TL;DR: Mortgage rates eased today, but borrowing costs are still expensive for many homebuyers.

Mortgage rates are lower today, but recent averages above 7% are still eating into buyers’ budgets.

The average interest rate on a 30-year, fixed-rate mortgage dropped to 7.13% APR, according to rates provided to NerdWallet by Zillow. This is 21 basis points lower than yesterday and 13 basis points higher than a week ago. (A basis point is one one-hundredth of a percentage point.)

Here are the average APRs we're seeing today, as well as movement over the past month for context:

» Take the next step: Compare mortgage rates from NerdWallet’s top lenders

Mortgage rates are constantly changing, since a major part of how rates are set depends on reactions to new inflation reports, job numbers, Fed meetings, global news ... you name it. For example, even tiny changes in the bond market can shift mortgage pricing.

On Friday, the Bureau of Labor Statistics released the Producer Price Index for October, which tracks the change in prices that U.S. producers are able to get for their products. This is one way to measure inflation on the market end, rather than the consumer end.

The results were mixed. While prices didn’t rise quite as high as economists anticipated month-over-month (0.3% vs. 0.4%), year-over-year price growth did reach 6.5% — the largest increase in four years. This points to even higher costs for consumers coming in the near future.

Investors are convinced that the Federal Reserve will raise overnight borrowing rates again in December to pull inflation down. And higher overnight borrowing rates — called the federal funds rate, which is what banks pay to fund products like mortgages — usually lead to higher mortgage rates.

» MORE: How the Federal Reserve affects mortgage rates

Refinancing might make sense if today’s rates are at least 0.5 to 0.75 of a percentage point lower than your current rate (and if you plan to stay in your home long enough to break even on closing costs).

With rates where they are right now, you may want to start considering a refi if your current rate is around 7.63% or higher.

Also consider your goals: Are you trying to lower your monthly payment, shorten your loan term or turn home equity into cash? For example, you might be more comfortable with paying a higher rate for a cash-out refinance than you would for a rate-and-term refinance, so long as the overall costs are lower than if you kept your original mortgage and added a HELOC or home equity loan.

If you're looking for a lower rate, use NerdWallet's refinance calculator to estimate savings and understand how long it would take to break even on the costs of refinancing.

» Time to refi? Compare refinance rates from NerdWallet’s top lenders

There is no universal “right” time to start shopping — what matters is whether you can comfortably afford a mortgage now at today’s rates.

If the answer is yes, don’t get too hung up on whether you could be missing out on lower rates later; you can refinance down the road. Focus on getting preapproved, comparing lender offers, and understanding what monthly payment works for your budget.

NerdWallet’s affordability calculator can help you estimate your potential monthly payment. If a new home isn’t in the cards right now, there are still things you can do to strengthen your buyer profile. Take this time to pay down existing debts and build your down payment savings. Not only will this free up more cash flow for a future mortgage payment, it can also get you a better interest rate when you’re ready to buy.

» Is now a good time to buy? See NerdWallet’s analysis

If you already have a quote you’re happy with, you should consider locking your mortgage rate, especially if your lender offers a float-down option. A float-down lets you take advantage of a better rate if the market drops during your lock period.

Rate locks protect you from increases while your loan is processed, and with the market forever bouncing around, that peace of mind can be worth it.

#3103. The Semiconductor ETF Is on Track to Beat the S&P 500 for a 4th Straight Year. It Has Never Done That Before.

The last time this chip fund beat the market three years running, the fourth year cost it around a third of its value.

By Daniel Sparks – Nov 19, 2026 at 6:23PM EST

10 stocks we like better than VanEck ETF Trust - VanEck Semiconductor ETF ›

The VanEck Semiconductor ETF (SMH -2.62%) closed on Nov. 17 at $460.10, putting it up around 28% in 2026. The S&P 500 (^GSPC -2.02%) rose about 7% during the same stretch.

With around six weeks left in the year, the chip fund is ahead by about 21 percentage points. If its lead holds through Dec. 31, it'll have beaten the index for a fourth straight calendar year, after winning in all of the last three. It's never strung together four in a row.

The last time it won three straight, the next year went badly. The fund dropped around 34% in 2022, while the S&P 500 lost about 19%.

I checked this using year-end closing prices from Yahoo Finance, with dividends left out throughout. That record begins in June 2000. Today's fund only dates to December 2011, though, when VanEck replaced the Semiconductor HOLDRS trust that had traded under the same ticker.

Either way, the fund's longest run of wins against the S&P 500 is three years. And including dividends doesn't change which years it won.

The two three-year runs look a lot alike. From the end of 2018 through 2021, the fund gained around 254%, versus about 90% for the index. From the end of 2022 through 2025, it climbed by about 255%, compared with about 78%.

Of course, what matters to a buyer is what came next. Every winning run in the data (six in all, including single-year wins in 2003 and 2005) was followed by a year when the fund's price fell. The declines ranged from below 3% in 2015 to the 34% drop in 2022.

And the industry's sales didn't give much warning. Worldwide chip sales hit a record $574.1 billion in 2022, up 3.3% over 2021, according to the Semiconductor Industry Association (SIA). The slowdown came only in the second half, while the fund had been declining since its Dec. 27, 2021, record close.

Then sales dropped 8.2% in 2023 -- the same year the fund gained around 72%. In other words, the stocks moved before the yearly sales numbers did, in both directions.

I think the main difference between 2026 and 2021 is the starting price. The fund finished 2021 only about 2% below its record close, so investors buying at the start of 2022 paid near-peak prices.

This year, the drop came early. The fund's record close was on June 22 at $668.91, up around 86% for the year. It's since lost most of that gain and is about 31% under the record.

Even so, it hasn't ended a single trading day in 2026 behind the S&P 500 on a year-to-date basis. A winning calendar year, in other words, can still hide a fall of around 31%, and the streak says nothing about the price an investor pays.

What's kept the fund ahead is spending on artificial intelligence (AI) data centers.

Showing how strong that spending still is, Nvidia (NVDA -3.30%), the fund's largest holding, posted fiscal third-quarter revenue (the period ended Oct. 25, 2026) of $115.8 billion after the close on Nov. 17, up 103% year over year. Its data center revenue climbed 110% to $107.6 billion, a small slowdown from 117% growth in fiscal Q2. But total revenue grew 20% from the previous quarter, slightly faster than the 18% sequential growth Nvidia posted in fiscal Q2. And management guided for about $130 billion in fiscal fourth-quarter revenue, a period that has an extra week.

These were also Nvidia's first results since Jensen Huang resigned as CEO. CFO Colette Kress is filling in as interim CEO. The fund climbed around 4% in after-hours trading that evening.

Much of the result may hinge on a few stocks. As of Nov. 16, Nvidia accounted for around 17% of the fund's assets, and Taiwan Semiconductor Manufacturing accounted for about 10%. Its 10 largest holdings, out of 25, accounted for about 69%.

A fourth straight win would be a first for the fund. But the record suggests a streak tells a buyer little about the year after, and the sales numbers gave little warning before the last one ended.

What a buyer gets now is a price around 31% under the fund's June 22 record close, in a group whose largest member just more than doubled its quarterly revenue. I think the fund is worth considering here, maybe added gradually over the next few months. I'd just size any position with a year like 2022 in mind.

Here are some of the key findings from the 2026 holiday shopping research.

Retailers that use AI shopping agents are seeing bigger orders and more loyal customers. The survey found that shoppers who use AI agent referrals are twice as likely to make a purchase. In addition, 39% of shoppers have used AI agents on an e-commerce site, and 80% had a positive experience, while 75% felt more loyal to the brand as a result of the AI agent experience.

#3101. Windows’ Baseline Protection Can Simplify Security, but There Could Be Pitfalls

Our gifting experts are obsessively searching for holiday gifts that are unique, thoughtful and suitable for any budget.

Our expert, award-winning staff selects the products we cover and rigorously researches and tests our top picks. If you buy through our links, we may earn a commission.

It makes security a little easier to manage, but apps can also refuse to work if your machine fails security checks.

Microsoft’s collecting all of Windows 11’s hardware-related security features under one roof starting in 2027. Announced during its Ignite developer conference this week, in addition to seven new AI models, baseline protection is a way to make Windows more secure out of the box.

The combination of core security safeguards into a single pass-or-fail device status is a boon, but it may also introduce problems, including for gamers, who tend to tweak aspects of the operating system environment, like UEFI BIOS settings.

A Microsoft spokesperson told CNET in an email that baseline protection is still in the preview stage and that the company will “continue to iterate and build upon this based on the feedback the company hears from customers, partners and developers.”

Currently, Windows’ eight key hardware security features are spread across the OS: the Trusted Platform Module security processor, Memory Integrity (which prevents unwanted alternation of data in memory), Kernel debugger protection (to guard the core code of the OS), Secure Boot (which ensures no tampering during system startup), driver security and a few others.

To manage or check these settings, you have to visit multiple locations, and if app developers need to verify them at runtime, they have to perform similar gymnastics.

The upcoming functionality will consolidate all those settings into a single control panel within Windows’ Security settings section, where you’ll be able to check their status and apply any necessary updates. Since it tracks all eight security features, developers will only need to confirm that baseline protection is met.

The feature is currently available in Windows Insider builds and is expected to roll out to the general public in 2027.

Baseline protection provides instructions for enabling these features if they’re not readily available. For example, enabling Secure Boot requires restarting directly into your BIOS. To save you time, the panel provides step-by-step instructions right on the screen, so you don’t have to look up how to do it yourself.

Application developers may have the biggest win here. The ability to poll just one security feature instead of eight individual ones streamlines the development process and allows developers to check security features quickly and easily. For instance, game anti-cheat software relies on multiple security measures to verify that no third-party code is running.

Microsoft has 11 initial software partners, including heavy hitters like Adobe, 1Password, Blizzard and Epic Games, each of which is incorporating support to help it identify risk faster, including detecting counterfeit and malicious software.

“A consistent security signal gives apps and organizations a shared foundation to build on,” said Michael Draper, vice president of Global Consumer Trust at Adobe, in a testimonial.

Power users and gamers potentially stand to lose the most from this new feature. Many of them intentionally disable certain security settings to dual-boot Linux, run custom hardware drivers or improve gaming performance by disabling Virtualization-Based Security, which can lower frame rates and cause visual glitches.

Also, since developers can perform a single pass-fail check for all the settings, users may be shoehorned into keeping all eight features enabled, even if the developer doesn’t need them all.

Microsoft is leaving enforcement up to the developer, though. For example, an application may check baseline protection, see that it’s not fully satisfied, but allow a user to run it anyway with a warning screen or another pop-up or reminder. Alternatively, the software may refuse to run until the user enables full baseline protection.

“Windows baseline protection gives the app information on each security requirement, and developers can choose to enable some or all requirements,” said a Microsoft spokesperson. “Microsoft still recommends developers embrace all requirements to meet the strongest security bar.”

Adobe, Blizzard, 1Password and most of Microsoft’s other partners haven’t expressly said they’ll lock users out of apps without complaints, but a few have strongly hinted that this will be the case.

Our gifting experts are obsessively searching for holiday gifts that are unique, thoughtful and suitable for any budget.

Just months after its release, Google is making its Spark agent free and officially renaming its capabilities “Tasks.” You can now toggle to it from the standard Gemini Chat setting. Reports show the rebrand started gradually in mid-October.

Also: Ready for a Siri AI agent? Apple under pressure to upgrade its assistant faster

(Disclosure: Ziff Davis, ZDNET’s parent company, filed an April 2025 lawsuit against OpenAI, alleging it infringed Ziff Davis copyrights in training and operating its AI systems.)

If Tasks sounds familiar, it should: The company already has a product called Google Tasks, which lets you turn emails into a checkable to-do list on the side of your inbox, among other places like Chat and Docs. This is the agentic version, obviously.

Gewirtz, ZDNET’s AI tester-in-residence, wasn’t blown away by then-Spark when he tried it last month, but had reason to believe in its eventual improvement. It’s unclear whether Tasks is meaningfully different from Spark, aside from being out of beta.

Abilities aside, what sets Tasks apart here is cost. Dots and Duet haven’t exactly impressed thus far, so free alternatives don’t have a high bar to reach yet.

The feature is free in the US, Canada, Korea, Japan, Australia, and India. US users can also start tasks by emailing or texting Gemini, and can have the agent call businesses for them (except in Indiana, Louisiana, Minnesota, Montana, and Nebraska).

Structure Research shows neoclouds like Sharon, which specialize in GPU-based services, gaining a share across every layer of the AI infrastructure. Within the cloud infrastructure space, the neocloud share is forecasted to roughly triple to about 16% by 2031, while the value of that share, as shown in the middle chart, is forecasted to grow roughly 18x from about $27 billion to over $480 billion. Our partner ecosystem has been critical to our success to date, and it's what makes our capital-light model possible. We orchestrate compute, data centers, networking, the data platform, integration, hardware life cycles around a single SharonAI platform, rather than owning every layer ourselves.

Our two platform partnerships are worth highlighting this quarter because both bear directly on how we scale. The first is VAST Data. In June, we committed to deploy 600 petabytes of VAST AI Operating System as the data foundation for our AI cloud. This is one of the largest sovereign AI data deployments in Asia-Pac. On VAST's benchmark of around six petabytes per 1,000 GPUs, that is the data center capacity support the needs of around 100,000 GPUs. Storage should not become the bottleneck as our GPU fleet grows. This quarter, we also launched DataEnclave with VAST, which brings leading AI models into a customer-controlled infrastructure.

The second is Rafay. in September, we signed a five-year strategic agreement under which Rafay's platform becomes the central orchestration and operational layer across our AI factories. Rafay standardizes how we provision, govern, monitor, and deliver capacity across sites, tenants, and workloads. The architecture is designed to support orchestration of up to 150,000 GPUs over the term of the agreement. In addition, we have and/or will be receiving customer deposits of approximately $800 million as we deploy.

Our approach is to match each source of funding to the stage of our company's growth. Equity and convertible debt funded the platform and our early deployments. GPU deployments are funded with asset SPV-level debt, secured against the GPUs and the contracts they serve. Let me be direct on one of the questions we hear the most from investors. SharonAI is not reliant on the unsecured debt market. The remaining build-out is being funded in the secured debt markets. That is, we will raise SPV-level debt facilities against signed take-or-pay contracts, and that are secured by the GPUs dedicated to them. The facility size to the compute dedicated to signed contracts. This is why the secured market is relevant for us. A dedicated SPV for each deployment, debt size to signed contracts, and security over the GPUs and their cash flows. Names and emails of some customers may have been compromised, but the bank's service is unaffected.

A third-party cyberattack may have compromised the names and email addresses of some JPMorgan Chase customers, the bank announced Thursday. Despite the announcement coming days after a technical glitch disrupted Chase services, the company said the breach is not related to the earlier issues.

Although limited details have been released, Chase said that the attack targeted a third-party provider that works with the bank and that no service disruptions are expected as a result of this breach.

Chase said that some affected customers will be contacted individually about the breach, and may be offered free credit monitoring. It’s unclear how many customers may have been involved.

A Chase representative did not immediately respond to a request for comment.

On Monday, thousands of Chase customers reported trouble accessing their online accounts. The company told CNET and said on X that a software bug caused those service disruptions, not a cyberattack. That problem also affected other banking platforms, including Bank of America and Zelle.

Read more: The World Didn’t End on Nov. 17, but Some Tech Chaos Did Go Down

The outages occurred on the heels of a nationwide flight grounding and the same week that a viral internet rumor stoked fear of a national blackout on Nov. 17, which didn’t occur. The rumor was tied to a scheduled test of the Emergency Alert System by FEMA in coordination with the FCC.

Despite official statements that the slew of technical issues was unrelated to a broader cyberattack, some pointed to the outages as evidence of a wider national emergency. Those fears did not materialize.

#3097. 5 new Apple Health features you should try in iOS 27.3 – if your phone qualifies

Our gifting experts are obsessively searching for holiday gifts that are unique, thoughtful and suitable for any budget.

Apple's redesigned Health app arrives in December with some major upgrades, but not every iPhone will get the full experience.

Apple is kicking off a new and improved Health app next month with the release of iOS 27.3. Instead of just recording and displaying your health-related stats, the app will tap into Apple Intelligence to analyze the data and dispense advice on how to improve your health and fitness. But that reliance on AI means you’ll need the right type of iPhone to enjoy all the benefits.

Also: Apple could build its AI health chatbot from this study – how to enroll

Here are five helpful new features built into the app, along with what you’ll need to access them.

First up, the app will offer suggestions based on data from different sources. For example, it might advise you to go for a walk at a nearby park if it detects that you’re not getting enough exercise. It may show you articles and videos about sleep if it finds that you’re not well-rested. It could also highlight possible conditions based on your lab and test results. You can easily view these recommendations from the Insights screen.

Also: Health is Tim Cook’s defining legacy – and your Apple Watch proves it

A new feature called Health Age compares your physical health to your actual age to show how you’re doing. The analysis draws on certain stats and lab data, such as your resting heart rate, sleep, heart rate variability (HRV), cholesterol, and A1C (average blood glucose levels), to deliver a health age, which may differ from your chronological age. The results can show you areas that may be of concern or that you need to focus on.

Also: Apple Watch Series 12 review: Finally, the health tracker I’ve been waiting for

With a new feature called Movement Evaluations and an iPhone and Apple Watch, the Health app can assess your flexibility, strength, balance, VO2 max (maximum oxygen absorption), and overall movement. You perform a physical routine while your iPhone “watches” you via the camera. Using built-in AI, the app will provide audio and visual feedback in real-time to tell you how you’re faring.

Apple promises that the analysis is performed on your device without recording, storing, or sharing the video.

The new app will be able to correlate your test results with data collected by your iPhone and Apple Watch to give you a more comprehensive picture of your health. Plus, Apple and Quest Diagnostics have teamed up to offer people in the US an optional $119 bloodwork panel that covers more than 50 biomarkers to scan for different health and medical conditions.

Also: I tested the Apple Watch Series 12 heart-rate claims against my gold-standard Polar strap

Normally, you need an Apple Fitness+ subscription to fire up workout videos to help you exercise. But the new Health app will come with its own comprehensive set of training videos. Scholarships are usually restricted to the necessary costs of attending college, but some scholarships let you apply the money to more than tuition.

Scholarships are meant to pay for the cost of attendance to study at a college or university. This often includes required bills and purchases, such as tuition, textbooks and on-campus living expenses.

Some scholarships restrict the funds to specific costs, such as tuition. How you can apply the money may depend on the scholarship’s requirements.

Here are the most common college costs you can pay with scholarship money.

Scholarships commonly pay toward the tuition and fees your college charges.

Tuition usually covers only the cost to enroll in classes. Your college will also charge fees for a variety of reasons, such as attending a lab portion of a class, access to on-campus technology, facility maintenance and student activities. You’ll have to pay many of these fees regardless of if you use those facilities or participate in campus activities. Fees are often charged with tuition on the same bill so that you pay them together.

Tuition and fees cost students at public four-year institutions an average of $32,730 for the 2026-2027 school year, according to College Board’s 2026 report. If you use scholarship money to pay for these costs upfront, it can help you save a good chunk of money.

Scholarship money also pays for textbooks and supplies you need to complete your courses. These can include physical books, e-books and software licenses to access online content.

Depending on the scholarship, the cost of additional supplies that are required for certain courses might be covered as well. For example, nursing students might have to purchase scrubs with their college’s logo or medical supplies such as stethoscopes for clinical shifts.

Some scholarships will pay for the purchase of a laptop because you’ll likely need one to complete your coursework; however, you’ll want to confirm that the money can be used for that purchase before buying one.

Your scholarship might help cover some of the costs of living on campus, including paying for a dorm room and meal plans (often called room and board). To apply the funds, you usually have to live in university housing, which might be in a dormitory or even university apartments.

Many students can purchase meal plans to eat meals in their college and university cafeterias. These plans are usually for a set number of meals each week and might be required for first-year students. Because meal plans are part of college expenses, some scholarships will let you apply the funds to purchase a meal plan.

Some scholarships might also allow money to pay for campus parking fees because those are paid directly to the college or university.

» MORE: What is need-based financial aid for college?

Scholarships are generally intended only for educational expenses such as those explained above, but there are some scholarships that want you to use the money for specific expenses. If your scholarship has this type of restriction, your award letter should outline how the funds must be used, such as paying for tuition and fees only.

If you aren’t certain whether there are restrictions on how you can spend your scholarship money and the scholarship was paid directly to your college, you can call your financial aid office to ask. But you’ll want to contact the organization that awarded you the scholarship to ask about restrictions if the scholarship money was sent to you instead.

Even if a scholarship is open to most educational costs, expenses that are rarely allowed to be covered by a scholarship include:

Some transportation costs such as car payments.

Non-essential supplies such as clothing or entertainment.

Scholarships can be paid directly to your college or to you, depending on the individual scholarship. If the money goes to your college, it’s applied to your account based on the scholarship’s requirements. For example, if the funds are only allowed to pay for tuition, the financial aid office will apply the money to your tuition bill to reduce how much you owe.

Scholarships work the same way for room and board. If your scholarship will pay toward the costs of living on campus, the money will reduce how much you owe or cover the costs entirely so that you don’t owe anything.

In some cases, you might be able to use your scholarship money to pay for books or supplies. If that’s allowed, the funds might be available on your account through the college bookstore. Instead of paying the entire cost of your textbooks with cash or your student loans, you can pay with the scholarship money.

If your scholarship sends you the money instead of giving it to your college, you’ll be responsible for using the funds to pay for eligible costs instead of your university automatically applying it toward your bill.

#3092. 90% of employers reject resumes that look like AI – yet half use AI to interview

Our gifting experts are obsessively searching for holiday gifts that are unique, thoughtful and suitable for any budget.

In today's job market, do applicants really have a choice of whether to comply with AI hiring tools?

Hiring managers are more suspicious than ever of AI use in applications, and it’s impacting who they consider. At the same time, they’re turning to AI to help screen more candidates — meaning those videos you’ve seen on the internet of people pranking AI interviewers aren’t going away anytime soon.

New data from hiring systems firm Greenhouse found that “nine in ten US employers (90%) believe they’ve turned away real candidates because those applications seemed fake or AI-generated.” Greenhouse clarified that it doesn’t know whether employers are putting applications through AI detection tools or not.

Also: How many jobs is your state losing to AI? This dashboard tracks the cuts – and the cost

“The survey data is self-reported, so it reflects what employers believe has happened, not a measured outcome,” Greenhouse’s Head of Voice AI Ophir Samson told ZDNET via email.

Employers are also reacting to AI by adjusting their hiring processes: 86% of those surveyed reported changes to account for AI’s impact. 57% of them did so by adding another human interview.

“As jobseekers rely more on AI to polish and send out their job applications, employers are finding it harder to tell who’s actually right for the role,” the report stated, echoing an ongoing push-and-pull between applicants and hiring teams. AI resume screeners automatically toss a majority of applications they deem unfit, so applicants try not to get tossed by formatting their material for the screener, which then backfires anyway.

The report shows how a tough economy and an influx of AI hiring tools are colliding, arguably to benefit employers over applicants. Greenhouse noted that, ironically, AI tools are helping hiring managers while also making resumes untrustworthy, and applicants would rather be interviewed by AI than not at all.

Also: How to beat the AI algorithm and get the job of your dreams

“A growing number of employers are using AI not just to filter candidates out, but to have conversations with more candidates, earlier, through AI-powered voice technology,” Greenhouse said, adding that “half now use AI interviews to hear from more candidates, and 40% of those have found strong candidates they would have missed.”

Greenhouse itself offers a voice AI screening interview tool. Samson told ZDNET that an HR professional ran 200 candidates she’d rejected through Greenhouse’s tool, and it suggested 19.

“All five of the finalists came from that group, and she ultimately hired one from the group,” Samson said.

What we don’t, and maybe can’t, know is the inverse: whether AI screeners influence hiring managers to turn away candidates they actually should have considered. At least in Greenhouse’s case, Samson said Voice AI doesn’t make hiring decisions or “automatically advance, reject, or rank candidates.”

“Recruiters review every output, and one recruiter owns the outcome and can explain how they reached it,” he said.

Greenhouse’s report surveyed 1,347 hiring managers and recruiters across the US, UK, Germany, Australia, and Ireland from late September to mid-October, and found that half of employers using voice AI “say the early-stage candidate experience has improved.”

Also: ‘So perfect, they are literally identical’ – Your AI-polished resumes are recruiters’ new top stressor

It’s unclear what “improved” means there, though, and whether applicants themselves would agree with that. Still, when given the choice, only 7% of applicants in the US would turn down an AI interview, per an earlier Greenhouse report. Additionally, “70% of those who’ve had a live AI interview say it helped them show their skills,” that report said.

But how swayed is that by the state of the US job market? October’s job report was better than expected, but it’s still been a tough year overall for job-seekers. Greenhouse’s findings could be as much a reflection of how desperate applicants are as an endorsement of or comfort with AI screenings.

“The job market could be a factor. Our Future of Hiring Candidate Report shows 81% of job seekers were rejected from a job in the past year without speaking to anyone at the company, human or AI,” Samson said. “But I’d be careful about reading the data as desperation. Candidates are setting clear conditions: nearly half (49%) want to know if a human will review their responses and 40% want to know how they’ll be evaluated.”

Also: Why replacing staff with AI backfires – and 5 ways smart leaders generate real value instead

Samson said that a software engineer named Ryan Quinlan, who was hired at Blissway, initially thought “talking to an AI” sounded stranger, but that it ultimately “felt like a conversation” that let him mention skills he’d forgotten to include on his resume. Samson said that Ryan has been “a ‘maybe’ on paper,” but that the AI interview helped him get over the line to be considered.

“For most applicants, a human conversation was never on the table,” Samson said. “The real choice is a resume lost in a pile, or 15 minutes to tell their story.”

Greenhouse found that while employers are using AI to screen more candidates, most are maintaining human oversight over the most important decisions in the hiring process.

“Of all the tasks employers would hand to an AI agent, deciding which candidates to advance came last, at just 7%,” Greenhouse said.

A recent California law aims to protect employees from being fired by AI systems that make determinations about their performance without a human co-signing the assessment. As with many AI productivity tools in the workplace, proper adoption ideally equates to more time for human workers to handle more important tasks.

Also: 92% of HR say staff can train for AI jobs – but half of companies still hire outside

“Of employers who’ve saved time with AI, 85% put it back into candidates, most often by spending more time with shortlisted candidates (45%) and interviewing more candidates earlier (40%),” Greenhouse said.

The main question around AI interviewers remains whether they’re correctly capturing your interview the way you’d hope a human interviewer would (though that’s still deeply subjective and out of applicants’ control anyway).

“When AI interviews are implemented thoughtfully and transparently, they pay off for both candidates and recruiters,” Samson said. “Every candidate who uses our Voice AI can opt out, and about 90% rate the experience as excellent.”

#3090. Meta Is Trying to Woo Teens to Instagram Through Schools

Our gifting experts are obsessively searching for holiday gifts that are unique, thoughtful and suitable for any budget.

Our expert, award-winning staff selects the products we cover and rigorously researches and tests our top picks. If you buy through our links, we may earn a commission.

Project Gryffindor is an initiative intended to make Instagram popular by marketing "school communities" on the platform.

Meta has justifiably attracted more scrutiny than ever this year, along with multibillion-dollar judgments and settlements, over how its business practices affect young social media users. The company, however, is not retreating.

In fact, the tech giant has made a major push toward drawing teenagers to one of its flagship platforms, Instagram, by targeting them at their schools.

According to documents obtained and reported by NPR, Meta launched an initiative called Project Gryffindor, named after a Hogwarts house in the Harry Potter series, to create school communities on Instagram in order to boost user counts and engagement on the platform.

Meta’s goal of approaching young users where they spend the most time offline was not a secret. As recently as late September, the company said it was expanding its School Partnership Program, which includes 17,000 schools, with a stated goal to “help students and parents stay informed.”

The company’s internal documents reveal some of the motivations behind Meta’s push for school adoption and Project Gryffindor’s proposed features, such as school banners on teen profiles and the ability to search school directories by class year. The details were acquired as part of discovery in a multistate lawsuit over whether social media platforms are designed to be addictive to users under 18. Meta is a defendant in the case, along with other companies, including TikTok, Snap and Google.

In 2024, Instagram introduced Teen accounts and has since been trying to assure parents they’re safe while rolling out additional protections. Studies, however, have suggested that young teens regularly encounter unsafe content or deal with unwanted contact. Recruiting more users at an early age without resolving these risks could make teens more vulnerable to mental health issues and increase the chances of being bullied or harassed.

A representative for Meta did not immediately respond to a request for comment.

Like other social platforms, Instagram primarily makes its money from targeted advertising. User retention is a key part of Meta’s strategy.

In one of the document slides, titled “Why schools, why now?” which preceded Gryffindor’s launch, Meta said, “Competitors are exploring school social use cases, but IG may be better positioned for school connections thanks to our differentiator of meeting new people and building relationships with acquaintances.” In other words, Instagram’s size and scale, with about 3 billion active users globally, automatically make it a draw for students.

The NPR report comes within a week of a filing against Meta alleging that it’s withholding evidence in a major case involving social media’s effects on teenagers.

One of Meta’s marketing pitches for its School Partnership Program is that it’s trying to create online safe spaces for students, while giving parents and schools more oversight on what’s accessible on the platform. But experts warn that Meta’s history makes it hard to trust the company with protecting kids from predators or scammers.

Katie Paul, director of the Center for Accountability’s Tech Transparency Project, which has been researching how Meta handles child-safety issues, said that Instagram Teen accounts “are not safe as advertised” and that nothing is “legally requiring the company to make these safe.” Paul pointed out that Instagram launched these accounts only when lawsuits over social media harm started rolling in.

“It’s all part of a broader marketing (effort) to claim that these are just safer for kids because they are Teen accounts,” Paul said. That marketing effort has included paid endorsements from therapists, psychologists and parent influencers to promote Teen accounts. The case for building up partnerships with schools is a way of “passing the buck on responsibility” to schools and parents, Paul said.

Parents, in particular, have less power in Instagram’s school groups: Unlike the school administrators tasked with managing school groups, parents have no powers to moderate or manage those groups; they can only view them. For Teen accounts in general, parents can’t view direct messages sent to or received by their children.

Meta’s business interests in its push for student engagement and school partnerships are easy to see through. Because kids are likely to be lifetime users on these platforms, getting them hooked early has long-term financial value.

“Ultimately, Meta is the one profiting off of the data collection of these kids while simultaneously failing to keep them safe,” Paul said.

The analyst raised his 2027 revenue and EPS estimates by 7% and 9% to $33 billion and $8.88, respectively. Yang also increased his 2028 revenue and EPS estimates by 7% and 8% to $36.6 billion and $9.89, respectively.

"It's the cleanest way to play AI-driven 3D scaling across memory, foundry/logic, and packaging," said Yang about LRCX.

#3088. The Flipper One is more than a Zero 2.0 – it’s a $399 Linux computer with a $13M Kickstarter

Our gifting experts are obsessively searching for holiday gifts that are unique, thoughtful and suitable for any budget.

Tech > Services & Software > Operating Systems > Linux

Backers are going big on the $759 Ultimate Bundle, but Flipper warns that rising RAM prices could affect production.

The Flipper One crowdfunding campaign has broken the $13-million mark, smashing the funding raised for previous Flipper devices and demonstrating strong interest in the successor to the Flipper Zero. The $399 Flipper One is a pocket Linux computer focused on networking, with delivery estimated for July 2027. But it isn’t simply an updated version of the Flipper Zero. It’s a very different animal and a much more serious bit of kit.

The thing that made the Flipper Zero so popular was how easy it was to use. You could fire it up and turn the volume down on the TV at your parents’ place, see the radio waves coming from your car’s key fob, and copy hotel room key cards.

Also: The Flipper One may be the ultimate Linux PC for hackers in 2026 – and I’m excited

It could do a lot, there wasn’t a steep learning curve, and you didn’t need to buy anything else. Did the fake videos on TikTok from people claiming they could change the prices at gas stations (I wish!) or start cars remotely help make the Zero more popular?

Unfortunately, yes. But what made it successful was that it packed a lot of power into a package that was small, fun, affordable, and easy to use.

If the Flipper Zero, with its NFC, RFID, sub-GHz, and IR, was kindergarten, the Flipper One is a college degree: a pocket Linux computer focused on networking.

This is reflected in the price. You can pick up a Zero for $169, while the Flipper One is $399.

What this buys you is the Flipper One base computer with a 256 × 144 grayscale LCD, Rockchip RK3576 8-core ARM SoC with NPU, a low-power MCU for handling the LCD and user interface, 8GB of LPDDR5 RAM, 64GB of UFS 2.2 storage, and a microSD slot.

If that $399 feels like a lot, it’s worth keeping in mind that, according to Flipper, the price only covers production costs and that the RAM and UFS storage account for at least half of the total hardware cost.

If you think this is a lot, you could spend a lot more. Adding a LoRa, SDR, or 5G module will push the total up a lot higher. And if you want all three modules, you’re looking at $759 for the Flipper One Ultimate Bundle.

Also: The Flipper One is the Linux cyberdeck I wish my Raspberry Pi could be

The reception has been strong enough that pledges have flown past the $300,000 goal that Flipper initially set, with over 24,000 backers pledging over $13 million. Close to 5,300 backers have gone for the Ultimate Bundle, compared to just over 4,300 choosing the bare Flipper One.

This suggests that backers really want the radio capabilities that this new platform offers.

If you want one, this crowdfunding run is a good time to get one because it’s a Kickstarter Special slashing 25% off an estimated retail price of $550.

The response over on Reddit has been a little more subdued, with some being taken aback by the price of the Zero’s bigger sibling.

Also: 7 useful things I can do with my Flipper Zero – as someone who’s used it for years

As someone who homebrews a lot of electronics, I’m going to say that the price is justified, and this project goes far beyond something you could put together with a Raspberry Pi and some code.

The Flipper One campaign runs until Dec. 17, 2026, with delivery estimated for July 2027.

Keep in mind that this is a Kickstarter pledge, not a purchase, and that rewards aren’t guaranteed. Flipper also says on the Kickstarter page that component shortages are the biggest risk to the project and that they “could cause significant delays to production and delivery.” It also says that if RAM prices continue to rise, it cannot “rule out adjusting some product specifications, including reducing the amount of RAM.”

Also: Is the Flipper Zero the best multi-tool for hacking?

And the good news here is that I’ve seen several analysts predicting that RAM prices will begin to go down in 2027 as demand eases off.

#3087. I Didn’t Know Southwest Points Could Be This Valuable

We believe everyone should be able to make financial decisions with confidence. While we don't cover every company or financial product on the market, we work hard to share a wide range of offers and objective editorial perspectives.
