#3068. With Mortgage Rates Rising, Should You Hibernate Until Spring?

We believe everyone should be able to make financial decisions with confidence. While we don't cover every company or financial product on the market, we work hard to share a wide range of offers and objective editorial perspectives.

So how do we make money? Our partners compensate us for advertisements that appear on our site. This compensation helps us provide tools and services - like free credit score access and monitoring. With the exception of mortgage, home equity and other home-lending products or services, partner compensation is one of several factors that may affect which products we highlight and where they appear on our site. Other factors include your credit profile, product availability and proprietary website methodologies.

However, these factors do not influence our editors' opinions or ratings, which are based on independent research and analysis. Our partners cannot pay us to guarantee favorable reviews. Here is a list of our partners.

Higher borrowing costs aren't the whole story. Here's what to consider before putting your house hunt on hold.

Mortgage rates are back up this week, wiping out modest relief from a monthlong drop that began in mid-October.

The average rate on a 30-year fixed-rate mortgage shot up 29 basis points to 7.28% APR in the week ending Nov. 19, according to rates provided to NerdWallet by Zillow. (A basis point is one one-hundredth of a percentage point.) We calculate our weekly average using daily APRs recorded over the past five business days.

A mortgage is a big ol’ loan, so when rates go up, those fractions of a percentage point add up fast. Say you’re borrowing $400,000 on a 30-year fixed-rate mortgage. Compared with last week, your monthly principal and interest payment would be about $78 higher today.

One bad week doesn't make a trend, but a jump like this can make putting your house hunt on hold until spring feel like a safer bet. So … is it?

Before deciding whether to buy a house now or wait, it helps to know what's pushing mortgage rates higher.

Right now, mortgage rates are still feeling the aftershocks from two major inflation reports last week. First, the Consumer Price Index (CPI) showed consumer prices rose more than expected in October. Then, the Producer Price Index (PPI) showed wholesale inflation climbed 6.5% over the past year — its biggest annual increase in nearly four years.

While CPI shows how prices have changed, PPI can offer clues about what's coming next. Faced with higher costs, businesses may raise their own prices to compensate, keeping inflation elevated. Federal Reserve policymakers aren't expecting much relief anytime soon, either. According to meeting minutes released Nov. 18, they expect inflation to remain elevated above their 2% target for a while.

To cool rising prices, the Fed can raise the federal funds rate, which is the benchmark interest rate banks charge each other for overnight loans. The Fed doesn't set mortgage rates, but lenders anticipate its decisions, so mortgage rates often move before the Fed acts. A rate hike is widely expected at the Fed's Dec. 8-9 meeting.

Even after a Fed rate hike, there’s no telling how quickly inflation will cool — or whether mortgage rates will follow. (Inflation is just one of many forces that affect mortgage rates, after all.) So if you do wait until spring to buy a house, don't do it just because you're betting on a cheaper mortgage.

If you're not in a rush to move, winter can be a good time to regroup. Fewer homes typically go up for sale from November through February, so waiting until spring could give you more options.

But new data from the National Association of Realtors suggests this year's slowdown goes beyond the usual seasonal lull. High mortgage rates and home prices are making it tough for many buyers to make the numbers work. For some buyers, waiting isn't a strategy — it's the only option.

Pending home sales, a measure of homes under contract, fell 16.7% in October compared with a year earlier, NAR reports. All four U.S. regions saw declines. At this rate, NAR chief economist Lawrence Yun warned that annual home sales could fall to their lowest level since the mid-1990s.

“Either sizable housing demand is building in the background, or the dream of homeownership is increasingly out of reach for many Americans,” Yun said in a news release.

Whether you're waiting by choice or necessity, you can use the time to strengthen your finances. Paying down debt, strengthening your credit score or saving for a bigger down payment could help you qualify for a better mortgage deal.

Every little bit helps when today’s mortgage rates are this high.

Mortgage preapprovals typically expire after 60 to 90 days. If you're already preapproved, why not keep an eye on listings this winter? (Hey, I’m an optimist. All it takes is one house.)

Think like a seller for a second. If you're listing your house in the dead of winter, you're probably not doing it just for fun. You might have a deadline, and you’re probably more willing to negotiate. In the winter, buyers have less competition — and more room to negotiate a lower price, closing cost credits or repairs. Those savings on the sticker price might help offset today's higher borrowing costs.

Spring typically brings more homes for sale, but it also brings more buyers competing for them. And if mortgage rates end up dropping this spring, you won't be the only one coming out of hibernation.

#3067. Ray Dalio says Bessent move is sign that a debt crisis is getting closer; recommends gold and bitcoin

Treasury Secretary Scott Bessent's debt buyback announcement this week fits into a broader pattern that can signal a forthcoming crisis, according to billionaire investor Ray Dalio.

The Bridgewater Associates founder said Bessent's plan to increase government debt purchases may portend trouble for the U.S. economy. Coupled with the Japanese government reducing its U.S. bond market exposure and surging long-dated American bond yields, Dalio said investors may want to prepare their portfolios for increased risk by owning cryptocurrencies and gold.

"I am confident that the government's financial condition is at an inflection point," Dalio wrote in a LinkedIn post published Friday. "If this is not dealt with now, the debts will build up to levels where they can't be managed without great trauma."

Dalio noted that the Treasury Department has "only limited capacity" to buy back bonds. Bessent told CNBC on Thursday that his team was going to "make a market" and that the purchases would likely top $4 billion.

The U.S. is spending about 40% more than it's bringing in, resulting in the burgeoning budget deficit, Dalio said. The U.S. budget deficit topped $432 billion in July, but Bessent told CNBC that it's likely peaked under President Donald Trump's administration.

Bessent said in the interview that a team was looking at ways to shrink spending by hundreds of billions of dollars. But Dalio said there is "very little ability" to do so given that it is either committed or considered essential.

After years of overspending, Dalio said total debt now dwarfs what the U.S. brings in each year. If the U.S. government was a business, Dalio said debt service payments would come in at roughly $11 trillion — about 200% of annual revenue.

Dalio, 77, warned the cost of repaying principal and servicing the debt will only grow over time.

To solve this, Dalio said the U.S. needs to carefully employ a three-part strategy to get the budget deficit down to 3% of gross domestic product.

First, Dalio said the U.S. government needs to reduce its spending. Second, he said tax revenue needs to be raised. Finally, the New York native and Harvard Business School alumni said lower interest rates were needed.

"All three need to happen concurrently so as to prevent any one from being too large," Dalio said. "If any one is too large, the adjustment will be traumatic."

Dalio cautioned against ramming through these adjustments by "force." For instance, "it would be very bad if the Federal Reserve unnaturally forced interest rates down," he said.

Dalio said it's important to to take steps now, while the economy is healthy. An economy in recession requires increased government spending, he said.

Dalio said the exact timing of a debt crisis can be swayed by variables ranging from military conflict to political change. On its current trajectory, the U.S. could enter such a crisis in as early as one year or as late as five. "My guess, which I suppose will be a bad one, is that it will come in three years, give or take two, if the course we're on is not changed."

To prepare, Dalio recommended investors are underweight debt assets, such as bonds.

As much as 10% to 15% of a portfolio could land in gold, as well as "a bit" of bitcoin, the hedge fund founder said.

Dalio's post came at the tail end of a volatile week for U.S. financial markets. Rising long-term Treasury yields have pressured stocks, leading the S&P 500 to snap a a three-week-long advance.

#3065. Beyond Detecting Fakes: Assuring Identity And Verifying Authorization

Krishnaveni Palanivelu, SVP Cybersecurity Architect, Financial Services.

​Imagine a bank’s fraud team reviewing two incidents. In the first, an applicant cleared onboarding using a synthetic identity assembled from stolen personal details and fabricated supporting documents. In the second, a finance employee released a payment after hearing an AI-cloned version of a familiar executive’s voice. The executive never requested it.

Both involved convincing fakes. But they exposed different failures: accepting an identity that did not represent a real applicant and accepting instructions that did not come from the person supposedly giving them. Stronger onboarding addresses the first. It cannot, by itself, prevent the second.

Generative AI reduces the time, effort and expertise required to create believable documents, faces, voices and messages. The FBI has warned that criminals use these capabilities to expand fraud and make their approaches more convincing. The Financial Crimes Enforcement Network has also reported suspicious activity involving fraudulent identity documents used to bypass verification.

Attackers can vary their material, repeat attempts and exploit whichever channel offers the weakest challenge. Training employees to notice an unnatural pause or a distorted image may help today, but it is a fragile foundation for tomorrow’s payment controls.

Detection still matters. However, making it the deciding control leaves the organization dependent on recognizing the next forgery before accepting it. Leaders should ask: What independent evidence must exist before we establish a relationship or allow a consequential action?

Identity assurance establishes confidence that someone is who they claim to be. It connects the applicant, supporting evidence and subsequent credentials to a real identity. The next checks concern authorization and intent: Is this person permitted to act, and what evidence shows they knowingly approved this specific request?

A customer can authenticate successfully and still be manipulated into paying a criminal. An employee can recognize a voice and mistake familiarity for permission. Authentication establishes control of a credential, but it does not establish informed intent.

In my article on non-human identity, I argued for attributable actions, defined permissions and accountable ownership across machines and agents. The same discipline must govern human interactions: establish who is acting, preserve that identity through the workflow and verify authority at the point of consequence.

In banking, account opening and authorized-push-payment fraud require different interventions. Onboarding should corroborate identity evidence against trustworthy sources and examine whether the applicant, device and submitted material belong together. A payment from an established customer requires transaction context: a new beneficiary, an unusual amount or signs that someone is directing the customer through the process. Another login challenge may add little protection against persuasion.

In healthcare, identity assurance can help prevent an impostor from gaining access to a patient portal, but releasing records or changing a caregiver’s access requires a separate authorization decision. Confirming the patient’s identity does not automatically establish that another person should receive their information.

Benefits administration presents a similar split. Establishing that a claimant exists does not prove eligibility, and verifying eligibility does not authorize every later change. Redirecting a benefit payment should trigger verification tied to that change, using contact details established before the request.

Across these settings, assurance belongs at the decision where harm becomes possible.

I would start with the highest-consequence journeys: opening an account, recovering access, changing payment details, releasing sensitive records and moving money. For each, identify the evidence required, the accountable owner and the conditions that should pause execution.

Layer identity checks deliberately. Document validation, authoritative-source checks, liveness, device signals and behavioral history should contribute different evidence. Five checks derived from the same compromised document do not create five independent reasons for confidence. Liveness detection, which confirms a real, live person is present (rather than a photo, replay or synthetic video), also needs protection against injected media; a live-looking face is insufficient if the capture process itself can be bypassed, for example, by injecting a pre-recorded or AI-generated video directly into the system rather than presenting it to a real camera. NIST’s identity-proofing guidance explicitly addresses forged media and injection attacks.

Consequential actions require confirmation through a separately established channel. A voice or video call should never, by itself, authorize a payment or sensitive change. Present the actual recipient, amount and action in a trusted application, and require approval bound to those details.

Independence is essential. Calling a number supplied during the suspicious conversation simply returns the organization to the attacker. Account recovery and contact detail changes deserve equivalent scrutiny because they can undermine every later confirmation.

Even a transaction-specific approval cannot prove that someone understands a scam. Unusual payments may require a cooling-off period, a targeted warning or a conversation with a trained specialist.

I previously argued that security reviews should follow information through its lifecycle. Fraud assurance needs that perspective too.

Govern your own generative AI with equal care. Inventory customer-facing assistants and internal agents, restrict their access and prevent conversational output from becoming authority to change records or release funds. Test whether manipulated inputs can persuade an assistant to bypass verification or expose information useful for impersonation.

These controls carry costs. Additional checks can delay customers, exclude people with limited documentation and generate false positives. Provide accessible alternatives and measure abandonment and mistaken rejection alongside fraud outcomes.

As I argued in my ORF America commentary, cybersecurity affects economic security because failures undermine the services and confidence on which commerce depends.

The fraud metrics reported to the board should lead with realized fraud losses reported both before recoveries and after recoveries, measured against transaction value and broken out by fraud type. Track customer harm, recovery time and legitimate activity blocked alongside them. Detection rates remain diagnostic measures; they are not the outcome. The practical test is whether fewer fraudulent actions succeed, less money is lost and legitimate people can still get things done.​

#3064. Applying for Spousal Social Security Benefits in 2027? 3 Things You Need to Know.

Spousal benefits have some unique rules that are worth knowing before you sign up.

By Kailey Hagen, CFP® – Nov 19, 2026 at 7:00PM EST

Spousal Social Security checks tend to be a lot smaller than retirement benefits, averaging just $988 in October 2026 compared to $2,092 for retirement checks. But they can still make a meaningful difference to your household's budget in 2027.

Spousal benefits have a few rules that make them different from retirement benefits, and it's important to understand them if you plan to apply for these checks next year. Here are three of the biggest differences you should be aware of.

You must be at least 62 or older to claim a spousal Social Security benefit. But even at this age, you can’t sign up if your partner is not yet receiving the partner's own retirement benefit. If you're eligible for a retirement benefit on your own work record, you may claim this in the meantime. Otherwise, you have to wait for your partner to apply first.

It's important that you and your spouse are both on the same page about when each of you will apply so that you can maximize your household income. If you haven't already talked through your plans, now is a great time to do so before you try to apply for Social Security benefits in 2027.

Spousal benefits are also available to ex-spouses if you were married to a qualifying worker for at least 10 years before divorcing and you haven’t remarried. Your ex's remarriage will not affect your eligibility to claim benefits on the ex's work record.

Benefits for ex-spouses work almost exactly the same as benefits for current spouses, except you don't need to wait for your ex to sign up for benefits first. As long as you've been divorced for at least two years and are 62 or older, you can claim a spousal benefit on your ex's work record, provided it's worth more than your own retirement benefit.

Social Security retirement benefits continue to grow for every month you delay your application until you qualify for your maximum checks at age 70. But spousal benefits only grow until you reach your full retirement age (FRA). This is 67 if you were born in 1960 or later.

Make sure you sign up by this point at the latest, unless you can’t because your spouse hasn't applied yet. If you fail to sign up by your FRA, contact the Social Security Administration right away to get the process started and to see if you qualify for any retroactive benefits.

#3063. The Inventory Accuracy Problem Smart Fulfillment Centers Still Need To Solve

Amruth Puppala | Senior Engineering Manager | Walmart.

​Walk into a modern fulfillment center, and you will see how much warehouse operations have changed. Robots move products, software coordinates thousands of orders and inventory systems track merchandise across receiving, storage and shipping.

Yet, even with these advances, a familiar problem remains.

A system shows that an item is available, but when someone goes to pick it, the product is not there. The inventory record may be correct on paper, but the physical reality is different. What seems like a minor discrepancy can quickly turn into additional searches, picking delays, order reallocation or missed shipping commitments.

This raises an important question. Instead of simply knowing how much inventory we have, shouldn’t we also know how reliable that information is?

Fulfillment centers and distribution centers handle enormous volumes of inventory movements every day. Products are received, stored, replenished, picked and shipped, often through a combination of manual processes and automated equipment.

Even with well-designed systems, discrepancies can occur.

A pallet may be placed in the wrong location. A receiving transaction might be completed before the merchandise is physically verified. Damaged inventory may not be removed from available stock immediately. Sometimes, a picking exception is recorded without the underlying inventory issue being resolved.

Warehouses already have processes to investigate these situations. Cycle counting, reconciliation and exception management are essential parts of daily operations.

However, many discrepancies are discovered only after they begin affecting order fulfillment.

By that point, the operations team is responding to a problem rather than preventing it.

One idea worth exploring is assigning a confidence score to inventory records based on the operational evidence supporting them.

Consider two storage locations, each showing 100 units available. The first location was recently verified, and its last several picking transactions were completed successfully. The second location has experienced repeated picking failures, unexplained quantity adjustments and an unresolved exception.

Both locations show the same available quantity, but they clearly do not carry the same level of operational confidence.

Today, many inventory decisions focus primarily on quantity, location and availability. Adding a confidence score could give warehouse systems another useful signal when making those decisions.

The score would not represent a new inventory balance. It would indicate how much confidence the system has in the existing record.

This could help teams identify which locations need verification and which inventory discrepancies are most likely to affect upcoming orders.

Recent advances in AI create an opportunity to evaluate these signals continuously rather than relying entirely on scheduled checks.

A system could monitor receiving transactions, inventory movements, picking results and adjustment history to identify patterns that deserve attention.

For example, repeated picking failures at the same location might suggest a discrepancy. An unusual sequence of inventory adjustments could indicate a process issue. A location that has not been physically verified for an extended period could warrant additional scrutiny, particularly if the inventory is needed for upcoming shipments.

Rather than treating each event independently, the system could examine the broader history and determine whether further verification is justified.

Newer AI models can also help interpret exception notes and other information that traditional rule-based systems may struggle to analyze consistently. Where cameras or robotic sensors are available, their observations could provide additional supporting evidence.

The important point is that AI should help identify where to investigate, not make inventory adjustments without verification.

Cycle counting is one area where this approach could have immediate practical value.

Most distribution centers already use scheduled counting programs, often based on inventory value, product movement or operational requirements. Those methods are useful and should continue.

However, a fixed schedule does not always account for problems developing during the day.

Imagine a location that reports 100 units in stock. Several picking attempts fail within a short period, but the inventory quantity remains unchanged. Instead of waiting for the next scheduled count, the system could recommend that the location be checked sooner. The priority could increase if those units are needed for orders approaching their shipping cutoff.

This would allow inventory teams to focus attention where a potential discrepancy is most likely to cause operational disruption. It could also help avoid unnecessary checks in locations where recent transactions consistently support the recorded inventory.

I would not recommend introducing another large platform to solve this problem. Most warehouses already generate much of the information needed. The opportunity is to make better use of it.

A practical starting point would be to combine inventory movement history, picking exceptions, recent count results and upcoming order demand.

Simple rules could first identify obvious discrepancies. Machine learning could then help recognize less predictable patterns, while newer language models could assist with interpreting operational notes and explaining why a location has been flagged.

The warehouse management system would remain responsible for inventory records and transactions. Any quantity correction would continue through established verification and approval processes.

For an initial rollout, I would focus on a limited number of high-volume locations and measure whether the approach reduces repeated picking failures, shortens discrepancy resolution time and improves verification productivity.

Accuracy matters, but so does the amount of additional work introduced. If the system generates too many unnecessary checks, it has not solved the underlying problem.

Fulfillment technology has made progress in improving speed, automation and visibility. But visibility alone does not guarantee accuracy.

A warehouse can have a view of its recorded inventory and still make the wrong fulfillment decision when those records do not match physical conditions.

The next opportunity is to make inventory reliability a continuous part of warehouse operations, rather than something evaluated through periodic reconciliation.

The goal is not to eliminate inventory discrepancies. That would be unrealistic in a continuously operating facility. The goal is to recognize problems earlier, direct people to locations and prevent disruptions before they affect customer orders.

The recently renovated Signia by Hilton Diplomat Beach Resort offers great views, a well-equipped fitness center and delicious food.

Hilton is making a big play in South Florida with its Signia by Hilton Diplomat Beach Resort. The massive 1,000-room property — which underwent an $80 million renovation before opening under the Signia Hilton brand in May 2026 — sits on the beach in Hollywood, Florida, just outside of Fort Lauderdale.

The resort caters primarily to business and group travelers (it’s attached to a massive events space), but it’s also a strong option for vacationers looking for some R&R. The main downside: The location isn’t great if your trip primarily revolves around off-property excursions, dining and nightlife.

Room rates typically run $300 to $600 a night, depending on the season, but you can also use Hilton Honors benefits to make your stay more affordable. There’s also a resort fee of $59 per night — but Hilton waives that when you book using Hilton points.

Hilton covered the cost of my stay for two nights, but the opinions in this review are my own. Here’s what guests can expect at this oceanfront resort.

Since the Signia by Hilton Diplomat Beach Resort is part of Hilton Honors, there are several ways to book a stay there.

If you’re using Hilton points, expect to pay 70,000 to 80,000 points a night when standard rooms are available. Hilton elite status — a benefit you can earn by holding any Hilton Honors credit card — gets you the fifth-night-free perk, where you stay for at least five nights but pay for four when booking with points.

For example, if you were to stay five nights at 80,000 points a night, you’d pay 320,000 points total, bringing down your average nightly rate to 64,000 points.

You can also book using Hilton’s generous free night certificates, which can be used at almost any property in the portfolio. If you hold the Hilton Honors American Express Aspire Card, you automatically get a certificate each year. It’s also possible to earn certificates through reaching spending thresholds on the card and on the Hilton Honors American Express Surpass® Card. Terms apply.

Make sure to check the cash rate against the points rate to make sure you’re getting good value from your redemption. NerdWallet values Hilton points at 0.4 cent apiece.

For cash bookings of two nights or more, you might consider using The Hotel Collection via American Express’ travel portal for eligible cardholders. Eligible bookings come with benefits like a $100 property credit and other amenities subject to availability, including a room upgrade, early check-in and late checkout.

Keep in mind that third-party bookings typically don’t earn Hilton points or count toward elite status qualification.

It’s hard to miss the Signia by Hilton Diplomat Beach Resort, with its signature H-shaped facade and sleek white-and-glass exterior.

Stepping into the hotel, I was immediately struck by the lush greenery filling the entrance and indoor courtyard. The grand lobby has soaring glass ceilings, giving the space a greenhouse feel, although the strong air conditioning keeps you cool.

Despite its massive size, it doesn’t have a sprawling layout, which I appreciated. Everything is close together, and you can walk from the check-in counter to any of the indoor restaurants in under a minute.

I stayed in an oceanfront suite with a balcony, which was spacious and had a fun beachy vibe. To get to the rooms, you’ll need to use either the north or south tower elevator banks.

In the living room, there was a large sitting area featuring a TV, a couch, an accent chair and a four-person high-top table.

Although I didn’t spend too much time on the balcony — the October balminess was a bit too much for me — I enjoyed stepping out each morning to admire the view.

The bedroom had a king bed with extremely comfortable bedding and an oversized chair that was a great spot to relax and read a book by the window.

The bathroom was spacious, featuring a shower and a separate tub (something every room has).

Even the standard room I toured felt roomy. I liked that it shared similar elements with the suite, including the oversized lounge chair.

This is what you’d normally get when booking a room at the cheapest points price.

There are several dining venues on the property, ranging from a grab-and-go cafe to a high-end steakhouse. It is a luxury resort, so expect the prices to reflect that.

For breakfast, you can head to Palmea Kitchen, which is also open for lunch. I had the breakfast buffet, which offered a nice spread of classics, from hot food items and pastries to cold cuts and smoked salmon.

If you don’t have time for a sit-down breakfast, you can head next door to The Press, which offers made-to-order and grab-and-go food options throughout the day. You can also get smoothies, juices, snacks, pastries and other sweet treats.

The Canteen is another grab-and-go option that also sells snacks, drinks, souvenirs and sundries, similar to a convenience store.

For lunch and dinner, try Solara. It doesn’t have a traditional restaurant feel, as it’s mostly an indoor-outdoor bar space. One side connects to the lobby, while the other side faces the Solara adults-only pool.

It serves a lunch menu, as well as a substantial bar food menu that’s available late into the night.

You can also eat at Playa Beach Bar & Grill, a beachside restaurant serving Latin-inspired cuisine. I enjoyed spending a lazy lunch there and watching the waves crash onto the shore.

For a fancy sit-down dinner, go to Diplomat Prime, the property’s steakhouse. We had a group dinner at the restaurant, and the meats were, of course, the highlight. But don’t sleep on the seafood, which was also delicious.

One of the best parts of the Dip, as it’s affectionately known, is its location right on the beach. Guests can access the stretch of beach directly adjacent to the property. But it’s not a private beach, so you might encounter crowds.

I didn’t spend any time on the beach itself — it was extremely windy while I was there — but the hotel’s resort fee includes amenities like a beach lounge (umbrella not included), a daily one-hour kayak or paddleboard rental, and beachfront yoga classes.

If you don’t want to get sand everywhere, you can head to one of the three pool options: the adults-only Solara pool, the family-friendly lagoon pool and the Verandah Social Club for those 21 and older (requires paid access).

The family-friendly lagoon spans the length of the property and runs beneath the Solara pool. It also has its own hot tub.

I spent an afternoon in a cabana at the Verandah Social Club, which has some smaller plunge pools and a hot tub.

I appreciated the attentive service from the staff there, who constantly checked on whether guests needed anything.

If you’re looking for other ways to stay active, head to the two-story fitness center, featuring a variety of equipment like free weights, exercise bikes, a rowing machine and treadmills.

Next door, you’ll find the spa and wellness center. I had a relaxing massage that incorporated hot stones and aromatherapy.

The locker rooms come with a sauna and steam room, although I wished there were more amenities like a hot tub and cold plunge.

One of the resort fee inclusions is complimentary high-intensity interval training workout classes at the gym across the street. I signed up for an early morning class. The instructor was friendly, and it was a great way to start my day.

Other amenities include a complimentary one-hour e-bike rental each day, as well as a kids’ club with various activities (but drop-off fees apply).

I had a fantastic stay at this resort, but I’d recommend it for a specific traveler.

If you’re planning to stay on-property your entire trip, it’s a great option. That’s probably why it’s such a popular convention hotel, since everything you need is easily accessible.

I loved the hotel’s design, including the jungle-like atmosphere in the lobby, and I found the dining options to be tasty, albeit pricey.

But if your trip revolves around visiting Miami attractions, you’ll likely want to stay closer to the action.

#3060. Beyond Tokens: Why Intelligence Per Watt Is The Metric That Matters

By Dr. Steven Woo, fellow and distinguished inventor at Rambus.

​AI progress centers on tokens: tokens processed, tokens generated, tokens per second and tokens per watt. And because tokens are easy to count, they’ve become the default unit of AI performance. But token-based metrics are only part of the story and miss what users really want. A more useful metric, and one closer to the industry’s goal, is how much intelligence a system delivers per watt.​

“Intelligence Per Watt: Measuring Intelligence Efficiency Of Local AI,” published in November 2025 by a Stanford team, found that small local models can accurately answer 88.7% of single-turn chat and reasoning queries. Intelligence efficiency—capability delivered per watt—improved 5.3 times between 2023 and 2025, roughly 3.1 times from better models and 1.7 times from better hardware—factors that compound rather than add. This efficiency, not pure token throughput, will determine how well AI can keep scaling.​​

Ask a CFO, CIO or CTO running AI workloads what worries them, and it’s rarely whether they’re generating enough tokens. Although tokenmaxxing has become a metric that some companies use to measure AI engagement, others see the dangers of simply measuring token consumption independent of productivity and delivered value. Several companies are cutting back on token spending, with Uber among others stating in May 2026 that it had already spent its 2026 AI budget, and their COO adding it was becoming “harder to justify” their internal AI costs. There’s a growing call for valuemaxxing, which directs teams toward measurable outcomes based on the value being generated by these tokens.​

Concerns about measuring token usage are compounded by the fact that reasoning models don’t produce a single response per query; they work through an internal chain of intermediate tokens the user never sees. Published work on model development puts these generations in the thousands to tens of thousands of tokens. That means a query can consume far more resources than its visible output suggests.​

The pressure to continuously improve value and reduce the cost per token extends beyond inference bills. TrendForce expected server DRAM contract prices to rise 13% to 18% quarter over quarter in Q3 2026, so memory, one of the critical workhorses for AI processing, is getting more expensive as it’s being asked to do more.​​

For hardware companies, that changes the questions being asked. It stops being how many tokens a chip can generate and becomes how much bandwidth memory can deliver per dollar and per watt, and how these metrics will improve in the future.​

For decades, the semiconductor industry relied on Dennard scaling to improve power efficiency. As transistors shrank, they drew less power, so more compute arrived without a matching jump in energy use. That relationship broke down in the mid-2000s as transistors continued to shrink, but the automatic power benefit that used to come with each new process node no longer followed.​

With this lever gone, the industry had to substitute architectural changes for what used to be a by-product of process scaling. Memory is where much of that effort is going: Moving data is a major consumer of system power, making it one of the largest levers to pull.​

The case for stacking DRAM directly on top of a processor has been argued for years. The energy needed to move a bit scales with distance. A DRAM stack beside a processor sits 10 to 12 millimeters away. But stacking the DRAM on top of a processor cuts the distance to about a millimeter. Bandwidth improves separately: Memory beside the processor feeds data through the die’s edges, so interconnect scales with perimeter; stacking can move data through the whole face of a die, allowing bandwidth to scale with area.​

Stacking DRAM has become a focus topic of the semiconductor industry. At Hot Chips 2026, Samsung released more details about zHBM, which places the processor beneath the DRAM stack and claims roughly 70% lower I/O power than the previous generation. That’s what more bandwidth per dollar and per watt looks like.​

Stacking has manufacturing and engineering challenges. Although silicon conducts heat reasonably well, a stack of DRAM sitting on a hot processor acts like a blanket and prevents heat from being moved away. Samsung’s answer is thinner dies and smaller four-high stacks rather than the 12-high or 16-high configurations conventional HBM supports. The energy saved on data movement is coupled with less thermal resistance to achieve a high performance, thermally viable architecture.​

The same constraint is reshaping infrastructure above the die. Enterprise racks that once drew 20 to 30 kilowatts are heading toward hundreds of kilowatts, and eventually toward a megawatt. Power Electronics Magazine reported in January 2026 that 54 volt in-rack distribution “isn’t designed to support the megawatt-scale racks,” and that the transition to 800 volt DC begins in 2027. Copper is expensive and limits current, so when power demand climbs, voltage is the remaining variable that can rise.​

Delivering the most intelligence for a given dollar and a given watt used to be determined by two scaling trends running together: Moore’s law delivered more transistors per dollar, and Dennard scaling delivered them at lower power. Moore’s law continues, albeit at a slower pace. Dennard scaling doesn’t, so the power portion of that result now has to be engineered deliberately, architecture by architecture.​

The industry has hit walls like this before, and the solution was rarely a single breakthrough. It was a return to fundamentals: measuring the right thing and re-architecting around the real constraint instead of the metric that’s easiest to report.​

For the CFOs, CIOs and CTOs approving AI budgets, and for the hardware and software teams underneath them, the number worth tracking isn’t simply how many tokens a system produces. It’s how much usable intelligence and value these tokens return for the dollars and the watts spent producing them.

For our aerial division, during the quarter, we brought Teal Drones and FlightWave Aerospace together under Red Cat Aerial, creating a unified organization and a single point of engagement for customers across our aerial systems portfolio. Beyond organizational simplification, the combination is intended to improve the speed and consistency of product development, manufacturing, sales and customer support while enabling technologies and customer relationships to be leveraged across multiple platforms.

Efficiencies gained through this new structure effectuated a 10% reduction in workforce and recurring expenses. This structure is intended to strengthen execution across our aerial portfolio as we continue scaling manufacturing and supporting customer requirements. We also introduced TRICHON, a hand-launched, long-endurance vertical takeoff and landing tricopter designed for intelligence, surveillance and reconnaissance missions. TRICHON is the first new platform introduced under Red Cat Aerial and expands the mission profiles and customer requirements we can address. Now to discuss our Blue Ops maritime portfolio. Much of 2026 has been about launching Blue Ops and building the foundation required to support a meaningful maritime autonomy business through internal growth and targeted partnerships.

With our expanded portfolio of maritime systems, we introduced a unified naming convention and added new vessels to our offering, the Blue Ops B-Series portfolio of U.S.-designed and built uncrewed surface vessels. The portfolio includes the B-26, formerly Variant 7; the B-18 tactical and one-way attack platform; and the B-39 platform, purpose-built for logistics and persistent maritime defense missions. The B-18 entered sea trials ahead of its original schedule and the B-39 entered low-rate production. Both platforms are available for orders. We also continue building out our 155,000-square-foot facility in Valdosta, Georgia, to support production, integration and testing for U.S. and allied defense customers. Alongside expansion of our portfolio is our expansion into targeted partnerships.

Blue Ops entered a strategic partnership with Florida Atlantic University's Harbor Branch Oceanographic Institute to strengthen development, testing and system integration. This provides access to a secure deepwater facility, direct ocean access and specialized marine engineering resources. We also partnered with HavocAI to integrate collaborative autonomy, software and command and control capabilities across the B-Series portfolio, supporting coordinated multi-vessel operations and joint customer engagement. In addition, our partnership with Sine Engineering is focused on integrating advanced technologies across Blue Ops USVs and Red Cat Aerial's UAVs, reinforcing the cross-platform nature of our strategy. Also to address Steyr Motors, Steyr is not just a company who manufactures diesel engines for USVs.

Red Cat's acquisition of Steyr Motors adds a power systems company to its portfolio. Power Systems. Please let those words sink in for a moment. This is important -- this is important because power is what determines how far and how long an autonomous system can operate. Steyr's engines already propel Blue Ops' unmanned surface vessels, and the same technology extends across the broader autonomy stack, powering manned, unmanned ground and marine vehicles and further extension of autonomous reach through mobile power units.

This partnership is critical -- a critical enabler of range and endurance, extending the reach of autonomous platforms across the maritime, ground and expeditionary domains while strengthening European supply chain resilience, sales and integration across its product lines. Steyr's propulsion capabilities will support the continued development of Blue Ops, while Red Cat's autonomy portfolio and U.S. defense relationships can create new avenues and growth for Steyr technology. We are excited about the momentum we have established and look forward to carrying it into 2027 as we focus on converting a growing opportunity pipeline into funded programs, production orders and customer deliveries.

Our near-term operating priorities are clear: convert customer engagement into funded orders and scheduled deliveries; maintain disciplined inventory and working capital management; advance the commercialization and integration of Red Cat Aerial and the Blue Ops B-Series portfolio; continue strengthening quality, supply chain resilience and program execution. We believe the capabilities and infrastructure are in place to support a meaningfully larger business -- the next phase is about demonstrating repeatable execution, converting pipeline into funded backlog into on-time deliveries and higher volume into better gross margin and cash efficiency. Those are the operating proof points we expect investors and customers to use in measuring our progress. I'll now turn the time over to Christian to discuss our financial results.

Christian Morrison: Thank you, Chris. Red Cat's financial performance for the third quarter of 2026 reflects continued year-over-year revenue growth as we continue building a durable, combat-proven business and investing in the manufacturing capacity, product development and operating infrastructure required to support our long-term growth strategy. For the third quarter of 2026, revenue was $11.8 million, representing an increase of 22% from $9.6 million in the prior year period. For the first 9 months of 2026, revenue totaled $47.4 million compared with $14.5 million in the prior year period, an increase of 227%. The quarterly increase was primarily due to drone deliveries to the U.S. Air Force and other customers, while year-to-date growth reflects increased drone deliveries to the U.S.

Army, the commencement of deliveries to the Japan Ground Self-Defense Force and additional deliveries to other branches of the U.S. military and allied nations. While revenue fell below our expectations, these investments are building the foundation for sustained growth. Our priority is to translate that foundation into consistent deliveries, stronger margins and improved financial performance. We were disappointed that our FANG FPV offering was not selected as a finalist in the Drone Dominance II competition. Our third quarter revenue expectations included anticipated deliveries associated with this opportunity, which did not materialize and partially contributed to revenue falling below our expectations. Nevertheless, the evaluation identified meaningful strengths.

Teal's production capability scored at the very top compared to the field median, and operator feedback placed usability in the 91st percentile with training results as the strongest at the event. These findings provide a foundation for continued development, while the testing identified specific priorities for improvement in low-light operations and subterranean performance. Our focus is on building on those strengths and incorporating the evaluation feedback to enhance FANG's competitiveness. FlightWave's revenue also fell short of our expectations this quarter. We believe strongly in the product's potential, customer demand and remain committed to addressing the development, production and commercialization challenges that have affected its progress.

Through the integration of FlightWave into Red Cat Aerial, we are bringing together resources, technical expertise and leadership to advance our products with a focus on product reliability, consistent execution and customer readiness. As part of that integration, we eliminated overlapping roles and expect those changes to lower our ongoing operating costs. While meaningful work remains, we are optimistic about FlightWave's opportunity to deliver a differentiated capability to U.S. and allied customers and contribute to Red Cat's long-term growth. Gross profit for the third quarter was approximately $0.1 million, representing a 0.6% gross margin compared with gross profit of $0.6 million and 6.6% gross margin in the third quarter of 2025.

The decrease was primarily due to higher inventory scrap at FlightWave, warranty expense, increased returns and unabsorbed manufacturing overhead and labor resulting from excess production capacity. Our improvement efforts at our FlightWave division began in earnest in Q2 and have focused on ensuring we have the right managers in place to lead our FlightWave division while addressing the root causes of scrap and warranty claims and strengthening product quality before shipment. These actions are intended to improve product quality and manufacturing efficiency while preserving our ability to support higher volumes and deliver a reliable product for the warfighter or end user.

Capital expenditures totaled approximately $17.1 million during the first 9 months of 2026, which primarily includes building out manufacturing capacity and operating infrastructure at our 155,000-square-foot Blue Ops facility in Valdosta, Georgia. This facility gives us room to increase production as customer orders ramp. We are proud of what our Blue Ops team has built in Valdosta, and we're grateful to the city, local and state officials in Georgia for their support. Net cash used in operating activities was $156.8 million for the first 9 months of 2026 compared with $52.7 million in the prior year period. This increase was driven primarily by inventory purchases and operating investments, partially offset by accounts receivable collections.

Our strategic investments in future growth remained significant during the quarter. Total operating expenses were approximately $43.5 million compared with $18.2 million in the prior year period, reflecting continued investments in engineering personnel, prototype development and testing, sales and marketing resources and the corporate and technology infrastructure required to support our growth objectives. Operating loss was $43.4 million for the third quarter compared with $17.5 million in the prior year period. Net loss was $40.4 million or $0.26 per basic and diluted share compared with a net loss of $16.0 million or $0.16 per basic and diluted share in the third quarter of 2025.

We are prioritizing spending around existing customer commitments and development programs with the clearest path to commercialization. The integration of our Red Cat Aerial business has provided an opportunity to consolidate overlapping activities and direct resources towards our highest priority programs. Research and development expense increased to approximately $16.1 million during the quarter from $6.0 million in the prior year period. This increase was primarily due to engineering personnel costs at our aerial divisions, prototype development with a particular focus on Blue Ops prototypes, testing and other expenses associated with the development of new and enhanced drone platforms and related technologies. Our balance sheet strength and liquidity position continue to provide us with substantial financial flexibility.

As of September 30, 2026, we held $242.7 million in cash compared to $167.9 million at year-end 2025. Working capital totaled approximately $355.8 million, providing resources to support our operating requirements and strategic growth initiatives. This liquidity gives us flexibility to execute existing programs and selectively pursue opportunities that we believe can create lasting shareholder value. Our inventory strategy continues to be an important component of our growth, production readiness and investment in shorter delivery times. Inventory totaled approximately $117.2 million at quarter end, up from $23.5 million at year-end 2025. The increase in inventory during the quarter was primarily driven by the strategic procurement of key components and materials to support production of our Hellcat ISR drones.

Additionally, inventory levels at our Blue Ops division increased significantly as we prepared for anticipated customer deliveries while establishing appropriate safety stock levels to support production readiness. We remain focused on converting inventory into customer shipments while maintaining disciplined working capital management. We view our balance sheet and inventory position as strategic assets. With approximately $243 million of cash and significant investments in inventory, manufacturing and technology development, we believe we have the financial resources to support future growth opportunities as they emerge. At the same time, disciplined capital deployment and converting those investments into revenue and improved operating performance remains important priorities. Turning to our outlook. We continue to see substantial opportunities across domestic and international markets.

However, since we last provided our full year revenue target, anticipated funding and contract awards have not materialized on the timelines we expected, and the outcome of the Drone Dominance program's Gauntlet II has removed an anticipated contributor to our near-term revenue outlook. These developments have changed both the timing and expected contribution of the opportunities underlying our prior target, and we no longer expect to achieve our previously announced full year 2026 revenue target and are withdrawing that target. Uncertainty surrounding defense funding, customer procurement decisions, customer acceptances and delivery schedules limits our ability to predict the timing and amount of future revenue. Our focus remains on converting opportunities into funded orders and executing on customer deliveries.

Regarding our proposed acquisition of Steyr Motors AG, the acquisition adds an iconic brand to the Red Cat family, an established revenue base, which approximated 60% concentration in defense in 2025 and 2024 and reported an order backlog exceeding EUR 300 million, providing a substantial base of potential future revenue. Steyr also brings accretive gross margins and exposure to additional defense customers and programs. Our investment case centers on growing Steyr's external engine business, complementary synergies and strengthening propulsion capabilities for Blue Ops. We will evaluate success through cash generation, returns on invested capital and measurable operating improvements with particular attention to preserving sufficient liquidity to execute Red Cat's existing programs. Several factors support our long-term growth opportunity.

First, defense and national security customers continue to prioritize affordable, mission-ready autonomous and unmanned systems. Second, our expanded manufacturing footprint, inventory position and product portfolio provide the operational foundation to support higher delivery volumes as orders materialize. Third, our investments and partnerships across Red Cat Aerial, Blue Ops, Apium, HavocAI, Anduril, Sine Engineering and Quaze broaden our capabilities across aerial and maritime platforms, collaborative autonomy, command and control, cross-platform integration and wireless power. We continue to see multiple growth vectors across aerial and maritime autonomy, supported by an expanding product portfolio and continued customer engagement. Our focus is on translating those opportunities into funded orders, deliveries and stronger financial performance.

Market conditions continue to support long-term demand for autonomous and unmanned systems across U.S. and allied defense customers. Combined with our liquidity position, expanded product portfolio and manufacturing infrastructure, we believe Red Cat is positioned to participate in the ongoing modernization of defense technology while remaining focused on execution and financial discipline. With that, I'll now turn the call over to our CEO, Jeff Thompson.

Jeffrey Thompson: Thanks, Christian. Good afternoon, everyone, and thank you for joining us. Christian and Chris have reviewed our third quarter in detail. I will be brief and move on to Q&A. I'm going to review our opportunities going forward for both Red Cat Aerial and Blue Ops. At this time last year, our opportunity pipeline was 0 for Blue Ops. In 1 year, we've been able to prove ourselves repeatedly in exercises, crucibles, live demonstrations, private demonstrations and more. Our current opportunity pipeline for Blue Ops is approximately $2.3 billion, approximately $365 million in the U.S., with approximately $250 million funded in the U.S. INDOPACOM is approximately $2 billion and growing with approximately $1.1 billion currently funded.

This has been a great 6 months for Blue Ops and want to congratulate the team for getting their first B-26 purchase order, which will ship next week. We splashed our first boat last December and 11 months later, we have our first customer. Let's move on to Red Cat Aerial. The Red Cat Aerial opportunity pipeline is approximately $440 million. Almost all of this is in Europe and INDOPACOM. Most of these are unannounced tenders, so we will not put a number for funded opportunities until we have public acknowledgment of these opportunities by their governments, so we will consider them not funded. Some detail on Ukraine.

We have 4 letters of requests and expect a few more this month. The LORs add up to approximately $100 million. We expect to receive more as the Hellcat continues to perform in theater. We believe the Hellcat is the only made-in-U.S.A. Group 1 drone that is not an FPV drone working in the Ukraine front. This work in Ukraine and other theaters will benefit the U.S. warfighter. Finally, I want to congratulate Apium for getting downselected 3 times and heading to Crucible 4 of Swarm Forge with our partner, Anduril. This is a great achievement and a first in swarming. Jeffrey Thompson: Yes. So we -- well, we're starting to have revenue with Blue Ops. We -- I would say the mix is still going to be still dominated by aerial, but there will be a decent number that will be from the maritime division, and that will be growing throughout the beginning of 2027.

Mike Latimore: Got it. And talked about your first purchase order for the B-26. Can you just elaborate a little bit on that? What's the initial use case? And where could that expand?

Jeffrey Thompson: Yes. It's a traditional -- when people start buying from the government, they bought 2 B-26s. It's attached to a much larger order if things go well. But as we said, we're delivering next week immediately to start working with the customer; as things progress, it could turn into a much larger contract.

Mike Latimore: Great. And then with regard to Steyr Motors, a number of potential benefits there. I guess, are they -- like, how important is it for new USV or Blue Ops wins, let's say, closing new deals for the Blue Ops business?

And it also opens up Europe. We're very excited to invest in Austria and continue to build the efficiencies that in this company. Operator: Our next question comes from the line of Austin Bohlig with Needham.

Austin Bohlig: I guess first one, we'll just stay on Steyr Motors. Guys, like, what are the, kind of, the key milestones we should be looking for? And, like, how is that tender offer process going?

Jeffrey Thompson: Yes. So the first big milestone is December 18. The goal is to get 50% plus 1 share. So that will be the first large milestone to completing that acquisition.

Christian Morrison: And then, Austin, there's 4 weeks after that, that it has to pass regulatory approval, 4 weeks at a minimum. So we're being realistic. So actual close date could be as early as late January.

Austin Bohlig: Okay. Okay. Helpful. And I guess you would love to dive into, like, these 4 LORs you have within Ukraine. So, like, are these basically contract orders? And then all of a sudden, we were asked to include Sine technology, which delayed us a little bit because of integration, but Sine is such an important thing for the Ukrainians, and we're one of the first U.S. companies to ever integrate Sine technologies, and it's working incredibly well. There's a massive amount that are funded already, and we expect there's -- that are different schedules than our government to also be funded.

So we think that $2 billion plus in INDOPACOM is probably going to expand pretty rapidly through the first half of 2026. But we're just very excited that our boat continues to perform. We couldn't even get a phone call back from these folks when we were trying to get in there 6 months ago. Now after people have seen our boat perform in exercises, private demonstrations. Christian Morrison: And Craig, I'll add to that a little bit. I mean, between Q2 and Q3, Blue Ops inventory went up 7x. I mean we need safety stock. We need inventory in Blue Ops period. Christian Ericson: Absolutely. I mean this is an area of the market that's rushing towards us. And it's exciting. You've got a lot of these groups out there that traditionally had relied on U.S. protection, right? They're relying on the big boys overseas to help protect them, take care of them. We've got large systems that we were able to protect them with. But now as we are telling them, hey, you need to rely on yourself a lot more, they are very interested in what we have to offer. And so this has brought in a large amount of interest and a large amount of demand that's been building up.

Jeffrey Thompson: Yes. And Craig, just to add to that -- with those 7,000 islands, that's a lot of area to cover. Some great examples. Even the B-26 can go almost 2,600 miles at slower speeds. #3055. 1 Unstoppable Stock to Buy Before It Joins NVDA and AAPL in the $1 Trillion Club

AMD looks poised to reclaim a $1 trillion market cap as Nvidia turmoil creates an opportunity.

By Marc Guberti – Nov 19, 2026 at 7:32PM EST

10 stocks we like better than Advanced Micro Devices ›

Advanced Micro Devices (AMD -7.72%) briefly became a $1 trillion company in September, but it lost that milestone after a prolonged artificial intelligence (AI) stock correction. However, the chipmaker is set to rejoin Nvidia (NVDA -3.30%) and Apple (AAPL -0.92%) as a trillion-dollar company. These are the catalysts that can drive the stock higher.

AMD has been viewed as the No. 2 graphics processing unit (GPU) chipmaker for several years, with Nvidia comfortably holding on to the top spot. However, Nvidia suddenly faces significant uncertainty with former CEO Jensen Huang out of the company and angling for a comeback.

Nvidia currently doesn't seem receptive to a reunion, and that can cost the company. Some investors argue that Huang's departure will make it difficult for Nvidia to continue innovating despite the competitive edge it has already obtained.

The AI industry is moving rapidly, and leadership complexities can cost Nvidia valuable time. It can be the difference between missing out on the latest technology and watching hyperscalers turn to alternatives.

This scenario positions AMD as the chipmaker with the most to gain from the confusion, and the company has been taking major steps to close the gap. For instance, AMD is making its chip fleet more attractive by making it much easier for developers to port existing Nvidia CUDA applications to its HIP platform.

Nvidia's CUDA was previously a major moat. Moving to another software essentially meant rewriting vast amounts of code, but that's no longer the case. If AMD can win over more businesses with an easier migration, it creates more headaches for a company already full of them.

Although Nvidia has captured most of the headlines throughout the AI boom, AMD has been quietly accelerating its growth. Data center revenue surged by 97% year over year in the third quarter, while overall revenue reached $13.4 billion, up by 45% year over year. That also represents a 16% sequential boost.

AMD CEO Lisa Su told investors that demand for its AI products is still accelerating. The chipmaker also remains confident that revenue growth will surge in the coming years, along with higher net profit margins.

AMD trades at a 30 forward price-to-earnings (P/E) ratio, which may be higher than what some investors are willing to handle. However, this same company almost doubled its net income year over year. AMD wrapped up the quarter with an 18.2% net profit margin, and if it can get closer to Nvidia's 62% net profit margin, the stock should have an easy time reclaiming a $1 trillion market cap and marching toward new highs.

#3053. Top Wall Street analysts believe in the growth potential of these 3 stocks

Geopolitical uncertainty in the Middle East and soaring bond yields weighed on global markets this past week. And investors are closely assessing the valuations of artificial intelligence stocks amid concerns about the sustainability of high spending on AI infrastructure.

Despite those continued challenges, top Wall Street analysts are bullish on the prospects of several stocks due to their long-run growth potential and exposure to lucrative business lines, including AI.

Here are three stocks favored by some of Wall Street's top pros, according to TipRanks, a platform that ranks analysts based on their past performance.

Cybersecurity company CrowdStrike Holdings (CRWD) is this week's first stock pick. The company is scheduled to announce fiscal second-quarter results on August 26.

Ahead of Q2 FY27 earnings, Truist analyst Junaid Siddiqui reiterated a buy rating on CrowdStrike stock and raised his price target to $245 from $187.50. Following CrowdStrike's impressive fiscal first-quarter performance and guidance raise, Siddiqui expects another strong quarter.

The 5-star analyst's optimism is backed by continued strength in Falcon Flex adoption and encouraging large deal activity. Siddiqui also cited continued momentum across emerging products. With the FY27 outlook assuming persistent strength in CrowdStrike's net new annual recurring revenue (ARR), Siddiqui is more focused on the longevity of key growth catalysts such as Falcon Flex adoption, platform consolidation and AI-led demand.

The analyst highlighted that talks with partners were encouraging, with pipeline generation and momentum in large deals remaining healthy in the fiscal second quarter despite tough, year-over-year comparisons.

"We continue to view CrowdStrike as one of the primary beneficiaries of platform consolidation, though we expect investors to remain focused on competitive dynamics and whether current growth levels represent a new baseline or a period of demand acceleration," the analyst said.

Siddiqui ranks No. 226 among more than 12,400 analysts tracked by TipRanks. His ratings have been profitable 80% of the time, delivering an average return of about 40%. See CrowdStrike Financials on TipRanks.

Shares of personal computer maker Dell Technologies (DELL) have rallied 251% this year, driven by strong demand for AI servers. Recently, Evercore analyst Amit Daryanani reiterated a buy rating on DELL and raised his price target to $550 from $500.

The 5-star analyst contends that while Dell's AI compute segment is getting investors' attention, the company's Storage business is underappreciated and well-positioned to drive revenue and profit acceleration. Daryanani expects the storage business to see higher demand once enterprises start to bring workload back on-premises.

The analyst highlighted that Dell's Storage business, estimated to account for only 10% of FY27 revenue, is one of the factors that could help improve profit margins, given its higher profitability compared to AI servers. Daryanani estimates that the Storage business's operating margin is currently in the low-20% range, while margins for the AI server and traditional server businesses are in the mid-single-digit and mid-teens range, respectively.

Overall, Daryanani views the Storage business as an important catalyst for three reasons: Dell has one of the broadest storage portfolios in the industry; Storage has a significantly higher margin profile than AI servers; and the shift toward proprietary, software-defined storage and AI-focused platforms.

"We think DELL's storage business is becoming increasingly strategic as AI infrastructure deployments move beyond GPU procurement and toward full stack + AI-ready architectures," said Daryanani.

Daryanani ranks No. 19 among more than 12,400 analysts tracked by TipRanks. His ratings have been successful 71% of the time, delivering an average return of 38.70%. See Dell Technologies Statistics on TipRanks.

SanDisk (SNDK) is benefiting from AI-driven demand for its memory and storage products. Following the company's 2026 Investor Day event, J.P. Morgan analyst Harlan Sur resumed research coverage of SNDK with a buy rating (it was earlier, "Not Rated") and a price target of $2,250.

The 5-star analyst believes SanDisk is well-positioned to capitalize on a structural inflection reached in NAND demand, driven by strong growth in AI inference. Sur's bullishness is based on three key factors.

First, Sur believes that SanDisk's New Business Model (NBM) framework (or long-term agreements) has enhanced its margin profile and reduced cyclicality. SNDK's eight signed NBMs represent a total contract value of $94 billion and a gross margin of about 80%, even at the floor pricing.

Second, Sur highlighted the growing NAND market and expects the total addressable market to surge from about $70 billion in calendar year 2025 to over $300 billion in 2026 and about $500 billion in 2027. Importantly, the analyst noted that data centers are the largest driver of NAND growth, as hyperscalers increasingly deploy flash for AI inference workloads.

Finally, Sur is optimistic on SanDisk due to its technology dominance. The company's BiCS10 technology is sampling ahead of schedule and has 65% more bits per wafer than BiCS8, the analyst said. Also, Sur expects SanDisk's High Bandwidth Flash to become a differentiated memory platform for AI inference.

"Layered on top, mgmt's commitment to returning 100% of excess cash flow to shareholders should drive an aggressive share count reduction trajectory that further amplifies EPS growth on a per-share basis," said Sur.

Sur ranks No. 15 among more than 12,400 analysts tracked by TipRanks. His ratings have been successful 71% of the time, delivering an average return of 43.20%. See SanDisk Ownership Structure on TipRanks.

Atmos Rewards offers six communities, each with its own travel perks and opportunities to earn bonus points

Atmos Rewards is the airline loyalty program for Alaska Airlines and Hawaiian Airlines. One of its newer features is Atmos Communities, which offer additional rewards and benefits tailored to different travel interests.

There are six communities, including two reserved for Alaska and Hawaii residents. The other four are open to members regardless of where they live. But don’t get caught up in the community names. The best choice for you may depend more on your travel plans than the groupings suggest.

Here’s how to decide which Atmos Community best fits your travel patterns.

Atmos Communities are like groups within the Atmos Rewards program that offer additional benefits based on different travel interests.

They’re free to join for Atmos Rewards members. Four communities are available to all members, while community Club 49 is reserved for Alaska residents and community Huaka’i by Hawaiian is reserved for Hawaii residents.

You can belong to only one community at a time and switch communities once per calendar year. Consider your upcoming travel plans before choosing.

Joining a community is easy: Log in to your Atmos Rewards account and navigate to “Account overview.” Select “Join a Community,” browse the options and click the “Join” button under the one you choose.

Each Atmos Community has a list of 10 destinations where members can earn bonus points and status points. Although the destinations differ by community, the rewards structure is the same.

Through Dec. 31, 2027, members can earn up to 10,000 bonus points and 10,000 status points by visiting qualifying destinations.

Here’s how many points you’ll earn as you reach each milestone:

Visit one destination, earn 100 status and bonus points.

Visit two destinations, earn 200 status and bonus points.

Visit three destinations, earn 300 status and bonus points.

Visit four destinations, earn 400 status and bonus points.

Visit five destinations, earn 500 status and bonus points.

Visit six destinations, earn 750 status and bonus points.

Visit seven destinations, earn 1,000 status and bonus points.

Visit eight destinations, earn 1,250 status and bonus points.

Visit nine destinations, earn 2,500 status and bonus points.

Visit 10 destinations, earn 3,000 status and bonus points.

The first member of each community to visit all 10 qualifying destinations during the challenge period will also earn 100,000 bonus points.

New lists of qualifying destinations for each community take effect on Jan. 1, 2028.

Here’s a closer look at the six communities, their benefits and the destinations eligible for bonus points.

Global Locals is geared toward frequent international travelers. Benefits include:

Earn 10% more status points toward Atmos elite status on flights that begin and/or end outside the U.S., including award flights.

Earn 1 status point for every 25 points transferred to Atmos Rewards from Bilt or Marriott Bonvoy.

Get 20% off Atmos Rewards Unlocked experiences.

Through Dec. 31, 2027, these 10 Oneworld Alliance hubs count toward bonus points and status points. Qualifying layovers also count toward the destination challenge, so you don’t necessarily need to make these cities your final stop.

If you frequently travel internationally or have any upcoming flights through any of these airports, including qualifying layovers, Global Locals might be a fit for you.

If you have the Atmos™ Rewards Summit Visa Infinite® credit card, you’ll earn 3 Atmos points per $1 spent on eligible Alaska and Hawaiian Airlines purchases, dining and foreign transactions. The last bonus category can be especially useful for frequent international travelers.

This community has a similar setup to Global Locals, but most of its bonus destinations are in the U.S. Here’s what you can get:

Get 20% off Atmos Rewards Unlocked experiences.

Through Dec. 31, 2027, here are the 10 destinations that count toward the bonus:

This community would be an excellent choice if your upcoming travels include several of these airports, even if dining isn't the main reason for your trips. If dining out is one of your favorite activities, check out the best credit cards for restaurants.

Active Escapes focuses on airports in outdoor-oriented destinations that are all in the U.S., save one. Benefits here are:

Through Dec. 31, 2027, here are the 10 destinations that count toward the bonus:

While these airports are gateways to national parks and other natural attractions, you don’t have to be an outdoor enthusiast to benefit. Like before, don’t let the heading sway you. Rather, consider the destinations before you decide.

Families On the Go might appeal to you if you redeem Atmos Rewards for your children. Benefits include:

Get 20% of your points back on eligible award flights for kids 12 and under after you complete your trip.

Get 20% off Atmos Rewards Unlocked experiences.

Through Dec. 31, 2027, these destinations qualify for bonus points and status points:

This community may be especially valuable if you regularly book award flights for children 12 and under. Even if you don't travel with kids, it could be worth considering if its qualifying airports align better with your travel plans than those of other communities.

Exclusively for Alaska residents, Club 49 offers rewards that are focused on travel to, from and within the state:

Two free checked bags when traveling to or from Alaska on Alaska Airlines or Hawaiian Airlines.

Three free checked bags when traveling within Alaska on Alaska Airlines.

Two Travel Now discounts per year for 30% off one-way refundable Y-class fares on Alaska Airlines, booked within four days of departure for travel to, from or within Alaska.

Ship cargo within Alaska for $49 plus tax (weight, size and content limits apply).

Get 20% off Atmos Rewards Unlocked experiences.

Baggage benefits don’t combine with other free checked bag allowances, such as those that come with some Alaska credit cards. However, they apply to everyone traveling on the same reservation.

Through Dec. 31, 2027, here are the 10 destinations that count toward the bonus offers:

While this community is only for Alaskans, you might decide one of the other communities more closely matches your travel plans — especially if you already have an Alaska credit card with free baggage benefits. However, if you ship a lot of cargo or think you’ll use the Travel Now discounts, those are special benefits that may sway you to choose Club 49.

Hawaii residents have their own community just for them: Huaka’i by Hawaiian. It offers benefits focused on interisland travel:

Two free checked bags on neighbor island flights on Hawaiian Airlines, including sports equipment like surfboards and golf bags.

Quarterly fare discounts of 10% off one neighbor island booking, or 20% off for eligible Hawaiian Airlines® World Elite Mastercard® and Atmos™ Rewards Visa® cardholders.

Earn 50% more points and status points on flights between Hawaiian islands beginning Jan. 1, 2027.

Get 20% off Atmos Rewards Unlocked experiences.

The 10 destinations eligible for bonus points through Dec. 31, 2027 are:

Seven destinations are in Hawaii, with one on the mainland and two international cities. If you live in Hawaii and like to hop between islands, this community is a strong choice.

Don’t be persuaded by the names of the communities. Look a little deeper, because there’s a lot of overlap between destination lists. Compare the options against your upcoming travel plans.

You can change communities once per calendar year, so you aren’t locked in to your initial choice indefinitely. However, switching communities resets your destination-challenge progress, but you’ll retain any points you’ve already earned.

If your home airport (or one you visit frequently) is already on a community’s list, you may have an easier time earning points. Also consider whether a particular community benefit, such as free checked bags or points back on award flights for kids, outweighs the destination challenge.

Finally, pay attention to airport codes. For example, Tokyo’s Narita (NRT) and Haneda (HND) appear on different community lists. New York’s qualifying airport is JFK, while it is DCA in Washington, D.C. If you have a choice between airports, check which one qualifies for your community’s challenge.
