#3050. As Power Demand Surges, Energy Is Moving Closer To The Edge

Darren H. S. Tan. Chief Executive Officer at UNIGRID.

​Over the summer, Europe suffered a heat wave that strained its power grids, simultaneously increasing electricity demand and forcing some power plants to shut down.​

This isn’t the first time extreme temperatures have impacted the grid’s ability to deliver power. Many places around the world have experienced record-high or record-low temperatures in recent years, and the demand for heating or cooling reached levels that existing energy infrastructure wasn’t designed to handle. ​

The problem is being made worse by the construction of hyperscale AI data centers, which require massive amounts of electricity and further strain the grid. Completely rebuilding the grid to meet modern demands has proven fiscally impractical for many governments, forcing many places to solve the problem on the local level using distributed generation and storage.

Energy infrastructure across the U.S. and Europe was built over a century ago, when energy needs were much different. ​

Even so, studies have shown that we use only about 40% to 55% of the grid on average, and that’s by design, so it can handle spikes when they occur. But recent extreme weather events and data center demand are causing power needs to exceed even that generous buffer.​

For example, the Electric Reliability Council of Texas (ERCOT), which manages electricity in Texas, has said its interconnection queue currently includes over 1,800 projects totaling 474 gigawatts of power, over five times the state’s record peak electricity demand. Ninety percent of those requests come from data centers. ​

The cost to completely rebuild the grid to meet today’s needs is astronomical, with some estimates putting the total replacement cost in the trillions. Because of the potential cost and the fact that the aging grid is a chronic rather than an urgent problem, it receives patchwork upgrades as needed and as government budgets allow. ​

With a full rebuild out of the picture, several strategies are in play to work within the system we already have. When demand approaches available supply, energy companies offer rebates for reducing usage at peak times, implement peak pricing or, in more extreme cases, resort to rolling blackouts, which are planned outages to alleviate the demand during peak periods. ​

Beyond the grid itself, some areas are reducing their dependence on the centralized infrastructure by moving toward local power generation and storage.

Battery energy storage systems (BESS) can store electricity and discharge it when demand exceeds the grid’s capacity. ​

They are already showing promise in several states, such as California, where battery storage capacity has reached over 21,000 MW, equal to about one-third of the state’s peak demand. Eighty percent of that capacity is represented by grid-connected batteries, but smaller batteries are also enabling residents to increase their own energy storage capacity at home.​

As these batteries become cheaper and more reliable, it’s not out of the realm of possibility that these energy storage systems become a standard household appliance in the future, much like a refrigerator or washing machine is today. They can also play a role in energy needs for small businesses.

Being able to store energy and use it in an emergency is only half the equation. The other half is being able to generate electricity independently of the grid. ​

This isn’t a concept that should be unfamiliar to many, as many organizations and homes already have backup generators or solar panels. Although these methods can keep small businesses and homes powered up, they have their disadvantages. Generators are noisy, pollutive and can be dangerous, while solar has significant upfront installation costs. ​

Plug-in solar is emerging as another option for generating electricity locally that has already seen success in Europe and is starting to gain support in the U.S. as well. Instead of being installed on a rooftop, these smaller panels can be mounted on a balcony or a small section of a yard or business property and plugged into a wall outlet to help power homes and small businesses. ​

These systems cost significantly less than traditional solar and are portable, so people can move them around wherever they’re needed. These benefits open up power generation to a whole new segment of the country: commercial and residential renters alike who might never invest in a hardwired battery system or solar installation.

As energy demand continues to increase, expanding traditional grid infrastructure will remain important, but those projects can be expensive and take years to complete. Distributed generation and storage offer another way to increase resilience in the meantime. ​

By generating and storing more electricity closer to where it will be consumed, communities and business leaders can help reduce their reliance on the centralized grid during peak demand.​

We’re unlikely to solve growing power constraints with any single technology, but as local generation and storage become cheaper and more accessible, they can play a larger role in managing peak demand and making better use of the grid infrastructure we already have.​

#3049. Michael Burry Says He Tried to Warn You About Nvidia, CoreWeave and Nebius. Here's What the 'Big Short' Investor Saw

The famed investor took a victory lap as AI stocks slid again on Thursday.

By Jonathan Ponciano – Nov 19, 2026 at 7:43PM EST

Michael Burry, the investor made famous by "The Big Short," isn't shy about saying "I told you so."

"Coreweave, Nebius, NVIDIA, semis, I tried to warn you all," Burry posted on X on Thursday afternoon. "I didn't say short. But I provided the information one would need to sell."

He picked a good day for it. Nvidia (NVDA -3.30%) fell 3.3% on Thursday, CoreWeave (CRWV -6.11%) dropped 6.1%, and Nebius Group (NBIS -9.39%) sank 9.4%, as tech stocks gave up an early rally.

Here's what Burry saw, and what investors should do with it.

Michael Burry. Image source: Getty Images.

Burry's warnings came in pieces. In mid-October, he shared a Wall Street Journal story arguing that CoreWeave's sell-off showed the pressure from rising borrowing costs, adding his own commentary: "Dumb da dumb dumb da."

CoreWeave and Nebius are so-called neoclouds, companies that rent out Nvidia-powered computing to AI developers. Building their data centers takes enormous amounts of money, much of it borrowed, so higher interest rates hit them hard.

On Nvidia, his case is about the long run. He says he expects Nvidia's competitive edge to shrink over the next five years. In September, he also argued that its chips "may be economically depreciating waiting in warehouses while GAAP depreciation remains at zero," meaning the hardware could be losing value faster than the accounting shows.

The numbers have lent credence to his concern. CoreWeave closed Thursday at $44.91, down 76% from highs last year, and Nebius finished at $96.92, down 66% from its June peak. Nvidia has held up better but still sits 39% below its October high. The damage has spread across the chip industry, too: The VanEck Semiconductor ETF (SMH -2.62%), a basket of the biggest chip stocks, is down 33% from its June high.

As he laid out his long-term worries about Nvidia earlier this month, Burry said he imagined "the whole market is going to think this is a heck of a trade fairly soon." But since then, the stock has fallen another 16%.

Nvidia's business, meanwhile, hasn't cracked. Its revenue jumped 103% to $115.8 billion last quarter, and management raised its growth forecast for next year. The stock's slide this month coincided with Jensen Huang's sudden resignation as CEO, rather than a drop in sales.

If you own neocloud stocks like CoreWeave and Nebius, watch how much they borrow and what that debt costs them. If you own Nvidia, watch whether customers keep buying at today's pace, and whether the chips they buy hold their value.

The AI stocks that come out of this sell-off in good shape will be the ones with the best answers to those questions. For long-term investors, that's a better guide than any single post on X, even one from Michael Burry.

#3047. Bullish: 3 Key Takeaways for Long-Term Investors

By The Motley Fool Team – Nov 19, 2026 at 7:44PM EST

On its third-quarter 2026 earnings call, held on Nov. 18, 2026, Bullish (BLSH -1.97%) announced a $300 million share repurchase program and updated its financial outlook ahead of its pending Equiniti Group acquisition. The expansion into transfer agency services, which maintain official corporate shareholder registries, diversifies revenue beyond the volatility of digital asset trading cycles. Three takeaways from management show how the business is positioning for long-term growth.

Moving stock ownership onto public blockchains, where digital ledgers record share transfers instantly, requires direct participation from equity issuers rather than third-party entitlement tokens. By aiming to integrate tokenization directly into the share registers of roughly 3,000 public companies, the firm establishes a regulated foundation for digital share settlement.

Combining operations with Equiniti Group provides opportunities to eliminate redundant back-office expenses and automate share registry workflows using modern software. Management raised its expected net cost reductions over the medium term to range from $75 million to $100 million.

Navigating a broad downturn in digital asset trading volumes required management to tighten spending and reduce operational budgets. The board authorized an up to $300 million share repurchase program, demonstrating balance sheet flexibility to purchase undervalued stock while funding integration plans.

Depressed trading volumes drag near-term revenue, but digital share registration gains institutional traction. Integrating corporate share registries creates structural cost advantages over legacy operators.

Management is driving operational efficiency and expanding U.S. derivatives permissions. Unifying blockchain infrastructure with corporate registers sets up durable compounding.

I think UTI has a brighter future than the Thursday market reaction would indicate.

#3036. The S&P 500 Just Fell 4 Straight Weeks From a Record High. Here’s Why I’m Buying the Dip.

There's a big difference between a healthy pullback and the start of a bear market.

By David Dierking – Nov 19, 2026 at 7:50PM EST

10 stocks we like better than S&P 500 Index ›

The S&P 500 (^GSPC -2.02%) closed at a record 7,818.93 on Oct. 6. It finished that week higher, but from there it closed lower four weeks in a row, culminating in its post-election day drubbing.

As of now, the index is about 8% below its October high. The Nasdaq-100 and the tech sector are faring far worse, and investors are thinking about a potential bear market for the first time in over a year.

But if you go back several decades and look at situations like this -- the S&P 500 declining four straight weeks following a record high -- the outlook from here could actually be pretty bullish.

Since 1970, there have been 12 occasions when the S&P 500 has fallen four straight weeks right after hitting a new all-time closing high the previous week. Historically, the short term following these events has been more volatile. But it's the longer-term recovery period that's more meaningful.

Six months after the streak ended, the S&P 500 was higher in 10 of those 12 instances. The median gain was 13.4%, which is more than double the 5.2% median six-month gain during an average week since 1970.

Over the subsequent 12 months, the S&P 500 was higher on 11 of the 12 occasions, with a median gain of 16.5%.

I don't want to over-inflate the success rate here when the sample size is only 12, but I believe there's an explanation for this. Even bull markets have periods when stocks pull back. In many cases, it's not necessarily a sign that economic growth is stalling and a major bear market is imminent. It's just a normal part of the process of investing in risky assets. These are often normal market gyrations, and I think the data shows that over the long term, stocks tend to rise more often than fall.

Data source: Investing.com data and author's analysis of S&P 500 daily closing prices. "Streak ended" is the final trading day of the fourth losing week. Returns are measured from that close. Three months = 13 weeks; six months = 26 weeks; 12 months = 52 weeks.

One month from the streak's end, the chances of a positive return are pretty much a coin flip. It's not until three months out that, historically at least, the odds start to swing in your favor.

But I believe the overall trend is pretty clear and a good example of why a long-term buy-and-hold strategy is usually the best approach. In this scenario, the odds of generating a positive return have historically kept improving the longer you stay invested. That's a good framework to keep in mind whether stocks are steadily declining or near all-time highs.

History suggests that dips like these are much more likely to be healthy pullbacks during longer-term rising markets than a bear market warning.

Therefore, there's probably little need to make any major changes to your investment process. That means keeping your stock/bond allocations intact. Continue investing monthly or with every paycheck. Make sure your portfolio still aligns with your long-term goals.

If anything, you could consider positioning the equity segment of your portfolio a little more defensively. Moving from a core position in the Vanguard S&P 500 ETF (VOO -1.98%) to something like the Vanguard Value ETF (VTV -1.58%) or the Invesco S&P 500 Low Volatility ETF (SPLV -1.27%) could be a smart way to take some risk off the table while maintaining your equity exposure.

Market dips don't necessarily need to be feared. They can also be taken advantage of.

#3034. The 'debasement trade' returns after Bessent bond maneuver. Crypto and gold are back in style

The debasement trade is gaining new traction on Wall Street as concern over the size and cost of the budget deficit mounts.

The conventional wisdom behind the trade is that perceived hard assets, like cryptocurrencies and precious metals, gain as investors try to hedge against a weaker U.S. dollar and Treasury debt in the face of ballooning government spending. Those fears reached a fever pitch last week before, and after, the Treasury Department's unusual step of increasing debt buybacks under Secretary Scott Bessent.

"The size of the Treasury purchases announced so far by Bessent are trivial in comparison to the size of the overall market, but the [signaling] effect was very powerful," said Stephen Coltman, head of macro at 21Shares, a crypto-focused creator of exchange-traded funds.

Gold touched three-month highs Monday, building on last week's advance of more than 5%. The yellow metal has climbed for five straight weeks and in August is on track for its biggest monthly rise since 1999.

Bitcoin added 2% Monday, to the highest since May. Last week, the digital currency soared 22%, its biggest three-day rally since 2023. Overnight Tuesday, the crypto touched $80,000.

The U.S. dollar index, which tracks the dollar against six other leading currencies, hit three-month lows last week and recorded its third down week in the last four. The index was little changed on Monday as investors expressed little appetite to bid up the greenback.

The Treasury Department said last week that it would double the maximum size of its bond buyback, to at least $4 billion from $2 billion. Two senior Treasury officials told CNBC Monday that the department could use its General Account to help fund the plans.

Last week's announcement followed news that the monthly U.S. budget deficit in July reached a five-year high and came at the same time as total federal government debt topped $40 trillion. Bessent told CNBC last week that he wields a "big toolkit" to calm the government bond market amid concerns about the government's financial health.

Long-dated U.S. Treasury yields surged last week, at one point sending the 30-year yield to almost a 20-year high of 5.34%, up from 4.82% in late June. Yields dipped and then rebounded in the wake of the Treasury buyback move, a signal that bond investors believed Bessent's moves were inadequate.

"Markets are saying something," the billionaire philanthropist and former energy trader John Arnold said in a Friday post on X. The weaker dollar, lower Treasury prices and strengthening hard assets, are "all part of the debasement trade," he wrote.

The Treasury's moves could aid the bond market, but also translate into outsized pain for the dollar, according to Nohshad Shah, Citadel Securities' head of fixed income sales for Europe, the Middle East and Africa.

The stakes are high for monetary policymakers, as a weaker greenback can ease financial conditions, Shah said. U.S. inflation — above the Federal Reserve's 2% target for five years — could worsen.

The Fed might need to hike interest rates in response, Shah said. Fed funds futures reflect about a 56% chance the central bank raises borrowing costs at its October meeting, up more than seven percentage points from a week ago, according to CME's FedWatch tool.

"The bond market's message is straightforward: fiscal or monetary policy should be tighter," Shah said in a Monday note. "Households may ultimately pay for policymakers' unwillingness to fix the roof whilst the sun is shining."

Coltman at 21Shares said the appetite for alternative stores of value also stems from mounting geopolitical tension. The U.S. on Monday rolled out a global sanctions program focused on segregating Iran from the global economy, days after slapping 50% tariffs on billions of dollars in Canadian exports.

Still, assets that would benefit from a debasement trade have recently received votes of confidence on Wall Street.

Deutsche Bank analyst Michael Hsueh said in a Monday note that gold could surpass his target price of $4,800 an ounce. Already, that level suggests the precious metal only need to rise another 3% or so from where it closed on Friday. "We see the Treasury policy change as underlining the gold constructive view," Hsueh said.

Billionaire investor Ray Dalio recommended investors remain overweight gold and bitcoin ahead of what he warned could become a debt crisis in the U.S. as a result of unchecked government spending. Gold could account for as much as 15% of a model portfolio, the Bridgewater Associates founder said.

"The government's financial condition is at an inflection point," Dalio wrote on LinkedIn Friday. "If this is not dealt with now, the debts will build up to levels where they can't be managed without great trauma."

Others are less sure, devaluing the notion of a debasement trade.

It's probably too early to endorse the idea unless it's clear that the Fed will go along with the Treasury Department, said Alexander Lis, investing chief at Social Discovery Ventures.

10 stocks we like better than Anthropic ›

Shares of Anthropic (ANT +17.07%) jumped 17% from its initial public offering (IPO) price of $83 on Thursday. The gains capped off a blockbuster debut for the artificial intelligence (AI) pioneer on its first day as a public company.

Anthropic's stock price opened at $111.50 and rose as high as $115.10 following its listing on the Nasdaq stock exchange. The AI model developer's share price closed at $97.17, placing its fully diluted market capitalization at a staggering $1.8 trillion.

Although management expects the company's expansion to slow in the coming years, Anthropic is likely to remain one of the fastest-growing businesses in the world.

The recommendations of top Wall Street analysts can help inform investors in their search for attractive stocks from the vast universe of dividend-paying companies. These experts assign ratings after analyzing a company's financials and ability to consistently pay dividends while also seeking capital appreciation.

Here are three dividend-paying stocks that are highlighted by Wall Street's top pros, as tracked by TipRanks, a platform that ranks analysts based on their past performance.

Integrated oil and gas giant Exxon Mobil has increased its dividends for 43 consecutive years. At a quarterly dividend of $1.03 per share (annualized dividend of $4.12), XOM stock offers a yield of 2.6%.

In his latest research report on energy players, Morgan Stanley analyst Devin McDermott reiterated a buy rating on Exxon Mobil stock and increased his price target to $177 from $168.

The analyst raised his free cash flow estimates to reflect Q2 guidance and the oil price strip, with the largest increase noted for integrated players due to higher refining margins. Moving on to natural gas producer Expand Energy. The company announced a quarterly base dividend of $0.575 per share to be paid on Sept. 3. At an annualized dividend of $2.30 per share, EXE offers a yield of about 2.3%.

Recently, Goldman Sachs analyst Neil Mehta reaffirmed a buy rating on Expand Energy stock and increased his price target to $113 from $99. Mehta attributed his higher price target to cash flow improvement and a strong outlook for shareholder returns. #3011. The Sixers’ performance in crunch-time games is Good, Actually

At first, the Sixers appeared to be headed toward a blowout loss against the Orlando Magic on Wednesday. They were without all three of Tyrese Maxey, Jaylen Brown and Dean Wade (along with Dominick Barlow and Adem Bona), and they fell into a 27-12 hole less than eight minutes into the game. Instead, the Sixers proceeded to outscore the Magic by 20 points over the remaining 40 minutes, sneaking out of Orlando with a 121-116 win.

That was their 11th clutch win of the season, which the NBA defines as a game that gets within a five-point margin with no more than five minutes remaining in regulation. The Sixers are now 11-0 in such games this season, which is by far the best record in the league. In fact, that record in clutch games puts them in rarefied air, as Mike Lynch of Sports Reference shared after Wednesday's win.

Granted, that clearly unsustainable crunch-time record is also fuel for skepticism about how good the Sixers actually are. It's safe to say that their net rating of plus-46.1 in those situations probably won't hold up for an entire season, particularly given that their overall net rating is only plus-2.7.

None of this is breaking news or hard-hitting journalism. It's stating the obvious. The Sixers are running unsustainably hot in clutch situations and will eventually lose one of these games. However, anyone who's using that record to downplay what they've done thus far this season is missing two crucial points.

The new-look Sixers are still developing chemistry with one another. They're figuring out how best to optimize their schemes both offensively and defensively. That very much remains a work in progress over a full 48-minute game, but the fact that they've been able to lock in at the end of games bodes well. That speaks to an attention to detail that Sixers teams in the past have lacked.

Granted, it helps when you have LeBron James orchestrating your late-game offense. But that's also the point. The "who takes the last shot?" questions from the offseason haven't proved to be a concern at all yet. The answer, unsurprisingly, is that the Sixers don't have a designated last-shot taker. All five guys in their starting lineups are legitimate offensive threats, so they've been adept at hunting mismatches and attacking their opponents' weak spots. That is playoff basketball in a nutshell.

Would it be ideal if the Sixers started blowing teams out so they weren't so reliant on crunch time? Of course. Buying their starters extra rest throughout the grind of the 82-game season would be a godsend. However, there's also value in getting this much crunch-time experience in the regular season, particularly for a team that's working to incorporate so many new pieces on the fly.

"You've gotta go through shit," LeBron said in the season premiere of his Mind the Game podcast this offseason. "… Those are some of the moments that we have to be able to go through some real, live battle moments, in the fight, in order to know really who we are and what we want to become. We've gotta peel the onion. We have to."

Being in these close-and-late situations will help the Sixers develop muscle memory that they can tap into later in the season and in the playoffs. They can see which plays worked and didn't work in those gotta-have-it moments. The best teams use the regular season as a lab to experiment so they have as many answers to the test as possible before the playoffs begin.

There's also a psychological component to their crunch-time performance that could pay dividends down the line. The more close wins they rack up, the more belief they'll have in one another no matter the circumstances. They'll begin to believe that no lead is insurmountable and that they can overcome any obstacle thrown in their way.

In last year's playoffs, the New York Knicks overcame double-digit deficits in every Finals game. They were 6-2 in playoff games where they went down by 10 or more points, which was the best playoff record for any team in the 30 years of play-by-play data, according to NBA.com's John Schuhmann. That didn't just suddenly begin in the playoffs, though.

"What you have to respect about the Knicks, you have to put them away every single possession," Miami Heat head coach Erik Spoelstra told reporters after the Knicks overcame a double-digit deficit in the first half of a game last December. "You can't leave anything to effing chance with that team ever. That's what they do. What they have is a will to win, all right."

LeBron and the Sixers have spent all season discussing the need for them to develop championship habits. Their early-season level of crunch-time performance might not be sustainable, but the way that they're playing in those moments matters just as much. Valuing every possession on offense and locking in defensively are non-negotiables for them to accomplish their goal of winning a championship this year.

The added bonus is that by getting off to such a hot start, they've reduced the temperature under Nick Nurse's seat for the time being. Had they stumbled out of the gate like most early-LeBron teams tend to do, Stephen A. Smith and Kendrick Perkins would likely be all over ESPN's airwaves calling for his head.

The Sixers are by no means a finished product. They'd be the first ones to admit that. But learning to win in crunch time despite that bodes well for their long-term outlook, even if it means their actual record is misaligned with their expected record for the time being. (Don't worry, Cleveland, you can still be the reigning NBA Analytics Champions.)

#3010. Disney Just Raised Its Dividend 33% and Guided to Double-Digit EPS Growth. Here’s What Its Results Mean for Investors.

The media and entertainment stock is up 20% in four months.

By Neil Patel – Nov 19, 2026 at 8:45PM EST

10 stocks we like better than Walt Disney ›

On Nov. 17, shares of Walt Disney (DIS -1.72%) ended the day down 1.5%. This was despite the business reporting financial results for its fiscal 2026 fourth quarter (ended Oct. 3) that easily beat Wall Street estimates.

Revenue totaled $25.9 billion, rising 16% year over year. Adjusted earnings per share (EPS) of $1.77 was 59% higher compared to Q4 2025. Management guided this profit metric to grow in the double digits in fiscal 2027.

What’s more, Disney showed its commitment to shareholders by boosting the annual dividend by 33% to $2 per share. And stock buybacks will total $9 billion over the coming fiscal year.

These are all encouraging signs at the House of Mouse. Here's what the latest results mean for investors.

The latest results show healthy financial performance for a business that has been navigating a changing media landscape amid the decline of cable TV. Entertainment streaming video-on-demand (SVOD), which includes Disney+ and Hulu (excluding live TV), has become a real profit engine. Its operating income jumped 97% in fiscal 2027, with a 13.6% Q4 operating margin.

The downside, however, is a potential red flag regarding transparency. SVOD operating income will no longer be broken out starting with the current quarter's financial update.

The experiences segment is the bright spot. It's the primary financial contributor to the overall business. Revenue and operating income increased by 15% and 20%, respectively, in Q4. Domestic parks attendance (up 11%) was a positive development.

Capital expenditures will come in at $9 billion this fiscal year. It's mostly going toward bolstering parks and cruises. Disney's Avengers Campus in California, for example, will double in size in 2028, among other enhancements.

Capital returns remain a priority for the leadership team after investing in strategic initiatives. A 33% dividend hike is a major announcement. And Disney will also conduct $9 billion in share buybacks in fiscal 2027. This is an indication of strong financial health. Free cash flow is expected to total $11 billion next fiscal year.

The business told shareholders it plans to achieve annualized run rate cost savings of $3 billion by fiscal year 2029. "While these efficiencies will be used primarily to fund future growth, we do expect a portion to drop to the bottom line over time," the shareholder letter reads.

With adjusted EPS rising 18% year over year in fiscal 2026, Disney has now reported three straight years of strong double-digit profit growth. And its forecast calls for the trend to continue in fiscal 2027.

The momentum is worth highlighting. It's encouraging to see the company operate from a position of fundamental strength after years of questions about how it will navigate a streaming future.

This positive trend isn't making shareholders happy, though. It's going in one ear and coming out the other. In the last three years, Disney's stock price has risen 30%. It's down 22% in five years. Investors would've made a lot more money if they owned an S&P 500 (^GSPC -2.02%) exchange-traded fund.

Disney shares currently trade at a forward price-to-earnings (P/E) ratio of 15.8, well below the overall market. From a competitive standpoint, no other company can replicate what Disney offers, which should command more positive market sentiment.

But I think the market is hesitant to assign a higher valuation multiple to the shares because the business requires significant capital to run and grow. Disney is in the middle of a 10-year, $60 billion investment cycle to spruce up its experiences division. And because of its huge presence in sports programming, valuable rights that certainly don't come cheap, it will spend $26 billion in cash just on content in fiscal 2027.

The stock has risen 20% over the past four months (as of Nov. 17). It's still worth taking a closer look at. Just don't count on market-crushing gains from here.

Management reported that the company achieved its synergy savings targets and successfully exited its transition services agreement with Amcor, a process that involved migrating 11 ERP systems across 10 manufacturing sites. The company reduced its total debt by $122 million during the fiscal year while generating $115 million in free cash flow. For fiscal 2027, management provided a constant currency EBITDA growth outlook of approximately 6%, supported by the continued rollout of the Project CORE business excellence platform and targeted investments in high-margin innovation categories.

Operator: Good day, and welcome. Thank you for standing by, and welcome to the Magnera Fourth Quarter 2026 Earnings Conference Call. You can also go directly to ir.magnera.com to review the investor presentations from our recent conference attendance. Our annual report and proxy statements with the SEC can be found on our website under Investor Relations.

Additionally, a reminder that we will make certain forward-looking statements. These statements are made based upon management's expectations and beliefs concerning future events impacting the company and therefore, are subject to risks and uncertainties. Actual results or outcomes may differ materially from those expressed or implied in our forward-looking statements. Some factors that could cause the results or outcomes to differ are in the company's latest SEC filings and our news releases.

These statements speak only as of today, and we undertake no obligation to update them. I will now turn the call over to Magnera's CEO, Curt Begle.

Curtis Begle: Thank you, Robert. Good morning, and thank you for joining our call. I'm proud to present our fourth quarter and full year results and discuss the significant progress made against our stated objectives as we recently celebrated our second anniversary as a new company. Before turning it over to Jim for an update on our financial performance, I would like to share some thoughts on our strong fiscal 2026 performance and our outlook for 2027. First, our people have delivered on our optimization targets as we completed year 2 of our initial 3-year merger plan. We have delivered on our synergy savings commitment to date with the remaining value to be captured in fiscal year 2027.

We announced and executed on Project CORE to strengthen our competitive position, including several portfolio and footprint-shaping actions in Argentina, the U.K. and recently France. Our teams continue to take action as Project CORE has evolved into our business excellence operating platform. We exited our transition services agreement with Amcor on schedule, which required the migration of 11 ERP systems, including 10 manufacturing sites and 1 technical center. We accomplished all this while maintaining safety as a core value, demonstrated by an 18% reduction in our incident rate versus 2025, further positioning our safety results as an industry top performer.

Next, our strategic focus and execution delivered year-over-year earnings growth that enabled us to generate strong free cash flow and improve our balance sheet. We have made and continue to make the necessary investments in product leadership and commercial excellence to win with our customers. We delivered solid organic growth in our global wipes and infrastructure product lines. In addition, we launched a number of improvements across the portfolio, including an expanded filtration offering with our HighPleat advanced media, leveraging our expertise in absorbency by improving food packaging performance, providing expanded options for industrial wipes with our Universa platform and continued advancements in personal care with pH-neutral products and improved softness for our adult, baby and feminine care offerings.

These investments helped drive our positive earnings momentum. Our quarterly results delivered an impressive 8% improvement versus last year's quarter, and our full year results surpassed prior year by nearly 4%. We achieved $115 million of free cash flow, demonstrating our ability for a second year to deliver consistent industry-leading results. We also strengthened our balance sheet by reducing $122 million of debt during fiscal '26, including a $57 million repayment during the quarter. I'm very pleased with the solid year-over-year results and proud of our team's performance in continued challenging global environments. Shifting to fiscal 2027. I'll start by summarizing our outlook for the macro environment we operate in and then comment on our fiscal guidance.

Operating globally, we have visibility to the various stages of growth in each economic region. In the Americas, we have maintained cautious optimism based on a resilient consumer that continues to weather economic uncertainty while remaining disciplined in their spending habits. In our Rest of World region, where Europe and China both remain the most exposed to the economic implications of the Iran war, we foresee another year of various headwinds that will continue to put pressure on volume growth, resulting in a flattish outlook. Despite these challenges, our durable business model built for all economic cycles continues to provide opportunities.

We will build on our momentum with innovation as we bring softer and skin-friendly solutions to our personal care portfolio. Our adult incontinence and feminine care products sold through retail and away-from-home channels remain stable. The strength of these end markets supported our decision to install and commission a new high-performance blown film line at our Dombühl, Germany site, which I'm pleased to report will produce and ship commercial orders in the first calendar quarter of '27. For fiscal 2027, we are guiding to an expected EBITDA earnings improvement of 6%, driven by synergy realization, Project CORE initiatives and further advances in product mix and innovation. We expect to see continued demand strength in wipes and infrastructure.

As we further optimize our business model, we will leverage our innovative organizational culture to grow our share in core businesses where we maintain leading market positions to deliver on our customer commitments and position the company for future growth. Our commercial teams have been integrated to ensure consistent service. Operational metrics and processes are being standardized and efficiency initiatives are underway throughout the organization. I remain confident in our strategy and our ability of our team to execute. Our objective is to build a simpler, more agile and higher-performing Magnera, operating with common standards and positioned to deliver value across market cycles. We are pleased with the progress achieved, and we are focused on the opportunity ahead in fiscal 2027. Thank you to our employees, customers and shareholders for your continued support. Operator, please open the line for questions.

Operator: Our first question will come from the line of Kevin McCarthy from Vertical Research Partners.

Kevin McCarthy: Congratulations on your 2-year anniversary as well as the solid finish to fiscal 2026. I was hoping if you could perhaps comment on some of the key bridge items in your EBITDA guidance. For example, volume growth outlook in the Americas as well as the ROW segment and your thoughts on price/cost spread moving forward, please?

Curtis Begle: I can -- Kevin, thanks for the question, and good to hear from you. I'll turn it over to Jim after some comments related to what our expectations as it relates to the midpoint. Similar in terms of what we had discussed last year, essentially low single-digit growth in the Americas, slightly low single-digit negative or flattish in Europe. So just think about the midpoint being flat from a volume standpoint and then the upside or the higher point of the EBITDA range would be low single-digit positive and then low single-digit negative globally is how we've kind of outlined that bridge. And I think you talked about price cost.

Obviously, inflation has been paramount across the globe as it relates to some of the impact from the Iran war and just normal increases that you experience every year from wages, benefits, et cetera. We work really hard every year to offset much of those inflationary metrics with productivity. But we also need to work with our customers on price increases and passing those along. So as we bridge that, again, it varies by segment, timing of flow-through of materials. But for us, as we talked about historically, we're very efficient in our pass-through of raw material increases, which is the largest increases or decreases, which is the largest cost of our overall cost of goods sold.

But in terms of energy, in Europe in particular, we're roughly 70% hedged today for 2027, and we still have quite a bit of work to do in closing that gap. So as we look at our guide and where we sit today, working with our customers and our commercial teams on, passing through price increases where appropriate, but also being opportunistic in making sure that we're buying at the right price as there's a lot of fluctuations and certainly at an all-time high in certain areas over the past year or 2 years. So we continue to be down that path. I don't know, Jim, if you have anything to add?

James Till: That was a pretty good coverage. What I would say is we do have some energy inflation in Europe factored in, call it, maybe $10 million-ish or so as well as other inflationary pressures that are lapping that we saw in the back half of this year. But obviously, as Curt highlighted, that's being offset with productivity, benefits from CORE synergy realization, items like that, that will benefit us in the first half as we lap those items that we achieved this year. And we also have some mix benefit as well as some capital spending benefits layered in to get you to the midpoint of our walk.

And then as you think about the higher end of the walk and then the lower end -- I'm sorry, the higher end of the range and the lower end of the range, it's mostly volume driven. So to Curt's point, we're slightly positive at the midpoint and then the higher end of our range would be plus 2% on volume, whereas the lower end would be 2% less.

Kevin McCarthy: If I may follow up on the productivity side of things. Would you refresh us on the magnitude of synergies that you would expect to realize in 2027 versus 2026, be the first part of it. And then secondly, I think I heard that you're continuing to execute on Project CORE, including some actions in the U.K. and more recently, France. So in a similar vein, what is the amount of savings from Project CORE in '27 versus '26?

James Till: Sure. The rollover benefits are roughly $20 million from 2026 actions, and that is front-end loaded, front half loaded versus roughly $45 million of benefit that benefited us in 2026. The second actions related to kind of the extension of Project CORE, the cost-to-EBITDA benefit isn't quite as -- isn't quite the 1:1 that we achieved on our first wave, but it's all factored into our $400 million midpoint is what I would say.

Kevin McCarthy: And then if I may squeeze in one more. Your capital budget of $85 million was basically in line with our model, but it does reflect an increase versus the spend rate in fiscal '26 that you just reported. So maybe you could just unpack that a little bit. What does the split look like in terms of maintenance versus growth projects? And are there any sort of chunkier projects that you would call out in the growth category?

Curtis Begle: Yes. Kevin, thanks for that question. It is the step up of what we would anticipate this year really is primarily tied to some of the innovation projects that we have in the queue, what we're working on from an end customer standpoint and the attractive markets that, again, we continue to find differentiation as we talked about our Vitality Index a couple of quarters ago, that's increased now close to 30% of the portfolio from 22% when we kind of started out. But just in terms of our platforms are pretty broad across the globe.

And we found -- we're identifying some green shoots where supply-demand dynamics and just capacity utilization internally is putting a more attractive point in time for us to consider larger investments within certain more attractive end-use spaces where, again, we see a better right to win in our product lines, but overall improving the margin profile of our business. So that would be the difference from a year-over-year standpoint. But we'll remain disciplined. We want to make sure that we're doing the right -- making the right choices, highly focused on deleveraging to our stated objective of 3x. So we'll continue to focus on paying down debt.

But again, we're focused also on as we get through year 3 of the merger plan, it's looking to the future and where we have opportunities for organic growth, and that's what we're focused on.

Operator: Our next question will come from the line of Edward Brucker from Barclays.

Abanikash Rayaji: This is Abanikash Rayaji on for Ed. Maybe starting with volumes in the fiscal fourth quarter. How much of the volume weakness was driven by the underlying demand versus the lower-margin business that you chose to walk away from? And maybe how are your volumes tracking in October, November versus the industry across the regions?

Curtis Begle: Yes. I'll take this, Abanikash. Thanks for joining the call. As it relates to Europe and Jim called out the volume, we actually experienced throughout the quarter -- towards the tail end of the quarter, some pushouts of orders and softness in certain categories that we weren't necessarily anticipating in the quarter. I mean, obviously, we think about business over a 12-month time frame. For Europe, in general, we're already experiencing somewhat of a -- what I would consider a rebound in terms of demand. Again, we'll see how the balance of the quarter plays out. But that's why we're comfortable at least from a flattish outlook for 2027 as it relates to Rest of World.

There's also, again, a lot of work being done by customers on inventory rebalancing, and we're seeing that more in the Americas. So as we're ramping up for the 2027 season, we're in the middle of our bid season and actually normal course of business for us, finalizing negotiations as we get through the calendar year and the start of the next year. I would say early indications have been positive based on where we want to play, where we've been intending to move the portfolio and customer partnerships across the globe. So that's what's giving kind of a little bit more comfort to the outlook for '27. But again, the economy is dynamic.

Demand can fluctuate within certain categories in any given quarter, but we think about it more over a 12-month time frame and really line out our machine utilization rates as it relates to the bid season and where we're tying in a good portion of our portfolio to ensure that we're putting the right business on the right lines at the right time with the right customers.

Abanikash Rayaji: Got it. Does that mean like most of it was the underlying demand and very little to do with the volumes that you walked away from?

Curtis Begle: Look, there's certainly part of the work that we're doing from identifying areas that we want to -- we aren't necessarily making the -- getting the right value for the products that we're manufacturing in those spaces. In certain categories, we called out very strong, very robust. In others, you're seeing some softness. But in general, I would say that, that was a portion of the overall, but I'd also say it was order patterns in a normal kind of cycle. So a little bit of strength in Q3, softness in Q4, and we're seeing some recovery in Q1, particularly in Rest of World. And again, that can fluctuate by quarter, by region.

Abanikash Rayaji: Maybe just one on the synergies on the Project CORE. I think with much of those initiatives largely behind over the past couple of years, do you see any additional opportunities from here, like, say, over the next -- once you're done with these existing initiatives?

Curtis Begle: Yes. As we talked about, Project CORE is part of the DNA of the organization and part of our business excellence. So we'll continue to work toward and identify areas that can drive productivity for the business, make us a healthier organization. And that includes a lot of things, right? Some of the decisions are very difficult. We've made some challenging decisions in the past for the good of the organization moving forward. And that will be part of our operating model and what we put into our outlook and guidance in the future.

But in terms of just the rollover, the team executed extremely well over the past 12 months when we laid out the plans for it to take that first wave of those actions. And unfortunately, in an inflationary environment, a lot of that gets offset, and that's just necessary part of what we do every year is finding ways to be more productive, but more importantly, that we're investing in the right areas of the business that have greater margin profiles for us, more attractive spaces and a longer runway in terms of right to win.

Abanikash Rayaji: Maybe if I can just squeeze one more in. You mentioned like in the middle of the bid season, like could you give us an idea of like what percentage of contract negotiations have been completed? And maybe are you seeing any ability to push through some base price increases? Like what are you hearing back from customers like what is factored into your '27 guide based on that?

Curtis Begle: Yes. So the way our bid season works, again, we're right pretty much on schedule with where we normally are at this time. And this is for the calendar 2027 year. So we're finishing out contracts from '26. We've established another -- a number of them for '27. We're right in line with where we would expect it to be at this point. There are some bids that go into calendar Q1, but it's relatively isolated to certain regions, certain customer sets. But in general, I would say we're feeling comfortable with where we sit today. And customers, obviously, competitors are facing the same type of inflationary pressures.

I think the one thing that we've been able to stand behind and really focus on is our quality and service levels and areas that we had challenges in service last year, really tied to some of the impact that we received from the storm. So we put in programs here early on this quarter to make sure that we have the right inventory to be able to prepare for any fluctuations. Again, a lot can happen in a given year. I don't think any of us anticipated some of the challenges that the market faced over the past 2 years.

But as we've grown and learned and we stay very close to our customers, and we've been a reliable, consistent supplier. And that's really a testament to the work that we do as an organization, partnering with our customers, understanding their business as well or in some cases, better in forecasting than they are at times. And so we stay very close to them. And that's provided some benefit through the negotiations of new contracts and the outlook of our organization.

Operator: And our next question will come from the line of Roger Spitz from Bank of America.

Unknown Analyst: This is Ethan on for Roger. You said you repaid $57 million of debt in fiscal Q4. Which debt was that?

James Till: It was a combination of both bonds and term loan, but it was weighted towards the term loan.

Unknown Analyst: Okay. And then another one. Could you just discuss a little further the allocation of your '27 cash flow guidance towards debt reduction, so term loan versus bonds versus other cash priorities to get to your 3x leverage target?

James Till: Sure. So our -- at the midpoint of our free cash flow, it is about $120 million. We would intend to use all of those proceeds towards debt reduction. And so the natural walk at our midpoint is roughly 3.6x as we march towards our 3x target. And just to highlight the walk, I appreciate the question, it's $400 million at the midpoint, $125 million of cash interest, $85 million of CapEx, which we talked about, and then you have $50 million of tax integration, and then we have an additional $20 million of a rollover of additional items on Project CORE, which is a lot of European-focused actions.

Unknown Analyst: Okay. And then could you provide the split? You didn't break out cash taxes or working capital?

James Till: Sure. Working capital, we assume flat every year, so 0 on our walk each year, which is in an inflationary environment, obviously, is items that we have to work towards. We've highlighted that, that will be back half -- our free cash flow will be back half weighted. As we -- as Curt mentioned, we'll take some actions on inventories here in the first quarter to make sure that we have the appropriate levels so we don't get caught out like we did last year. And then the allocation of cash taxes, we're sticking with the 10% to 11% cash taxes as a percentage of EBITDA.

Operator: It looks like we have a follow-up from the line of Kevin McCarthy from Vertical Research Partners.

Kevin McCarthy: I was wondering if you could comment on your perception of industry operating rates as well as trajectory for your own operating rates as you've taken these capacity rationalization actions.

Curtis Begle: Thanks, Kevin. We've -- as we talked about, we intentionally have taken out various sets of capacity through Project CORE and other initiatives inside of the organization. We spent a great deal of time qualifying other raw materials and other products within the total network. So having the flexibility, not only the importance for us to operate most efficiently within the sites that we can produce those products, but that's a benefit to our customers as well. We have certain platforms, Kevin, within certain regions that I would say are nearing the mid-90% utilization rates, which is what we referred to as potential growth areas for us on investments.

And we've made some step changes internally with even some of the longer supply-demand dynamic markets where we're in the 80s for us. Now that doesn't necessarily mean the industry is there, but we have -- we would expect -- and again, we would expect our competitors to be doing the same thing of idling and taking out capacity, maximizing their footprint and operations. So I think there's been progress globally that's been made in that area, but the challenge is even with those capacity takeouts, it's the overall global demand and whether or not you're seeing step changes across the board within certain spun melt applications. But in general, we're well positioned from a cost competitiveness standpoint.

But overall, utilization rates for us continue to trend in the direction that we would like them to. Obviously, we'd like the entire market to continue to go up to those levels, but there's still capacity available in certain platforms in certain regions, and we monitor that. And we make choices in terms of can we get, again, the value for the products we're manufacturing? And is that a business that we have the right to win in. So we'll continue to evaluate those and take actions as necessary as we have done with the resources that we have available to us.

Kevin McCarthy: Excellent. And I want to also ask for your updated thoughts on supply chain inventory levels as you perceive them. As I look at your balance sheet, it looks like Magnera's own internal inventory is quite steady. But I guess the spirit of the question is more to do with thinking about how global markets have changed since the onset of conflict in the Middle East in March. Did you get the sense that your customers anywhere around the world are choosing to run with more safety stock? Or have there been difficulties in procurement anywhere such that inventory levels might be running leaner? And where do you think the balance of that shakes out?

Are we in a normal environment today as it relates to the level of product in the chain?

Curtis Begle: Yes. That's a great question. Kevin, I would say that we're going to be in a never-normal situation for the foreseeable future, and that's why you have to be very agile in the space. It does fluctuate quarter-to-quarter, year-over-year. I think that there were some maybe heavier pull-ins or panic orders toward the end of Q3. There's only so much we can supply during that period of time. And so as you would imagine, I'm going to avoid the old destocking term here and I just brought it up, we are seeing inventory rebalancing. And really, look, everybody has been impacted and continues to focus on offsetting inflation.

And as they do that, then they have to make choices in terms of where their inventory positions may be just from an overall -- their overall cash needs as an organization. The one thing that really helps from our standpoint is our regional footprint and proximity to our customers provides them with some of that flexibility to be able to swing. So we may maintain certain level of safety stocks or a certain level of inventory. They may work theirs down for a period of time. And we see that fluctuate again quarter-to-quarter.

I'd like to tell you that things will be normal, but we are seeing, again, as we experienced in Q4 with certain European customers that have pulled back and now we're seeing a snapback of some of those orders. We would expect to see some of that in Q4 for the Americas with anticipated snapbacks based on bookings and bid season for Q2, our fiscal Q2. So I'd like to give you a clean answer on that, Kevin. I think you can hear from customers, some of the larger CPGs that are public and communicate and maybe other folks in the packaging industry that are talking about what their outlooks are.

But in terms of where we're positioned, again, we manage to, again, be mindful of service levels and quality levels for our customers, response time, but the anticipation of what positive or negative that we may experience from an overall global demand standpoint. And that, again, varies by product, season and customer need.

Operator: It looks like we have another follow-up question from the line of Edward Brucker from Barclays.

Abanikash Rayaji: Maybe on -- like with much of the integration like moving towards a close, how are you thinking of inorganic opportunities here? Is that something that could be part of the strategy over the medium term?

Curtis Begle: Inorganic, is that what you said, Edward?

Abanikash Rayaji: Yes. I mean like -- go ahead.

Curtis Begle: Yes. We continue to evaluate opportunities on both sides of our portfolio. But I would say that doesn't take away from our focus and our commitment to deleveraging the balance sheet and making sure that, again, we get to our stated objective of 3x. Obviously, we're -- we have a lot of visibility and plenty of inbounds, the right opportunity that fits within our longer-term strategy and meets the various hurdles that we have put on ourselves for our organization. Again, we would consider that as part of the DNA of this organization of being able to have 1 plus 1 equals something greater than 2.

But again, I'm not here to say that there's anything that would be available that makes sense for us today, but we evaluate a lot of things through our corporate development organization.

Abanikash Rayaji: Got it. And maybe just one on valuations. Where do you think like the valuations of the multiples are in the space relative to where you trade right now? I think it's around 5x. So I just wanted to get a sense of where do you think the industry and market is?

Curtis Begle: Look, I can't necessarily comment on that in particular. We obviously believe that we have a very good organization and strength in the outlook for the business. But to comment on things that are in the market today and valuation expectations versus valuations in general, I don't really have anything to comment there. I don't think there's been anything that's been published with valuations that really are in our space as of late. So...

Operator: And it looks like we have a follow-up question from the line of Matthew Hettwer from Vertical Research Partners.

Matthew Hettwer: Is the impact of the extra shipping days that you have in your fiscal 2027 ratable? In other words, would you expect it to add about 2% to EBITDA in FY 2027 followed by a similar unwind in fiscal 2028?

James Till: Yes. Thanks for the question. Yes. So the extra shipping days will impact both Q1 and Q2. And I think I've penciled in around $5 million or $6 million of benefit. As we sit here today, that's being offset just with a little bit of FX headwind. So it's sort of a push. So depending on what assumptions you want to make going out 2 years from now on those items. But right now, like I said, it's those sort of offset each other, probably a little bit more headwind on FX versus our guide of a constant currency, but that moves from a daily-to-day basis.

Matthew Hettwer: And then one more from me. I just wanted to inquire about the $106 million impairment charge that you took in the quarter. Could you explain what the charge was related to and then why you felt it was necessary to assess it this quarter?

James Till: Sure. We've been signaling since last year as we lapped our second year as a public company that given where we traded our market multiple versus where the multiple was at the inception of the RMT that there would be pressure on our internal carrying value versus the fair value. And so that was the primary factor that resulted in the impairment.

Operator: And with that, this concludes the question-and-answer session. I would now like to turn it back over to Curt for any closing remarks.

Curtis Begle: Thank you, operator, and thank you all again for joining us today and for your continued interest in Magnera. We look forward to updating you on our progress at upcoming conferences in the next quarterly call. Everyone, have a great day.

Operator: Thank you for your participation in today's conference. This does conclude the program. You may now disconnect. Everyone, have a great day.
